text:
應天府鄉試錄序
國朝三年一開科以取士而於
兩京尤重必
命翰林儒臣二人為考試官盖
祖宗成法著之為令者也乃正德
五年秋八月適維其期應天
府臣先事以
===

應天府鄉試錄序

國朝三年一開科以取士，而於兩京尤重，必命翰林儒臣二人為考試官，盖祖宗成法著之為令者也。乃正德五年秋八月，適維其期，應天府臣先事以請。侍讀學士臣冕、侍讀臣希周寔奉命而来。至則與提調官府尹臣鳳、府丞臣玉，同考試官學正臣銘、臣思，教諭臣尚忠、臣春、臣源潔、臣世棻、臣璋、臣暘，訓導臣偉，監試官監察御史臣和、臣沾
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Our dynasty holds examinations once every three years to select men for service. Particular importance is attached to those at the two capitals, for which two scholarly officials of the Hanlin Academy must be appointed as Examiners. This is an established practice of the imperial ancestors, set down as a regulation. In the eighth month of autumn in the fifth year of Zhengde [1510], when the appointed time came, the officials of Yingtian Prefecture submitted a request in advance. Your servants Mian, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, and Xizhou, Reader-in-Waiting, duly came under imperial command. Upon arriving, they joined the Proctors, your servants Feng, Prefect, and Yu, Prefectural Adjutant; the Associate Examiners, your servants Ming and Si, Instructors; Shangzhong, Chun, Yuanjie, Shifen, Zhang, and Yang, Instructors; and Wei, Assistant Instructor; and the Examination Monitors, your servants He and Zhan, Investigating Censors …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
暨諸執事更相戒誓而後就
列乃窮日夜精校閱慎去取
之於四千一百四十卷中拔
其文之優者得百三十有五
人其卷若是乎其多也而所
拔乃僅止此非士之可取者
止於此也遵
===
制額而不敢過也文則錄而刻
者二十篇亦間舉其一二以
例之錄何能盡也然即其所
已錄者而觀之雖一出於風
簷短晷倉卒督迫所成率皆
明於理而達於辭蔚然鏘然
有可誦而傳者則其平日從

punctuated: 暨諸執事，更相戒誓而後就列，乃窮日夜精校閱，慎去取之。於四千一百四十卷中，拔其文之優者，得百三十有五人。其卷若是乎其多也，而所拔乃僅止此，非士之可取者止於此也，遵制額而不敢過也。文則錄而刻者二十篇，亦間舉其一二以例之，錄何能盡也？然即其所已錄者而觀之，雖一出於風簷短晷、倉卒督迫所成，率皆明於理而達於辭，蔚然鏘然，有可誦而傳者，則其平日從
translation_en:
…together with all the functionaries, admonished one another and pledged themselves before taking their appointed places. They then worked through day and night, scrutinizing the papers closely and exercising care in accepting or rejecting them. From 4,140 papers they selected those whose writing was superior, obtaining 135 candidates. So numerous were the papers, yet so few were selected. This was not because the scholars worthy of selection were limited to this number, but because they observed the imperially prescribed quota and dared not exceed it.
As for the essays, twenty were transcribed and printed. These, too, were only a few chosen here and there to serve as examples; how could the record include them all? Yet, looking at those already included, although every one was composed beneath wind-swept eaves, with little daylight and under the pressure of haste and supervision, they are generally clear in principle and fluent in expression, rich and resonant, worthy of recitation and transmission. Then, as for what they ordinarily compose at leisure…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
容展布之作將不有大且深
於此焉者乎即其在錄中者
而推其遺於錄外者使非限
於
制額則人之見取文之見錄雖
或倍蓰於此亦無不可然而
有所不敢者法之所在不容
===
以己意參乎其間也仰惟
皇上嗣大歷服以來無一政一事
不遵
祖宗成法至於試事尤切
惓惓屢
渙大號戒飭所司申條格謹防
範於凡徇情干正假公售私

或倍蓰於此亦無不可然而

===
以己意參乎其間也仰惟
皇上嗣大歷服以來無一政一事
不遵
祖宗成法至於試事尤切
惓惓屢
渙大號戒飭所司申除格謹防
範於凡徇情干正假公售私
punctuated:
容展布之作，將不有大且深於此焉者乎？即其在錄中者，而推其遺於錄外者，使非限於制額，則人之見取、文之見錄，雖或倍蓰於此，亦無不可。然而有所不敢者，法之所在，不容以己意參乎其間也。
仰惟皇上嗣大歷服以來，無一政一事不遵祖宗成法。至於試事，尤切惓惓，屢渙大號，戒飭所司，申條格，謹防範，於凡徇情干正、假公售私，
translation_en:
…works composed at leisure, with room to develop their ideas—would these not be greater and more profound than these examples? From those included in this record, one may infer the quality of those left out. Were it not for the prescribed quota, there would be nothing amiss even if the number of men selected and compositions recorded were twice or five times as great. Yet there are things we dare not do: where the regulations govern, we may not interpose our own judgment.
We reverently consider that, since His Majesty succeeded to the great dynastic mandate, not a single policy or undertaking has departed from the established laws of his imperial ancestors. He has been especially solicitous about examination affairs, repeatedly issuing solemn proclamations to admonish the responsible officials, reaffirm the regulations, and ensure rigorous safeguards against all instances of allowing personal considerations to compromise impartiality or using public office to advance private interests…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
者尤嚴其罰必如古所云無
情如造化至公如權衡者而
後已焉皆法之為也若乃解
額之在鄉試者則間增於北
卷額之在會試者則去中數
而以分屬於北南是雖法外
之意抑亦因時損益以至於
===
此蓋我
祖宗之法本之於身以達之家國
天下無一政一事不以公天
下之心處之萬世守之萬世
所不能易也豈獨試事為然
哉然姑即試事求之則凡法
之所在雖

天下無一政一事不以公天
下之心處之萬世守之萬世

translation_en:
…for such persons, punishments are especially severe. Nothing less will suffice than what the ancients called being “without partiality like the workings of creation, perfectly impartial like a balance.” All this is the operation of established law. As for the quota of successful candidates in the Provincial Examination, it is occasionally increased in the north; as for the quota of examination papers in the Metropolitan Examination, the central allocation is removed and apportioned between the north and south. Although this reflects an intention beyond the established law, it too has come about through adjustments to suit the times.
The laws of our imperial ancestors were rooted in their own persons and extended to the family, the state, and all under Heaven. There was no matter of government, no undertaking, that they did not handle with a commitment to impartiality toward all under Heaven. These laws are to be observed for ten thousand generations and cannot be altered in ten thousand generations. How could this be true only of examinations? Yet, considering examinations alone, wherever established law applies, although…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
朝廷之上亦未嘗輒以己意參
之也况有司乎有司之奉法
雖遠而藩服猶凛然如在
朝廷也况
畿甸乎法以嚴於
畿甸以率乎天下務期所取
之士無不得焉以取重於天
===
下以無負乎
朝廷所尤重之意此臣之志也
而士之所以自重則又係乎
士之所自立者何如是豈臣
之所能與哉士之所自立凡
處己待物事君治民之道亦
豈無成法哉自昔聖賢具載

畿甸以率乎天下務期所取
之士無不得其□以取重於天
===
下以無負乎
朝廷所尤重之意此臣之志也
而士之所以自重則又係乎
士之所自立者何如是豈臣
之所能與哉士之所自立凡
處已待物事君治民之道亦
豈無成法哉自昔聖賢具載
punctuated:
朝廷之上，亦未嘗輒以己意參之也，况有司乎？有司之奉法，雖遠而藩服，猶凛然如在朝廷也，况畿甸乎？法以嚴於畿甸，以率乎天下，務期所取之士無不得焉，以取重於天下，以無負乎朝廷所尤重之意。此臣之志也。
而士之所以自重，則又係乎士之所自立者何如，是豈臣之所能與哉？士之所自立，凡處己待物、事君治民之道，亦豈無成法哉？自昔聖賢具載
translation_en:
… even at the imperial court, no one has ever presumed to introduce personal discretion into the application of the law; how much less should the responsible officials do so? In upholding the law, officials even in distant outlying territories remain as reverently vigilant as though they were at court; how much more should those in the metropolitan region do so? The law is therefore enforced strictly in the metropolitan region to set an example for the realm. Every effort must be made to ensure that all the scholars selected are worthy, so that the selection commands respect throughout the realm and does not betray the court’s intention in attaching particular importance to it. This is your servant’s aspiration.
Yet how scholars uphold their own dignity depends in turn on the foundations they establish for themselves. How could this be something in which your servant can intervene? As for those foundations—the principles of conducting oneself, dealing with others, serving the ruler, and governing the people—are there not established standards for these as well? From antiquity, the sages and worthies have fully set them down …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
於經其本末次第可考而知
者士當敬以守之隨其職守
才力所至而皆求以不悖不
以利害為趨舍不以毁譽為
前却如此而始如此而終如
此而貧賤如此而富貴其有
所當為也如水之必寒如火
===
之必熱其有所不為也如騶
虞之不殺如竊脂之不穀有
斷斷乎其不可易者非可視
時高下而為之損益者也使
或悖乎此則非士之所以為
士者矣凡天下之士皆然而
況

punctuated: 於經，其本末次第可考而知者，士當敬以守之，隨其職守才力所至，而皆求以不悖。不以利害為趨舍，不以毁譽為前却。如此而始，如此而終；如此而貧賤，如此而富貴。其有所當為也，如水之必寒，如火之必熱；其有所不為也，如騶虞之不殺，如竊脂之不穀。有斷斷乎其不可易者，非可視時高下而為之損益者也。使或悖乎此，則非士之所以為士者矣。凡天下之士皆然，而況
translation_en: …in the Classics. Their fundamentals and ramifications, and their proper sequence, can be understood through examination. Scholars should reverently abide by them, seeking never to contravene them in whatever their official responsibilities, abilities, and strength enable them to accomplish. They must not let advantage or harm determine what they pursue or reject, nor let disparagement or praise determine whether they advance or retreat. Thus should they begin, and thus should they end; thus should they conduct themselves in poverty and low station, and thus in wealth and high rank. When something ought to be done, they must do it as surely as water is cold and fire is hot; when something must not be done, they must refrain as surely as the zouyu does not kill and the qiezhi bird does not eat grain. There are principles so firmly settled that they cannot be altered, neither diminished nor augmented to suit the changing circumstances of the times. Should scholars contravene these, they would forfeit what makes a scholar a scholar. This applies to all scholars under Heaven; how much more, then, to…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
畿甸之士乎哉試事既畢例
有録以
獻臣敢謹序于其首且用以為
諸士告云
翰林院侍讀學士奉訓大夫
蔣冕謹序
alt_text:
畿甸之士乎哉試事既畢例
有錄以
獻臣敢謹序于其首且用以為
諸士告云
翰林院侍讀學士奉訓大夫
蔣冕謹序
punctuated:
畿甸之士乎哉！試事既畢，例有録以獻。臣敢謹序于其首，且用以為諸士告云。
翰林院侍讀學士、奉訓大夫蔣冕謹序。
translation_en:
…the scholars of the metropolitan region! Now that the examination has concluded, a record is, by established practice, compiled for presentation to the throne. I, your servant, venture respectfully to place this preface at its beginning, also using it to address these scholars.
Respectfully prefaced by Jiang Mian, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Instructional Service.

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
上好禮則民易使也
誠之者擇善而固執之者也
舜發於畎畝之中傅說舉於版築之間膠
鬲舉於魚鹽之中管夷吾舉於士孫叔
敖舉於海百里奚舉於市
易
美在其中而暢於四支發於事業美之至
===
也
君子以正位凝命
是故四營而成易十有八變而成卦
天地定位山澤通氣雷風相薄水火不相
射八卦相錯
書
日宣三德夙夜浚明有家日嚴祇敬六德
亮采有邦
有言逆于汝心必求諸道有言遜于汝志

四書
上好禮，則民易使也。
誠之者，擇善而固執之者也。

Question: Our Emperor Taizu Gao once ordered Confucian court scholars to compile the two Records of Preserving the Mind (Cunxin) and Examining Oneself (Xinggong). They record all instances in which rulers of successive dynasties, in performing sacrifices, responded to calamities and auspicious signs, as well as instances from the Han, Tang, and Song onward in which calamities and auspicious signs manifested themselves in relation to officials. The guidance for these compilations came entirely from the imperial mind, and their titles were bestowed entirely through the imperial utterance. Their circulation at the time and transmission to posterity were intended solely to make rulers and officials, superiors and subordinates alike, share the same vigilance and reverence, devoting their efforts to cultivating themselves in person and mind, thereby transforming calamity into good fortune. Could the purpose have been merely to exercise care in sacrificial observances?

Yet I have ventured to consider reverently the intention behind the titles of these two books. In admonishing the ruler, they speak of the mind and wish him to preserve it; in admonishing officials, they speak of the person and wish them to examine themselves. Can it be that the ruler has no concern with his own person, and officials have no concern with their minds? Or are there also ways in which rulers and officials may apply their efforts to both? …who understand it, for they consider themselves exalted and important and regard the people as insignificant. Only when they understand that the people and they themselves depend upon one another will they surely avoid the fault of slighting the people. Thus it is said: ‘Is it not the ruler who deserves to be cherished? Is it not the people who deserve to be feared?’ How great are these imperial words! Since Shun and Yu personally transmitted rule from one to the other, their like has scarcely been seen in the ensuing thousands of years. Let us discuss this with you candidates. When our sagely founder spoke of fearing the people, did he truly regard the people as fearsome? Or was he merely stating the principle in these terms? Compared with the people at the founding of the dynasty, are the people of the realm today likewise to be feared, or is there nothing in them to fear? At the founding of the dynasty, warfare had only just been brought to an end, and there might indeed have been something fearsome about the people of that time. Now that peace has endured so long, not one of the people throughout the realm fails to bask and rejoice in profound benevolence and abundant bounty. What is there still to fear?

Yet our Emperor remains deeply concerned day and night, with no leisure to rest at ease. Whenever he hears reports of floods, droughts, or banditry in any quarter, he immediately refers the matter to the responsible authorities, directing them to devote their full attention to devising measures. The edicts expressing these concerns are too numerous to enumerate. Unless he took as his own the ancient emperors’ and kings’ fear of the people, and sought reverently to follow his ancestor’s footsteps, how could he attain this degree of care? Why, then, have we still heard of no prospect for those people in Chu and Shu who have fallen into banditry to return and settle in their home communities? In Suzhou and Songjiang…

Can it be that above there is a ruler who holds the people in awe, while below there are no officials who do so? Even among the ministers of earlier dynasties, there were those who dealt with the tangled cord of disorder in Bohai or went to Guangling in a single carriage, turning swords into ploughs and hoes. Mengzi spared no effort in refuting Yang Zhu and Mo Di, holding that anyone able to argue against their teachings was a follower of the sages; his rejection of Mo Di was especially vehement. Yet a later Confucian scholar declared: “Kongzi would certainly have employed Mozi, and Mozi would certainly have employed Kongzi.” How could his statements have become so contradictory? Had these words come from an ordinary person, there would have been no need to refute them. Yet this man had taken suppressing heterodoxy and upholding orthodoxy as his own responsibility, and had exalted Mengzi. Could he really have fabricated such reckless assertions without any insight? Are the ways of Kongzi and Mozi, then, the same or different? From this we cannot tell. Kongzi is the teacher of all ages: those who follow him are Confucians, and those who go against him are heterodox; anyone able to match his achievements is also a sage. In choosing what to pursue or reject, and whom to approve or condemn, one must indeed exercise careful judgment. You candidates all study and emulate Kongzi and must have reached a settled judgment on this matter. Analyze it for me.

text:
姦慝何由而詰乎雖使堯舜三王亦無
以治天下矣然宋儒之論顧以不盡人
之財不盡人之力不盡人之情者為賢
而以歸於漢世之君且慨其繼治者之
不能然何也然則治天下者於斯三者
果可以盡歟果不可以盡歟抑宋儒之
論雖曰論漢其實又借漢以論宋也宋
世之君於斯三者亦固有盡不盡焉者

姦慝何由而詰乎？雖使堯舜三王，亦無以治天下矣。然宋儒之論，顧以不盡人之財、不盡人之力、不盡人之情者為賢，而以歸於漢世之君，且慨其繼治者之不能然，何也？然則治天下者於斯三者，果可以盡歟？果不可以盡歟？抑宋儒之論，雖曰論漢，其實又借漢以論宋也？宋世之君於斯三者，亦固有盡不盡焉者矣。果孰賢而孰非賢歟？夫治道莫要於斯三者，漢宋諸君同以之治天下也，而其所行之得失乃不同如此，庸可不求其故歟？諸士子皆明於古今之故者，是固不容默矣。

問：士之窮理，於古昔人物臧否，皆所當知。然欲知其臧否者，亦惟考其行事之實焉耳。大抵君子之所為，必當於理者也；小人之所為，必背於理者也。然或忠貞鯁亮，勳德著聞，而其所行亦有不慊於
translation_en:
…How could wickedness be investigated? Even Yao, Shun, and the Three Kings would then have no means of governing All under Heaven. Yet in their discussions, Song Confucian scholars instead deemed worthy those who did not exhaust the people's wealth, did not exhaust their strength, and did not probe their feelings to the utmost. They attributed these qualities to a ruler of the Han, and moreover lamented that his successors could not do likewise. Why was this? In governing All under Heaven, then, may one indeed go to the utmost in these three matters, or may one not? Or did the Song scholars, though ostensibly discussing the Han, actually use the Han to comment on the Song? Among Song rulers, too, there were certainly those who went to the utmost in these three matters and those who did not. Which, then, were worthy, and which were not? Nothing is more essential to the way of government than these three matters. The rulers of both the Han and the Song relied on them to govern All under Heaven, yet the successes and failures of their conduct differed so greatly. How could one fail to inquire into the reasons? You candidates all understand the circumstances of past and present; on this matter you certainly cannot remain silent.

text:
公道者或憸邪讒慝人品汚下而其所
建白者乃有公平正大之論則賢否曷
從而定乎史所載賢者之過有說其君
背約而擊楚者有從其主背義而取益
州者疑不得為正有舍陸贄而薦竇參
者有舍李泌顏真卿而薦楊炎者疑不
得為明有殺張曇而僚佐多求去者有
殺曲端而軍士或叛去者則幾於暴矣
之數公者皆善之著者也而其所行顧
===

因贓吏之誅而諫陷人於法或論官豕

或以絶邪佞為太子箴或以預外事為
太子戒似得乎輔養之道或請蠲負而
釋繫囚或請罷兵而撫蠻寇則疑於仁
矣之數人者皆惡之尤者也而其所見

…public justice; others are deceitful, wicked, slanderous, and malicious, their personal character base, yet among the proposals they submit are arguments that are fair, impartial, upright, and honorable. On what basis, then, are we to determine whether they are worthy or unworthy?

Among the faults of worthy men recorded in the histories, some persuaded their rulers to break a covenant and attack Chu; some followed their lords in violating righteousness and seizing Yizhou. Such conduct seems hardly upright. Some passed over Lu Zhi and recommended Dou Can; some passed over Li Mi and Yan Zhenqing and recommended Yang Yan. Such conduct seems hardly discerning. Some killed Zhang Tan, whereupon many of their subordinate officials sought to leave; some killed Qu Duan, whereupon some soldiers rebelled and deserted. This verges on brutality. These gentlemen were all renowned for their goodness, yet their conduct was like this. Can it be said to accord with moral principle?

Among the good deeds of petty men recorded in the histories, some, on the occasion of a corrupt official’s execution, remonstrated against entrapping people under the law; some discussed the harm caused by government-owned pigs [?], extending their concern to other prefectures as well. These actions seem to fulfill the duty of correcting faults and remedying harm. Some admonished the crown prince to cut off wicked flatterers; some warned the crown prince against intervening in affairs outside his household. These actions seem to accord with the proper way of assisting and nurturing him. Some requested the remission of debts and the release of prisoners; some requested that military operations cease and that non-Han raiders be pacified. These actions appear benevolent. These men were all outstandingly evil, yet the views they expressed were like this. Can they be said not to accord with moral principle?

Certainly, a gentleman is not necessarily without minor flaws, and a petty man is not necessarily without a modicum of goodness. Judging from what has previously…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
上好禮則民易使也
沈瓉
同考試官教諭田批題本冠冕場中士子類
能發揮及細加檢閱未免熱腐相半晩得此篇詞語切
當趣味悠然覺出人表因錄之以範來學
同考試官教諭蔡批論語題似易實難連日
閱卷惬意者殊少此篇就題寫意辭不費而理獨到故
===
錄之
考試官侍讀朱批體貼易使二字明白
考試官侍讀學士蔣批辭順理明優於衆作
治人者能尚乎理之自然事人者斯安於分之
當然蓋禮出於自然之理而莫大乎分也上好
乎禮則禮達而分定矣又豈有難使之民哉昔
吾夫子之意若曰安上治民莫善於禮君子之
居上而臨下也不以禮為尚可乎必也出入起
居悉由乎矩範之中而惟禮是好于以踐履於

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
一身俾民有所式焉設施措置不出乎儀則之
外而所好惟禮乎以綱維乎庶政俾民有所守
焉蒞之以莊未也而所以動斯民者必於禮乎
是崇道之以德未也而所以齊斯民者必於禮
乎是尚上之好禮也如此則禮教達於下矣焉
有禮達而分不定分定而民不服者乎故凡民
之在所統者是惟無使也一有以使之則莫不
曰上之所以使我者分也分所當為吾何敢愛
其力邪民之在所治者是惟無役也一有以役

上者不患民之難使而患禮之不達盍亦知所

盡其道之當為而其應有必至耳若子犯之告
晉文公則曰民未知禮未生其共於是乎大蒐

punctuated: 一身，俾民有所式焉。設施措置不出乎儀則之外，而所好惟禮乎，以綱維乎庶政，俾民有所守焉。蒞之以莊，未也，而所以動斯民者，必於禮乎是崇；道之以德，未也，而所以齊斯民者，必於禮乎是尚。上之好禮也如此，則禮教達於下矣。焉有禮達而分不定，分定而民不服者乎？故凡民之在所統者，是惟無使也，一有以使之，則莫不曰：「上之所以使我者，分也。分所當為，吾何敢愛其力邪？」民之在所治者，是惟無役也，一有以役之，則莫不曰：「我之所以為上役者，職也。職所當盡，吾何敢顧其私邪？」使之興作也，則趨事赴功之恐後，而勞非所辭；不徒貌之從也，而實安於心焉。使之攻守也，則折衝禦侮之爭先，而危非所避；不徒法之畏也，而實勇於義焉。是則為人上者，不患民之難使，而患禮之不達，盍亦知所務哉？雖然，上之好禮，豈以欲民易使而然？亦惟盡其道之當為，而其應有必至耳。若子犯之告晉文公，則曰：「民未知禮，未生其共。」於是乎大蒐
translation_en: …in his own person, giving the people an example to follow. His arrangements and measures remain within the bounds of proper forms and standards, and he cherishes ritual propriety alone, using it to order the many affairs of government and give the people rules to observe. Presiding over them with dignity is not enough: to move these people, he must exalt ritual propriety. Guiding them through virtue is not enough: to bring these people into accord, he must esteem ritual propriety. When those above cherish ritual propriety in this way, its teachings reach those below. How could ritual propriety reach them without their allotted duties becoming settled, or their duties become settled without the people submitting? Thus, whenever the people under his authority are called upon to serve, they all say: “Our superior calls upon us because this is our allotted duty. How dare we spare our strength in doing what our duty requires?” Whenever the people under his governance are called upon to perform labor, they all say: “We labor for our superior because this is our responsibility. How dare we attend to private interests when our responsibility must be fulfilled?” When he sets them to building and other works, they hurry to their tasks and strive for accomplishment, fearing to lag behind and refusing no toil. Their obedience is not merely outward: they are truly content at heart. When he sets them to attack or defense, they vie to be first in repelling enemies and resisting aggression, shunning no danger. They do not merely fear the law: they are truly emboldened by righteousness. Thus, those who rule others should worry not that the people are difficult to employ, but that ritual propriety has not reached them. Should they not recognize where to direct their efforts? Yet does a ruler cherish ritual propriety simply because he wants the people to be easy to employ? He merely fulfills what the Way requires of him, and the corresponding response will inevitably follow. As for Zifan’s counsel to Duke Wen of Jin, he said: “The people do not yet understand ritual propriety; their reverence has not yet arisen.” Thereupon the duke held a great military hunt…

text:
理之實於已也不亦難哉中庸引孔子荅哀公
之問政言誠者誠之者有天道人道之分而此
則釋誠之之事何則誠之原於天也本無不同
而其在乎人也不能無異誠之者知理之間以
欲也欲變其異求與誠者同歸知理之雜以人
也欲反其同求與天道一致是果何如其用力
哉以為擇之不精則天下之理必將錯雜於是
非之間而心體終於昏昧矣何以知其善之所
在而詣之哉於是辨真偽於疑似之間務求何

物凡天下之理皆有以究析其幾微今日致一

奧夫然則有以真知善之所在而有誠之地矣

之餘而表裏終於扞格矣何以得其善於吾心
而安之哉于是擇之於始者執之於後而持守

punctuated: 理之實於已也，不亦難哉？《中庸》引孔子荅哀公之問政，言誠者、誠之者，有天道、人道之分，而此則釋誠之之事。何則？誠之原於天也，本無不同，而其在乎人也，不能無異。誠之者，知理之間以欲也，欲變其異，求與誠者同歸；知理之雜以人也，欲反其同，求與天道一致。是果何如其用力哉？以為擇之不精，則天下之理必將錯雜於是非之間，而心體終於昏昧矣，何以知其善之所在而詣之哉？於是辨真偽於疑似之間，務求何者為是，何者為非，不底於至當之歸不已也；審取舍於隱微之際，務求何者為真，何者為妄，不造於至善之地不已也。今日格一物，明日格一物，凡天下之理，皆有以究析其幾微；今日致一知，明日致一知，凡天下之理，皆有以窮極其蘊奧。夫然，則有以真知善之所在，而有誠之地矣。以為執之不固，則所擇之理必將得失於苟且之餘，而表裏終於扞格矣，何以得其善於吾心而安之哉？于是擇之於始者，執之於後，而持守
translation_en:
…for principle to be fully realized in oneself—would this not be difficult? The Doctrine of the Mean quotes Confucius’s response to Duke Ai’s question about government, distinguishing sincerity as the Way of Heaven from making oneself sincere as the Way of humanity. This passage explains the work of making oneself sincere. Why is this so? Sincerity originates in Heaven and is fundamentally the same in all; yet as it exists in human beings, it cannot be without differences. Those who strive to make themselves sincere recognize that desires intervene in principle. They wish to transform what differs and attain the same end as those who are sincere. They recognize that human interference mingles with principle. They wish to restore its original sameness and become fully consonant with the Way of Heaven. How, then, do they exert themselves?

They consider that, unless their discernment is exact, the principles of all things under Heaven will become confused amid right and wrong, and the substance of the mind will remain benighted. How could they then know where goodness lies and reach it? Thus they distinguish the genuine from the false amid doubtful appearances, striving to determine what is right and what is wrong, and not stopping until they reach what is perfectly fitting. They scrutinize what to accept and what to reject at the subtlest, least apparent points, striving to determine what is true and what is delusive, and not stopping until they reach the utmost good. Today they investigate one thing, tomorrow another, so that they can examine and analyze the finest subtleties of all the principles under Heaven. Today they extend one item of knowledge, tomorrow another, so that they can fathom the deepest implications of all the principles under Heaven. In this way they can truly know where goodness lies and establish a basis for making themselves sincere.

They consider that, unless they hold fast firmly, the principles they have discerned will be grasped and lost through careless laxity, and their outward conduct and inward state will remain at odds. How could they then apprehend that goodness within their own minds and rest secure in it? Thus, what they discern at the outset they hold fast to thereafter, preserving it…

之也堅，務使心與理融，不隨□□□□□□。於昔者，執之於今，而操持之也篤，務俾理與心契，不或在而或亡也。時有久暫，而執之之功不以久暫而或殊；事有常變，而守之之力不以常變而或異。夫然，則有以造詣乎善之所歸，而入誠之域矣。誠之者而能至是焉，則與誠者同其歸，而與天道無二致矣。反其異以歸於同，擇善固執之功焉可誣哉！大抵聖賢之學，未有不以知行為要者。《虞書》之惟精惟一，《大易》之學問寬仁，顏子之博文約禮，曾子之格致誠正，孟子之盡知存養，皆是物也。然則吾夫子擇善固執之說，豈獨哀公之所當知哉？宜子思引之以明道之費隱也歟！

…holding to it firmly, striving to unite the mind with principle, without following [six illegible characters]. What was [chosen?] in the past is held to in the present, and maintained with steadfast resolve, so that principle accords with the mind and is not sometimes present and sometimes absent. Periods of time may be long or short, but the effort of holding to it does not vary with their length; circumstances may be ordinary or exceptional, but the strength devoted to preserving it does not vary with those circumstances. Only then can one reach the ultimate destination of goodness and enter the realm of sincerity. If those who work toward sincerity can attain this point, they reach the same destination as those who are naturally sincere, and their attainment is no different from the Way of Heaven. Turning back from difference to arrive at sameness—how could the efficacy of choosing the good and holding firmly to it be denied?
Broadly speaking, the learning of sages and worthies has always taken knowing and acting as essential. The Documents of Yu speaks of being discerning and single-minded; the Book of Changes, of learning, inquiry, generosity, and benevolence; Master Yan, of broadening one's learning through cultural refinement and restraining oneself through ritual; Master Zeng, of investigating things, extending knowledge, making intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind; and Master Meng, of fully realizing the mind, knowing one's nature, preserving the mind, and nurturing one's nature. All concern this same matter. Thus, surely our Master's teaching on choosing the good and holding firmly to it was not something that Duke Ai alone ought to understand? It was fitting that Zisi should cite it to illuminate the Way's extensive manifestations and hidden subtlety!

大賢述古人之亨於困，有統治於上者，有輔治於下者。蓋舜以聖人治天下，而傅說諸賢則皆隨時輔治之臣也。其亨皆未始不由於困，何莫而非天意之所在哉？孟子之意如此。誠以富貴福澤，固天所以厚乎人，而困窮拂鬱，天亦何嘗薄於人邪？是故舜，聖人也，受堯禪而膺曆數之歸，之中國而踐天子之位。人知舜之登庸也，而不知四岳之舉實始於歷山之耕，側陋之揚實由於往田之日。舜蓋發於畎畝之中焉。傅說身胥靡，築于傅巖之野，陋矣。高宗則舉之以作相，舟楫資
translation_en:
…It is as though the writer had personally met these men, learned the particulars of their deeds, and recorded them. An excellent composition!

Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: “The discussion of the sages’ and worthies’ success and adversity is lucid and exhaustive. The phrase ‘yi ge’ [?] especially displays learning and discernment. Is this perhaps someone who, discussing the men of antiquity, can find teachers for himself among them?”

Associate Examiner Han, Instructor, comments: “The two words ‘rose’ and ‘was raised’ in this topic are perfectly clear in the original text. Yet writers invariably confuse them in their discussions, which is most tiresome. Can many compositions be found that comprehend the topic’s meaning and express it as elegantly and fluently as this one?”

Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “The exposition of Mencius’s meaning is detailed, elegant, orderly, and clear. This must be an accomplished writer.”

Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “It brings out what Mencius meant.”

The great worthy recounted how men of antiquity attained success through adversity: some presided over government above, while others assisted in governing below. Shun governed All-under-Heaven as a sage, while Fu Yue and the other worthies were all ministers who assisted in government as their times required. Their success invariably arose from adversity. In what instance was Heaven’s intention absent? Such was Mencius’s meaning. Wealth, rank, blessings, and bounty are indeed ways in which Heaven treats people generously; yet in hardship, poverty, frustration, and distress, when has Heaven ever treated people ungenerously?

Thus Shun was a sage. He received Yao’s abdication and accepted the succession ordained by Heaven; he went to the central realm and ascended the Son of Heaven’s throne. People know of Shun’s elevation to office, but do not know that his recommendation by the Four Mountains began with his plowing at Lishan, and that his advancement from humble obscurity originated in his days of working in the fields. Shun indeed rose from among the furrowed fields. Fu Yue was a convict laborer, building walls in the countryside at Fuyan—a humble station indeed. Yet Gaozong raised him to serve as chief minister, relying upon him as a boat and oars …

舉之以為政或藉之以先後也或藉之以疏附

之以作也，鹽梅資之以和也，則捄度之處，非其夢弼之地乎？膠鬲身鬻魚鹽，其事𤰞矣，文王則舉之以為政，或藉之以先後也，或藉之以疏附也，則貿易之塲，非其奮跡之所乎？齊桓公以管夷吾為相國，舉之果何所自邪？則拘於士師之官，而縲紲方且困繫也。楚莊王以孫叔敖為令尹，舉之抑何所從邪？則困於隱處之地，而海濱且將終身也。以至百里奚之賢，而為秦穆公之舉，得非混跡於商賈之區，屈志於懋遷之市，而始出哉？是則亨不遽於亨也，而必始於困；困不終於困也，而卒至於亨。古之聖賢，大率類此，謂非天意可乎？雖然，舜大聖人也，以傅說、膠鬲擬之，固已非其倫矣，況夷吾輩區區霸者之佐哉？而孟子乃一律言之，何也？盖雜舉小大之成就，皆出於困窮憂患中，用以示學者堅志熟仁之一助耳。然則有志之士，其可以憂患而自沮哉？

《易》
君子以正位凝命。
translation_en:
…he relied upon him to perform this role; as salt and plums, he relied upon him to bring harmony. Was not that place of rescue [?] the very place where the helper seen in his dream was found? Jiao Ge himself sold fish and salt, a humble occupation; yet King Wen raised him to participate in government, relying on him either to guide and assist or to draw others close in support. Was not that marketplace the place from which he rose to distinction? Duke Huan of Qi made Guan Yiwu his Chancellor. From what circumstances, indeed, did he raise him? He was in the custody of the judicial authorities, still held fast in bonds. King Zhuang of Chu made Sunshu Ao his Chief Minister. From what circumstances did he raise him? He was confined to an obscure retreat and was about to spend his entire life by the seashore. Even the worthy Baili Xi was raised up by Duke Mu of Qin: was it not only after mingling among merchants and suppressing his aspirations in the trading markets that he emerged?

Thus success does not come immediately as success: it must begin in adversity. Nor does adversity end in adversity: it ultimately leads to success. The sages and worthies of antiquity were generally like this. Can one say that this was not Heaven’s intention? Nevertheless, Shun was a great sage. To compare Fu Yue and Jiao Ge with him is already to compare men who were not his peers; how much less were men such as Yiwu, mere assistants to hegemonic rulers, his equals! Why, then, does Mencius speak of them all alike? He brings together examples of achievements both small and great, all arising from hardship and distress, simply to offer learners an aid in strengthening their resolve and bringing their benevolence to maturity. How, then, could a man of aspiration allow distress to discourage him?

Book of Changes

君子體鼎之象，必端其身之所履，以承乎天之所祐。盖位者，身之所履，而命則天之所祐也。天位正，則天命有歸矣，豈不足以凝之哉？且下巽上離，卦名曰鼎。吾夫子係之以象，盖謂木上有火，鼎象也。鼎之為物，非安重而不動者乎？有天下之君子觀斯象而體之，必也齊莊中正，端居乎五位之尊；嚴肅整齊，高拱乎九重之上。大寶至貴也，正以持之而不敢慢，所以為天下之大觀者，屹乎其鎮重而有威之可畏焉。神器至重也，正以守之而不敢忽，所以為萬物之利見者

Hua Jin 華金

Comment by Associate Examiner Tian, Instructor: “The language and reasoning are refined and precise, capturing profoundly the Master's meaning in the Commentary on the Images. Commendable.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: “The mandate is something the gentleman has already received from Heaven; the point is simply that he should consolidate it. Most writers lack clarity in grasping this. This essay alone brings out the original meaning and deserves inclusion among the selected answers.”

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-Waiting: “Clear and ample in exposition; worthy of selection.”

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: “Its discussion of rectifying one's position and consolidating the mandate is beyond the other papers.”

When the gentleman embodies the image of the Cauldron, he must rectify the position he occupies, thereby receiving Heaven's blessing. For position is what one occupies, while the mandate is Heaven's blessing. When the heavenly position is rectified, Heaven's mandate has somewhere to settle. Is this not sufficient to consolidate it? With Xun below and Li above, the hexagram is named the Cauldron. Our Master appended an explanation of its image, saying in effect: ‘Above wood there is fire: the image of the Cauldron.’ Is not the cauldron an object that rests firmly and remains unmoving? The gentleman who possesses all under Heaven observes this image and embodies it. He must be reverent, dignified, centered, and upright, occupying with rectitude the honored fifth position; solemn, disciplined, and composed, he sits aloft with hands folded within the ninefold palace. The great treasure of the throne is supremely precious: he upholds it with rectitude, never daring to be remiss. Thus, as the grand exemplar for all under Heaven, he stands firm in his gravity and possesses an awe-inspiring majesty. The sacred vessel of sovereignty is supremely weighty: he guards it with rectitude, never daring to be careless. Thus, as the one whom it benefits all beings to behold …

…solemn in his reverent conduct, presenting a deportment that others can emulate. Where the sovereign’s position resides, there too resides the Mandate. Is rectifying his position not the means of securing his Mandate? The Mandate is indeed difficult to sustain: only steadfast gravity suffices to bear it and consolidate it in the august serenity of the court. The Mandate is indeed inconstant: only reverent conduct suffices to receive it and gather it within profound stillness. The dignity of the great treasure—the throne—is truly what Heaven cherishes and protects. By thus upholding it and making it secure upon a mighty rock, the ruler can forever preserve prosperous government. The weight of the sacred vessel—sovereign authority—is truly what Heaven entrusts to him. By thus receiving it and making it as firm as a clump of mulberry roots, he can forever enjoy the blessings of happiness and greatness. Rectifying the sovereign’s position resembles setting the cauldron upright; consolidating the Mandate resembles the cauldron’s consolidating its contents. How well the gentleman embodies the Changes!
To discuss this further: the gentleman rectifies his position not for outward embellishment; this is simply the outward manifestation of his reverent virtue. The Master once praised the great Shun for reverently composing himself and taking his proper position facing south. Thus, reverently composing himself was precisely how Shun rectified his position. When emolument, rank, renown, and longevity all converged upon him, the evidence that he had secured the Mandate was surely no falsehood. Can a ruler fail to take Shun as his model?

The Great Commentary discusses the method of counting yarrow stalks, tracing how the changes arise and bringing together the means by which the lines are completed. Counting yarrow stalks is the means of obtaining a hexagram. Yet unless one investigates the beginnings of the process that produces a change, how can a hexagram be formed? Now, the number of the Great Expansion is fifty, of which forty-nine are used. What, then, should be the sequence for using them? The method of manipulation begins by dividing them into two groups, next setting one stalk aside, and then counting them off in fours: these constitute three operations. It concludes by setting aside the remainders: these constitute four operations. In this way, the method of numerical intercomparison can be unfolded, and the actual quantities, greater or smaller, can be verified. Five or four produces the odd result of a single change; nine or eight produces the even result of a single change. At this point in counting the yarrow stalks, a fresh beginning is made, and the successive steps are all in place. If even one operation were incomplete, how could a change be accomplished? After the first change, a total of three changes must be undergone before one line is formed; nine changes must be undergone before the inner trigram is obtained. …are thus complete. In this way, the inner and outer trigrams are at last joined, and the structures of the lower and upper trigrams become whole. From the first line to the topmost, root and culmination are fully displayed; from beginning to end, the relationships of riding upon and supporting other lines have their proper order. Here the procedure of manipulating the milfoil stalks reaches its conclusion, and the full structure is complete. If even one transformation were missing, how could a hexagram be formed? One who can maintain constancy in virtues already attained will assuredly be effective when put to use in the future. This is a matter of discerning men’s abilities. For accomplished virtue must be manifest and constant. If it is not, how can it serve a noble house or a state and bring about government that is profoundly enlightened and carries out its duties faithfully? Gao Yao offered counsels to Shun, and here he spoke of discerning men’s abilities. Was his meaning not this: a person of accomplished virtue is certainly capable of working toward good government, but in the manifestation of that virtue, constancy is especially to be prized?
Among the nine virtues, some men possess three. Unless these three virtues are displayed daily, those who have attained them will merely remain at that level. If such a man is appointed a grand officer, how can he bring profound enlightenment to the affairs of his noble house? He must surely renew himself daily and flourish monthly, so that his efforts at self-cultivation increase without ceasing; he must advance daily and gain monthly, so that his exertions to extend and develop his virtues grow stronger without declining. What he has attained within himself becomes ever more brilliant as he brings it to light; what appears in his conduct becomes ever greater as he gives it fuller expression. In this way, the three virtues become manifest in his person and endure with constancy.
If such a man is employed as a grand officer, I envisage him sitting up awaiting dawn, further enhancing the excellence of government and moral instruction; continuing through the night the work of the day, he makes the brilliance of his discerning administration abundantly manifest. Through exercising the three virtues, he adds lustre to his noble house. The employment of the three virtues must indeed be like this. Is this not where the usefulness of constant virtue lies? Among the nine virtues, some men possess six.…

punctuated:
是六德也，不日嚴之，則成於六德者亦終於六德矣。以之而為諸侯，有邦之政伊何而亮采乎？殆必檢束而不敢肆，素有者保守不遑，而未至者恒拳拳也；矜持而不敢放，夙成者操執匪懈，而有歉者每切切也。如此，則六德著之於身而有常矣。斯人也，用之而為諸侯，吾見邦圻之内，燦然德教之流行；邦域之中，蔚然治化之浹洽。以六德之祗嚴，足以表一邦之有又。用六德而心如是，常德之可用者不在是乎？是則謂之曰「日宣日嚴」，則彰而有常；謂之曰「浚明亮采」，則吉而可用。人君欲盡知人之事，其可忽於此哉？雖然，知人則哲，惟帝其難。臯陶陳知人之謨，推而至於官人之要，似不以為難者，豈臯陶之明顧有出於帝堯之上哉？蓋帝之所難，難於心也；臯陶之所易，易於事也。體堯之難其心，而法臯陶之詳於事，知人之道其庶矣乎！

translation_en:
…As for these six virtues, unless one attends to them with reverence each day, one who has attained six virtues will go no further than those six. If employed as a feudal lord, how could he faithfully discharge the duties of governing a state? Surely he must restrain himself, never daring to indulge himself: he must tirelessly preserve what he already possesses and remain ever earnestly intent upon what he has yet to attain. He must maintain his discipline, never daring to let himself go: he must hold fast without slackening to what he has already achieved and remain constantly concerned about his deficiencies. In this way, the six virtues will become manifest in his person and endure. If such a man is employed as a feudal lord, I see moral instruction spreading brilliantly within his borders, and the transforming influence of good government flourishing throughout his domain. His reverent attention to the six virtues will suffice to exemplify orderly government throughout a state [?]. If his application of the six virtues is thus guided by his heart [?], is this not where enduring virtue proves fit for employment? Thus, the words “daily manifest them and daily attend to them with reverence” mean that the virtues become evident and enduring; the words “illuminate them deeply and faithfully discharge one’s duties” mean that they are auspicious and fit for employment. Can a ruler who wishes fully to accomplish the task of knowing men neglect this?

Nevertheless, “To know men is wisdom; even the emperor found this difficult.” When Gao Yao set forth his counsel on knowing men and extended it to the essentials of appointing men to office, he seemed not to regard it as difficult. Could Gao Yao’s discernment actually have surpassed Emperor Yao’s? The difficulty the emperor perceived lay in his own heart; the ease Gao Yao perceived lay in practical affairs. If one embodies Yao’s sense of difficulty in one’s heart and follows Gao Yao’s thoroughness in practical affairs, one will perhaps approach the way of knowing men!

“Distinguish the good from the wicked; mark their dwellings and neighborhoods. Make goodness manifest and punish evil, establishing a reputation that influences public conduct. For those who do not follow the established teachings, separate their lands and boundaries, so that they may come to feel fear and admiration. 賢王命大臣，既欲明勸懲之政以化殷民，尤欲嚴根本之地以安天下。盖勸懲既明，則民之區別者未必皆能自安也。使非嚴根本之地，亦何以防未然之釁，以安天下哉？康王命畢公保釐東郊，而勉之以此，若謂予命公以周公之事者，豈有他哉？亦惟望公盡保釐之責耳。彼商民之中，不有淑者乎？則旌之而不沒其善；不有慝者乎？則別之而不宥其惡。旌淑何如？盖率汝訓典而不違，民之淑者也。則表其宅里，于焉顯其善

…the boundaries; carefully strengthen the defenses of the territory, so as to bring peace to all within the Four Seas.
Yu Yi 喻義.
Comment by Associate Examiner Shou Lu [?], Assistant Instructor: “The topic itself is stately. In treating [?] the recognition and differentiation of the good and wicked, the commendation of goodness and punishment of evil, and the passage on carefully strengthening territorial defenses, the author’s analysis is clear and exhaustive. He grasps King Kang’s intention to transform the people of Yin and secure the foundations of rule. This essay is therefore selected as a model for later students of textual exposition [?].”
Comment by Associate Examiner Geng, Instructor: “The language is concise and the meaning fully expressed. It captures admirably the manner appropriate to charging a minister with his duties. I admire it greatly, greatly!”
Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-waiting: “It skillfully develops the meaning of King Kang’s address to the Duke of Bi.”
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-waiting: “The composition is closely interconnected.”
When a worthy king charged a great minister with his duties, he wished both to make clear the policies of encouragement and punishment, thereby transforming the people of Yin, and, above all, to secure the region that formed the foundation of his rule, thereby bringing peace to the realm. For even when encouragement and punishment had been made clear, the people thus differentiated might not all remain content in their stations. Without securing the region that formed the foundation of rule, how could he forestall troubles before they arose and bring peace to the realm? King Kang charged the Duke of Bi with protecting and governing the eastern suburbs and exhorted him in these terms. It was as though he said: “In entrusting you with the work of the Duke of Zhou, could I have any other purpose? I hope only that you will fully discharge your responsibility to protect and govern. Among those people of Shang, are there not good people? Recognize them, so that their goodness does not go unnoticed. Are there not wicked people? Distinguish them, and do not pardon their wickedness. How should the good be recognized? Those who follow your instructions and established rules without transgressing are the good among the people. Mark their dwellings and neighborhoods, thereby making their goodness manifest…”

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以病其惡使為善之風聲聳然而樹挺然而立
有以播今而傳後也別之何如盖達厥訓典而
弗率民之惡者也則殊其井疆子以區其惡不
雜於善使為惡之頑民畏禍於已慕福於人莫
不警悚而悔悟也然既兼舉夫旌別之政則當
潜消其覬覦之心故郊圻之制昔固規畫矣公
必思其歲久則易湮而申明之有章封域之險
昔固有守矣公必念其時平則易玩而戒嚴之
有備王畿既尊則居重以馭輕而四海之遠可
===

邑既嚴則宅中以制外而天下之大可寧謐也

懲以化殷民又嚴根本以防殷民保釐之政尚

者康王生重熙累洽之後能不以宴安自怠保

punctuated: 以病其惡，使為善之風聲聳然而樹，挺然而立，有以播今而傳後也。別之何如？盖達厥訓典而弗率，民之惡者也，則殊其井疆，子以區其惡，不雜於善，使為惡之頑民畏禍於已，慕福於人，莫不警悚而悔悟也。然既兼舉夫旌別之政，則當潜消其覬覦之心。故郊圻之制，昔固規畫矣，公必思其歲久則易湮，而申明之有章；封域之險，昔固有守矣，公必念其時平則易玩，而戒嚴之有備。王畿既尊，則居重以馭輕，而四海之遠可康乂也，況商民之見旌者，孰不益勉於善乎？京邑既嚴，則宅中以制外，而天下之大可寧謐也，況商民之見別者，安敢復肆其惡乎？吁！既明勸懲以化殷民，又嚴根本以防殷民，保釐之政，尚有要於此哉？大抵旌別不明，則善惡必至於混殽；根本不固，則姦宄必至於窺伺。是以古之人君，未有不以勸善懲惡、脩內攘外為治道之要者。康王生重熙累洽之後，能不以宴安自怠，保釐之命，拳拳以是望之畢公，盖非徒以警畢公
translation_en:
…thereby putting their wickedness to shame, so that the influence and reputation of doing good rise prominently and stand firmly established, spreading in the present and passing down to posterity. How should the wicked be distinguished? Those who understand the instructive statutes yet do not follow them are the wicked among the people. Their field boundaries should therefore be separately marked, thereby [?] setting the wicked apart so that they do not mingle with the good. This will make the obstinate people who do evil fear calamity for themselves and desire the blessings enjoyed by others, so that all become alarmed and repent.

Yet once the measures for both honoring the good and distinguishing the wicked have been put into effect, their covetous ambitions must also be quietly dispelled. Thus, although arrangements for the capital’s suburban territory were certainly laid out in the past, you, my lord, must consider how easily they become obscured over the years, and reaffirm them in clear regulations. Although the strategic positions within the territory certainly had defenses in the past, you must remember how easily these are neglected in times of peace, and enforce vigilance and preparedness. Once the royal domain commands respect, its preponderant authority can control the lesser regions, and even the distant reaches within the Four Seas can enjoy peace and good government. How much more, then, will those among the Shang people who have been honored strive to do good! Once the capital is securely guarded, it can control the outlying regions from its central position, and the vast realm can enjoy tranquility. How, then, would those among the Shang people who have been set apart dare again to give free rein to their wickedness?

Ah! Having made encouragement and punishment clear in order to transform the Yin people, and having also secured the foundations of the realm in order to guard against them, could anything be more essential to the work of protecting and governing? In general, if honoring the good and distinguishing the wicked are not clearly carried out, good and evil will inevitably become confused; if the foundations are not secure, evildoers will inevitably watch for opportunities. Thus, among the rulers of antiquity, none failed to regard encouraging good and punishing evil, maintaining order within and repelling threats from without, as essentials of government. King Kang, born after successive generations of flourishing peace and harmonious rule, was able to avoid growing indolent amid ease and comfort. In his charge to protect and govern, he earnestly placed these expectations upon the Duke of Bi. Surely his purpose was not merely to admonish the Duke of Bi…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
命而代商者皆由於此以戒成王此則言大命
福周之遠其意謂夫我文王以亹亹之德膺天
心之眷豈徒尊榮其身而已哉是故麟趾振振
衍瑞慶於無窮何者非我文王之孫子瓜瓞綿
綿垂休禎於不竭何者非我文王之子孫有宗
子焉莫不出震繼離而統馭乎萬方將使歷百
世之遠永傳帝王之曆數也有支庶焉莫不分
茅胙土而君臨乎一國將使歷千載之久永為
王室之蕃衛也豈但已哉彼疏附先後我文王
===
有一代之王也濟濟乎其多矣奔走禦侮我文
王有一代之士也藹藹乎其眾矣今皆自天佑
之使周士之後昆亦顯顯乎世脩其德上有是
君下有是臣將永保至治之休而與周家媲美
於無疆焉自天申之使周士之後嗣亦昭昭乎
世濟其美君明於上臣良於下將永保太平之
盛而與我周匹休於無窮焉是則本支百世固
福周也不顯亦世亦福周也文王盛德格天之
至有如是哉大抵帝王大業未有不由於祖宗

punctuated: 命而代商者，皆由於此，以戒成王。此則言大命福周之遠，其意謂：夫我文王以亹亹之德，膺天心之眷，豈徒尊榮其身而已哉？是故麟趾振振，衍瑞慶於無窮，何者非我文王之孫子？瓜瓞綿綿，垂休禎於不竭，何者非我文王之子孫？有宗子焉，莫不出震繼離而統馭乎萬方，將使歷百世之遠，永傳帝王之曆數也；有支庶焉，莫不分茅胙土而君臨乎一國，將使歷千載之久，永為王室之蕃衛也。豈但已哉？彼疏附先後，我文王有一代之王也，濟濟乎其多矣；奔走禦侮，我文王有一代之士也，藹藹乎其眾矣。今皆自天佑之，使周士之後昆亦顯顯乎世脩其德，上有是君，下有是臣，將永保至治之休，而與周家媲美於無疆焉；自天申之，使周士之後嗣亦昭昭乎世濟其美，君明於上，臣良於下，將永保太平之盛，而與我周匹休於無窮焉。是則本支百世，固福周也；不顯亦世，亦福周也。文王盛德格天之至，有如是哉！大抵帝王大業，未有不由於祖宗
translation_en: …that Zhou received the mandate and supplanted Shang all arose from this; thus he admonished King Cheng. Here he speaks of the far-reaching blessings bestowed upon Zhou by the great mandate. His meaning is this: Our King Wen, through his unremitting virtue, won Heaven’s favor. Could this have served merely to bring honor and glory to his own person? Thus, like the auspicious lin’s hoofprints, his worthy descendants extend auspicious blessings without end: which of them is not a grandchild of our King Wen? Like an unbroken succession of melons upon the vine, they perpetuate blessings and good fortune inexhaustibly: which of them is not a descendant of our King Wen? Those of the principal line all come forth as Zhen and succeed to Li—the eldest son inheriting the sovereign’s radiance—and govern the myriad regions, so that through a hundred generations they may transmit the imperial succession forever. Those of the collateral branches all receive grants of thatch and territory and rule over individual states, so that through a thousand years they may forever serve as bulwarks of the royal house. Yet is this all? Those who drew the distant near, attached the people to him, and assisted him before and behind—our King Wen had the kings of an age [?], so numerous and distinguished were they. Those who hastened about in his service and warded off aggression—our King Wen had the worthy men of an age, so abundant were their ranks. Now Heaven protects them all, causing the descendants of Zhou’s worthy men likewise to cultivate their virtue illustriously from generation to generation. With such rulers above and such ministers below, they will preserve forever the blessings of perfect government and rival the house of Zhou in excellence without limit. Heaven renews its favor toward them, causing the heirs of Zhou’s worthy men likewise to carry forward their excellence brilliantly from generation to generation. With enlightened rulers above and good ministers below, they will preserve forever the flourishing of great peace and match our Zhou in glory without end. Thus, for the main trunk and its branches to endure for a hundred generations is indeed a blessing upon Zhou; for the illustrious likewise to continue through the generations is also a blessing upon Zhou. Such was the utmost power of King Wen’s abundant virtue to reach Heaven! In general, the great achievements of emperors and kings have never failed to derive from their ancestors…

…won it through their abundant virtue; nor has it ever been lost except through the arrogance and extravagance of their descendants. In admonishing King Cheng, the Duke of Zhou said, on one occasion, “Continue to cultivate that virtue,” and on another, “Will you not bear your ancestor in mind?” Why did he speak so earnestly of taking one’s ancestors as models? When ancestors won it through abundant virtue in earlier times, their sole wish was that their descendants should preserve it through abundant virtue thereafter. Ah! How supremely loyal and loving was the Duke of Zhou’s heart!

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:

桓公帥三國之師以救之於是乎聶北有次焉
夫春秋於後此陘亭之役嘗以次為美矣而此
則譏之者何耶盖以邢人之難朝不及夕桓欲
救之不可以不速也使公也邊塵既警而倍日

懷養亂之志偕宋及曹力非不足也乃逗遛而
不前攘外安內事非可疑也乃玩寇而待斃及

…his encampment failed to fulfill the ritual duty of relieving distress, whereas his subsequent encampment during the campaign against Chu fulfilled the benevolent duty of caring for the people. Could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to censure the one and praise the other? Alas, when Xing suffered an attack by the Di, Duke Huan of Qi led the armies of three states to rescue it and encamped at Niebei. In the later campaign at Xingting, the Spring and Autumn Annals treated his encampment as praiseworthy. Why, then, did it censure this one? Because the people of Xing were in such peril that they could not be sure of surviving from morning to evening. If Duke Huan wished to rescue them, he had to act swiftly. Had the duke, once alerted to trouble on the frontier, marched double stages with redoubled haste, what would the Spring and Autumn Annals have censured? Why did he merely proclaim his intention to relieve distress while actually harboring the intention of letting disorder grow? Allied with Song and Cao, he certainly had sufficient strength, yet he lingered without advancing. Repelling outsiders and securing the states within was unquestionably his business, yet he trifled with the enemy and waited for Xing to perish. Only when Xing’s plight grew more desperate by the day and it could scarcely survive did he slowly bestir himself to build its walls. Such was his lack of resolve in relieving distress! In compiling the classic, the Sage considered rescuing those in distress and sharing the burden of calamity urgent duties under ritual propriety. Yet in rescuing Xing, Duke Huan deliberately delayed when he should have acted swiftly. With such an encampment [text illegible, ?], could he escape censure? Thus the encampment is recorded first and the rescue afterward. As the Commentary says: “In recording a rescue, an encampment is not mentioned; mentioning the encampment conveys censure.” This is precisely the point.
As for Chu’s bringing trouble upon Zheng, Duke Huan of Qi led the armies of □ states to attack it and encamped at Xingting. In the earlier campaign at Niebei, the Spring and Autumn Annals treated his encampment as grounds for censure. Why, then, did it praise this one? Because the people of Chu could hardly be won over by force. If Duke Huan wished to punish them, he had to act cautiously. Had the duke sent his army deep into enemy territory, far from support, determined to use [three illegible characters, ?] …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
春秋奚美焉幸而謀欲出于萬全志不快于一
逞嚴兵固圉非畏縮也將以慎用吾民脩詞問
罪非迂緩也將以柔服乎遠逮夫楚人震恐遣
使如師即退舍以禮之非有志於愛民者能如
是哉聖人脩經以為好攻樂殺於世為大而桓
之伐楚能全師愛民如此欲不美之可乎故先
書伐而後書次者傳曰伐而書次以次為美是
矣是則救邢不譏則凡急恤患之義者無所懲
伐楚不美則凡存愛民之仁者無所勸褒貶在
===
一人而無窮之勸懲以寓然則聖人之義其可
以一端求之哉抑救邢之後始之次也固可罪
矣而終之城也亦可罪乎伐楚之役終之次也
固可美矣而始之專也亦可美乎故觀夷儀之
役而繼有三師之城使蔡之次而敢專八國之
伐則桓公之功過得失當相準矣噫功不足以
掩過得不足以救失伯者之事大抵皆然吾於
桓公乎何尤
晉人宋人衛人陳人侵鄭〔宣公二年〕

逞嚴兵圍圍非畏縮也將以懾用兵民偷詞問
罪非迂緩也將以柔服乎遠迷夫楚人震恐遣
使如師即退舍以禮之非有忘於愛民者能如

一人而無窮之勸懲然則聖人之義其可
以一端求之哉抑救邢之後始之次也固可罪
矣而終之城也亦可罪乎伐楚之後終之次也
固可美矣而始之專也亦可美乎故觀夷儀之
後而繼有三師之城使蔡之一而取專入國之
伐則桓公之功過得以當相準矣噫力不足以
掩過得不足以救失伯者之事大抵皆然吾於
桓公乎何尤
晉人宋人衛人陳人侵鄭〔宣公二年〕
punctuated:
春秋奚美焉？幸而謀欲出于萬全，志不快于一逞，嚴兵固圉，非畏縮也，將以慎用吾民；脩詞問罪，非迂緩也，將以柔服乎遠。逮夫楚人震恐，遣使如師，即退舍以禮之，非有志於愛民者能如是哉？聖人脩經，以為好攻樂殺於世為大，而桓之伐楚能全師愛民如此，欲不美之可乎？故先書伐而後書次者，傳曰：「伐而書次，以次為美。」是矣。是則救邢不譏，則凡急恤患之義者無所懲；伐楚不美，則凡存愛民之仁者無所勸。褒貶在一人，而無窮之勸懲以寓。然則聖人之義，其可以一端求之哉？抑救邢之後，始之次也固可罪矣，而終之城也亦可罪乎？伐楚之役，終之次也固可美矣，而始之專也亦可美乎？故觀夷儀之役而繼有三師之城，使蔡之次而敢專八國之伐，則桓公之功過得失當相準矣。噫！功不足以掩過，得不足以救失，伯者之事大抵皆然，吾於桓公乎何尤？

晉人、宋人、衛人、陳人侵鄭。〔宣公二年〕
translation_en:
…what would the Spring and Autumn Annals have to praise? Fortunately, his plans sought complete security, and his ambition was not to be gratified by a single show of force. Readying his troops and securing his defenses was no shrinking from danger: it was intended to exercise care in employing his people. Preparing diplomatic language and calling the offender to account was no dilatory roundabout approach: it was intended to win the submission of distant peoples through conciliation. When the people of Chu became terrified and sent an envoy to his army, he immediately withdrew his encampment to receive the envoy with due courtesy. Could anyone without a commitment to cherishing the people have acted thus? In compiling the Classic, the Sage regarded delight in aggression and killing as a grave matter for the world. Since Duke Huan’s campaign against Chu preserved his army and cherished the people in this way, could the Sage refrain from praising him? Thus, concerning the recording of the attack first and the encampment afterward, the Commentary says: “When an attack is followed by a record of encampment, the encampment conveys praise.” This is precisely the point.

If the relief of Xing were not censured, there would be no admonitory lesson for those concerned with the duty of urgently relieving distress; if the attack on Chu were not praised, there would be no encouragement for those who preserve the benevolence of cherishing the people. Praise and blame concern a single man, yet embody encouragement and admonition without end. Can the Sage’s moral judgments, then, be sought through a single principle? Moreover, in the relief of Xing, the initial encampment certainly deserved blame; but did the eventual building of fortifications also deserve blame? In the campaign against Chu, the eventual encampment certainly deserved praise; but did the initial unauthorized action also deserve praise? Thus, consider the undertaking at Yiyi, followed by the building of fortifications by the armies of three states, and the encampment at Cai [?], with his daring to undertake on his own authority an attack by eight states: Duke Huan’s merits and faults, successes and failures, should then be weighed against one another. Alas! Merit cannot conceal fault, nor can success remedy failure. Such is generally the case with the deeds of hegemons. Why should I single out Duke Huan for reproach?

Men of Jin, Song, Wei, and Chen invaded Zheng. 〔Second year of Duke Xuan.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: Candidates writing on this topic often divide into two separate arguments the discussion in Hu’s Commentary concerning an unjust cause and rectifying the root. This essay alone treats them as an integrated whole, allowing the commentary’s meaning to emerge naturally. I single it out for recognition [?].
Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-Waiting: The Sage’s principle of condemning those who side with evildoers is fully elucidated.
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: The composition displays decisive judgment.

When a hegemonic state punishes divided allegiance yet lacks justification, the Spring and Autumn Annals records the facts directly to convey its censure. Here we see that Zheng had a sound case for attacking Song on Chu’s behalf, whereas Jin lacked justification for siding with Song and oppressing Zheng. Could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to hold Jin gravely accountable? Why is this so? When Zheng defeated Song at Daji, it was indeed allied with Chu. Jin wished to retaliate against Chu and assembled an army to attack Zheng. Thus Guisheng’s defeat of Song amounted to following the barbarians, while Zhao Dun’s punitive attack on Zheng amounted to preserving the Chinese states. Once Jin’s army marched out, three states joined it. Why, then, in recording this campaign, does the Spring and Autumn Annals designate the ministers merely as “men” and describe the army’s action as an “incursion”?

Righteousness is the impartial principle shared by all under Heaven; profit is the selfish impulse of human desire. The crimes of Bao of Song were beyond pardon under the king’s law. Why did Jin’s ruler and ministers undertake no expedition to punish this traitor, but instead negotiate a covenant that consolidated the disorder? They had thereby already abandoned the great obligations of righteousness before all under Heaven.

Although Guisheng’s attack on Song at Chu’s command might be called leading barbarians to ravage the Chinese states, this overlooks the fact that anyone may punish a perpetrator of high treason—and Chu did punish him. Although Zhao Dun’s attack on Zheng on Song’s behalf might be called chastising a Chinese state for following the barbarians, this overlooks the fact that a state harboring the chief evildoer…

text:
義不容於黨之而晉則黨之矣夫師必理之直
而氣始壯事必始之慎而終斯善晉之始也以
貪利而廢天討之刑則何有於慎繼焉以黨惡
而發憑弱之旅又何有於直惟理不直而曲故
師雖盛而老是以棐林之役未克稱兵討罪而
鬬椒之來遽爾卷甲旋師向使盟扈無貪賂之
失則晉師方強何乃至於畏楚向使侵鄭非黨

謀始謀始所以慮終晉君何有焉故春秋於此

而深譏之以為末流之戒也吁一書法間而討
賊之義貪利之戒謹始之訓正本之道咸寓焉

亦不能成討賊之義鄭之所行果何為者哉春

punctuated: 義不容於黨之，而晉則黨之矣。夫師必理之直而氣始壯，事必始之慎而終斯善。晉之始也，以貪利而廢天討之刑，則何有於慎？繼焉以黨惡而發憑弱之旅，又何有於直？惟理不直而曲，故師雖盛而老。是以棐林之役，未克稱兵討罪，而鬬椒之來，遽爾卷甲旋師。向使盟扈無貪賂之失，則晉師方強，何乃至於畏楚？向使侵鄭非黨惡之行，則列國咸在，何以不能服鄭？君子作事謀始，謀始所以慮終，晉君何有焉？故《春秋》於此，列卿特以人稱，討鄭又以侵錄，蓋因其本不正而深譏之，以為末流之戒也。吁！一書法間，而討賊之義、貪利之戒、謹始之訓、正本之道咸寓焉。《春秋》謂非聖人莫能脩，信夫！抑晉之罪固不可逭，而鄭之所行，要亦非盡善者。彼晉靈貪污，誠不足與，而楚莊裔夷，是豈宜從？而且今日動眾以虐陳，明日勞師以掠宋，既不免犯於華之愆，亦不能成討賊之義。鄭之所行，果何為者哉？《春秋》於侵鄭責晉者，特為黨惡而然耳，非謂鄭本
translation_en:
…righteousness does not permit taking its side, yet Jin took its side. An army’s cause must be upright before its spirit can be strong; an undertaking must be begun with care if it is to end well. At the outset, Jin coveted gain and abandoned the punishment required by Heaven: where was its care? Subsequently, it sided with evil and dispatched an army to oppress the weak: where was its uprightness? Precisely because its cause was crooked rather than upright, its army, though mighty, was exhausted. Thus, in the campaign at Feilin, before it could raise arms to punish wrongdoing, the arrival of Dou Jiao prompted it hastily to pack away its armor and withdraw. Had there been no fault of coveting bribes at the covenant at Hu, Jin’s army would have been strong: how could it have come to fear Chu? Had the incursion into Zheng not been an act of siding with evil, then, with all the allied states present, why could it not subdue Zheng? When a gentleman undertakes something, he plans its beginning; planning the beginning is how he takes thought for the end. What trace of this was there in the ruler of Jin? Thus, in this passage the Spring and Autumn Annals refers to the various ministers merely as “men” and records the punitive expedition against Zheng as an “incursion.” Because its foundation was unsound, the text censures it severely, as a warning against the consequences that follow. Ah! Within a single instance of its manner of recording events are contained the duty to punish rebels, the warning against coveting gain, the lesson of taking care at the outset, and the way of setting the foundation right. How true the saying that none but a sage could compile the Spring and Autumn Annals!

Yet although Jin’s guilt certainly cannot be excused, Zheng’s conduct, upon consideration, was not wholly good either. Duke Ling of Jin was greedy and corrupt, and indeed unworthy of association; but King Zhuang of Chu was a barbarian of the outer regions—was he someone whom Zheng ought to follow? Moreover, today Zheng mobilized its forces to ravage Chen; tomorrow it wearied its army to plunder Song. It neither escaped the offense of attacking the states of the Hua cultural realm nor fulfilled the righteous duty of punishing rebels. What, indeed, was Zheng trying to accomplish? text:

…overstep their prescribed bounds? In distinguishing close from distant relationships and following principle as circumstances require, people recognize righteousness, yet do not realize that the rites governing close and distant relationships firmly possess fixed standards. In distinguishing the noble from the lowly and determining what is appropriate to the occasion, people recognize righteousness, yet do not realize that the rites governing rank clearly possess fixed regulations. How, then, can this be demonstrated? Rites cannot arise arbitrarily. Yet if, after consideration and assessment, a practice accords with righteousness, then even though the former kings had no such rite, one may deliberate upon righteousness and establish a new regulation. What constraint need there be? Rites cannot be devised arbitrarily. Yet if, after weighing and deliberating, righteousness is brought into accord with circumstances, then even though the former kings never established such a rite, one may weigh righteousness and establish a new rule. What grounds for objection need there be? For example, the ritual preference for simplicity did not exist under the Xia. The Shang instituted it to accord with righteousness, without being bound by the Xia emphasis on wholehearted sincerity. The ritual preference for refinement did not exist under the Shang. The Zhou instituted it to accord with righteousness, likewise without clinging to simplicity. Rites arise through righteousness, and righteousness is put into practice through rites: thus we can see that rites are the concrete embodiment of righteousness. Could the former kings’ insistence on cultivating rites first, when regulating human feelings, have been without reason? Generally speaking, rites and righteousness must accompany one another and cannot exist apart. Without rites, righteousness has no means of embodying its constant principles; without righteousness, rites have no means of adapting to change. Thus [?], in regulating human feelings, the former kings necessarily took rites and righteousness as their guiding framework and never failed to follow them. Let those who aspire to establish rites examine this.

“To fathom the root and understand change is the essential nature of music; to manifest sincerity and eliminate falsity is the guiding principle of rites.”

To regulate the feelings so that none fail to accord with one another is the spontaneous effect of music’s transforming influence; to regulate the feelings so that none fail to be good is the proper effect of ritual’s ordering. The gentleman in the Record of Music means this: people know that ritual and music encompass human feelings, but who understands how ritual and music govern them? Consider human feelings: in terms of their principle, they are originally alike. Because they are alike, their root is one. It can comprehend the differences in their transformations, enabling the nature that has gone astray in feelings to recover the goodness of its original substance.

text:
與情會而情自得於樂之化凡所以安久天神
一皆感通之自然者耳謂非樂之情而何人之
情理存於中而甚微微則誠隱也欲動於物而
甚危危則偽生也禮以辨異故能著其理之誠
而使微者以顯純乎天理之流行去其欲之偽
而使危者以安絕無物欲之留滯夫著誠去偽
則情無不善矣此豈事之可已哉盖辨異者禮
之用也禮必達於情而後情之發始著其誠則
著誠之功何可無情必治於禮而後情之用始
===
去其偽則去偽之功何可少凡所以莊敬嚴威
一皆脩為之當然者耳謂非禮之經而何是則
禮樂之能治乎人情如此此其所以不可斯須
去身也歟雖然禮樂一道也而以為有情有經
若不同焉何也盖自天地之高下散殊周流合
同而禮主於收斂樂主於發達固已有不同者
此禮所以能脩外而樂所以能脩內也至其交
錯於中而發形於外恭敬而温文焉則又何可
以異視哉學者析其異而會其同則得之矣

雖然，禮樂一道也，而以為有情有經，若不同焉，何也？盖自天地之高下散殊、周流合同，而禮主於收斂，樂主於發達，固已有不同者。此禮所以能脩外，而樂所以能脩內也。至其交錯於中，而發形於外，恭敬而温文焉，則又何可以異視哉？學者析其異而會其同，則得之矣。

All that brings enduring repose and heavenly spirituality [?] is simply the spontaneous working of sympathetic response and communion. What could this be called but the essential character of music? In human feelings, principle resides within and is exceedingly subtle; because it is subtle, sincerity remains hidden. Desire is stirred by external things and is exceedingly perilous; because it is perilous, falseness arises. Ritual distinguishes differences. It can therefore make manifest the sincerity of principle, bringing what is subtle into view, so that there is nothing but the free operation of heavenly principle. It removes the falseness of desire, bringing what is perilous to rest, so that material desires leave no lingering obstruction. When sincerity is manifested and falseness removed, no feeling is other than good. How could this work ever be abandoned? For distinguishing differences is the function of ritual. Only when ritual reaches the feelings does their expression begin to manifest sincerity: how, then, could the work of manifesting sincerity be dispensed with? Only when the feelings are ordered by ritual does their operation begin to shed falseness: how, then, could the work of removing falseness be neglected? All that produces solemnity, reverence, dignity, and awe is simply what cultivation and practice properly require. What could this be called but the constant norm of ritual? Such is the capacity of ritual and music to order human feelings. Is this not why one must never depart from them, even for an instant?

Nevertheless, ritual and music constitute a single Way. Why, then, speak of the one as having an essential character and the other a constant norm, as though they differed? The distinction already exists in Heaven and Earth: their high and low positions, their dispersed differentiation, and their all-pervading circulation and union. Ritual chiefly gathers in and restrains; music chiefly unfolds and gives expression. This is why ritual can cultivate the outward person, while music can cultivate the inner person. Yet when they interweave within and take outward form as reverence and refined gentleness, how could they be regarded as separate? If students distinguish their differences and comprehend their unity, they will grasp their meaning.

translation_en:
…the laws recorded in books can certainly still be examined. If later rulers have no wish to bring peace and order to the realm, there is nothing more to say; but if they aspire to good government yet abandon the great laws of the sages, how can they even speak of governing? Master Cheng, discussing the learning of emperors and kings, said: “The sages’ great laws for ordering the world are fully preserved in books. If one grasps their essentials, putting them into practice presents no difficulty.” How fine these words are! Allow me to unfold their meaning.

Heaven, in protecting the people below, necessarily brings forth sages to serve as their rulers and teachers, governing and instructing them. When the sages undertake their work in accordance with Heaven’s intent, theirs is a responsibility they cannot decline. Accordingly, they regulate and bring to fruition the Way of Heaven and Earth, assist what is fitting to Heaven and Earth, and thereby order this world and establish great laws for it. Concerned that the world might lack sustenance, they institute the well-field system to support it; concerned that it might lack instruction, they establish schools to teach it. Concerned that it might lack encouragement, they distinguish the five grades of official robes to encourage goodness; concerned that it might lack restraints, they make the five punishments clear to prohibit evil. Concerned that people might deceive one another, they provide tallies, seals, weights, and measures to ensure trustworthiness; concerned that people might encroach upon one another, they provide inner and outer city walls, armor, and weapons to protect them.

By attending to the astronomical instruments [?], they bring the celestial governing bodies into accord, and the Way of Heaven is made manifest in the world. By regulating the calendar and celestial observations, they announce the seasons, and human affairs are duly ordered in the world. They use the eight instruments of authority to govern their ministers, so that all who serve as ministers obey their commands, none daring to confer favors or wield coercive power on their own. They use the eight unifying principles to govern the myriad people, so that all the people follow their Way, none daring to act upon private likes or dislikes. As for the prescribed ceremonies for court audiences, diplomatic visits, assemblies, and gatherings, and the established forms for cappings, weddings, funerals, and sacrifices…

…and distinctions of rank governing carriages, horses, palaces, and dwellings: in everything constituting the great laws for ordering the world, was anything left unprovided for? Thus benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music extended in all directions without conflict, and all things under Heaven were encompassed within these great laws. Yet why is the world not always well governed, and why are its laws not always observed? When a sage is born but does not attain the proper position, can he alone remain indifferent to the world? He therefore takes the former kings’ great laws for ordering the world and entrusts them to the classics to instruct later generations. Although these laws are not put into practice in his own time, they are all preserved in written records. Thus, in elucidating the Book of Changes, he traced matters from Fuxi and Xuanyuan onward, embedding their great laws for ordering the world in the Changes; in arranging the Book of Documents, he traced matters from Yao and Shun onward, embedding their great laws for ordering the world in the Documents; in editing the Book of Odes, he traced matters from Kings Wen and Wu onward, embedding their great laws for ordering the world in the Odes. In compiling the Spring and Autumn Annals, he traced matters from Duke Huan and Duke Wen onward. Although that age lacked the government of a sage, our Master used the text of the historical records of Lu to embody the great laws for ordering the world. Of the sage’s laws, not one fails to express what resides in his heart, and not one fails to embody the Way. These are what is meant by laws that, “established before Heaven and Earth, do not conflict with them; tested against ghosts and spirits, admit of no doubt; and awaiting a sage a hundred generations hence, occasion no perplexity.” Can those who later rule all under Heaven fail to seek their guidance here?
The human heart is vast and boundless, endowed with every goodness; abundant virtue and great achievements all proceed from it. That the sage’s laws can be transmitted through myriad generations without becoming defective is assuredly due to the extension of this heart. Then can those who wish to transmit the sage’s Way and put his laws into practice fail to consider how to expand…

translation_en:
…extend that heart to its fullest? To develop this heart fully, one must begin with learning. Yet the learning of emperors and kings does not consist in searching out passages and picking out phrases; it lies in grasping the essentials. If I grasp the essentials and fully develop this heart to put them into practice, my virtue will be the virtue of the sages, and my achievements will be their achievements. Who, then, could say that the government of the Two Emperors and Three Kings cannot be restored? Alas! Since the Three Dynasties, there have indeed been rulers who loved learning. Men such as Emperor Wen of Wei and Emperor Yang of Sui, who devoted their talents to literary composition and calligraphy, are certainly unworthy of discussing the Way of the sages. As for Emperor Wu of Han’s promotion of the Six Classics and Emperor Ming’s lectures on the classics at the Biyong, the imperial academy, these suggest an aspiration toward sagely learning. Why, then, did their government ultimately fail to equal that of antiquity? Because they did not fully develop their hearts, and their learning failed to grasp the essentials.

Thus, anyone wishing to implement the great institutions of the former kings must first devote himself to the teaching of being discerning and single-minded and holding fast to the Mean. Without this heart, even if one adopts these institutions and implements them, they remain mere institutions. How could one rival the flourishing government of Tang and Yu—the ages of Yao and Shun—and the Three Dynasties? Master Cheng said, “It is also said [?] that only when one possesses the spirit of ‘The Ospreys’ Cry’ (Guanju) and ‘The Qilin’s Hooves’ (Linzhi) can one implement the regulations of the Offices of Zhou.” Profound indeed is this argument tracing things back to their root.

translation_en:
…the numinous longevity of the dynastic succession, extending its radiance abundantly to the most distant descendants and diffusing its blessings to bathe the countless multitudes. It illuminates the flourishing ancestral legacy, displaying the proliferation of the greater and lesser lineage branches; it sets forth anew the grand principles, showing the importance of recording matters specially and repeatedly. Resplendent are its inscriptions on precious jade; copious are its words establishing rules and models. Dates and times are recorded, with orderly arrangement and essential points. Commands were renewed for its compilation in the Palace Library, and its exposition at the historians’ desks was conducted with solemn care. The lineage branches are distinguished by their alternating generational ranks, arrayed like stars about the Purple Pole; close and distant kin are differentiated, bringing daily greater stability to the grand dynastic design. Flourishing is the spirit of benevolence and generosity; radiant is the reign of supreme harmony. The Silver River of imperial descent flows broad and shimmering; the jade tablets are comprehensive and solemn. In the enfeoffment of eighteen hundred states, imperial kinsmen take precedence over those of other surnames; the records of the Five and Three [?] and the Six Classics truly accord with this. Illustrious ancestors and cultured descendants possess the excellence of continuing succession from a single root; imperial branches and imperial undertakings sustain the grandeur of a foundation lasting ten thousand years. Joy fills officials and people, and radiance suffuses all within the seas.
We reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor, through abundant grace, brings harmony to the imperial clan …

translation_en:
…grandly following your forebears and carrying forward their foundation. As the hereditary lineage continues unbroken, you perceive how branches and leaves support trunk and roots; as your imperial designs embrace all in their vastness, you seek to follow established patterns and standards. Your greatness is too boundless to name, yet your affection for your kin observes due order. The principal lineage succeeds to the throne as Son of Heaven, maintaining unified rule for ten thousand years; the collateral branches receive territories as imperial princes, perpetuating the dynastic mandate to match the Three Dynasties. On this radiant day, you reverently honor your ancestors and proclaim the grand enduring ordinances. The august compilation is completed, and Heaven and humankind rejoice together.
We, your servants, have undeservedly received appointments among your attendants and discharge our duties as compilers. Our talent falls shamefully short of Liu Fang’s, yet the Tang imperial house’s new chart, termed a record [?], seems meager by comparison; our learning falls shamefully short of Ban Gu’s, yet the compilation [?] of the Han house’s genealogy seems paltry. Fortunately, these precious jade-like writings are now set forth, and we look up toward the palace court as we present them.
We humbly pray that the One Man may enjoy blessings, and that all regions may look up together to your splendid and enlightened rule; that the states throughout the four quarters may serve as bulwarks, and that all the Nine Regions may attain good order and peace together. Gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your Sagely Majesty, we, your servants, cannot contain our fervent emotion and profound trepidation. We respectfully submit what we have compiled …

At the end, it again presents preserving the mind and examining one’s conduct as aids to bringing about harmony today; its intent is especially earnest. Should this candidate one day hold office at court, he will surely serve his sovereign by adhering to the admonition to examine his own conduct.

text:
力於身心則無以盡其忠如是而欲望夫
弭災致祥以回天意亦何可得哉此我
太祖高皇帝存心省躬二錄所以不容於不作
而萬世
聖子神孫與夫佐理承化者皆所當深念而不
可忽焉者也仰惟
聖祖在御之時嘗
命儒臣編葺存心錄一書凡歷代帝王祭祀
而有感於災祥者皆載焉既而又
===
命儒臣編葺省躬錄一書凡漢唐宋以來災
祥之應於臣下者皆載焉二書雖皆主於
祀事而作然究其宏綱大義只指授出於
聖心者則拳拳乎天人之理懇懇乎災祥之應
無非欲天下後世之為人君者知天心之
仁愛也一遇夫日月之薄蝕星辰之凌犯
山崩川竭水湧地震與夫恒雨而恒暘恒
燠而恒寒凡人事乖於下而天變應於上
則必專精礪志察事求端思所以致感之
