山崩川竭水湧地震與夫恒雨而恒暘恒
燠而恒寒凡人事乖於下而天變應於上
則必專精竭志察事求端思所以致感之
punctuated:
力於身心，則無以盡其忠。如是而欲望夫弭災致祥，以回天意，亦何可得哉？此我太祖高皇帝《存心》《省躬》二錄所以不容於不作，而萬世聖子神孫與夫佐理承化者，皆所當深念而不可忽焉者也。
仰惟聖祖在御之時，嘗命儒臣編葺《存心錄》一書，凡歷代帝王祭祀而有感於災祥者，皆載焉。既而又命儒臣編葺《省躬錄》一書，凡漢唐宋以來災祥之應於臣下者，皆載焉。二書雖皆主於祀事而作，然究其宏綱大義，只指授出於聖心者，則拳拳乎天人之理，懇懇乎災祥之應。無非欲天下後世之為人君者知天心之仁愛也。一遇夫日月之薄蝕、星辰之凌犯、山崩川竭、水湧地震，與夫恒雨而恒暘、恒燠而恒寒，凡人事乖於下而天變應於上，則必專精礪志，察事求端，思所以致感之
translation_en:
…exert himself in cultivating body and mind, he has no means of fully realizing his loyalty. Under such circumstances, how could one hope to avert disasters and bring auspicious signs, thereby turning Heaven’s intent? This is why our Emperor Taizu Gao could not but have the two Records, Preserving the Mind and Examining Oneself, compiled. His sage sons and divine grandsons through all generations, together with those who assist in governing and carry forward his transforming influence, must ponder them deeply and never disregard them.
We reverently recall that, while the sagely founding emperor occupied the throne, he once commanded Confucian court scholars to compile the Record of Preserving the Mind (Cunxin lu). It included all instances in successive dynasties in which emperors’ sacrifices were associated with responses in the form of disasters or auspicious signs. Subsequently, he again commanded Confucian court scholars to compile the Record of Examining Oneself (Shenggong lu). It included all instances from the Han, Tang, and Song onward in which disasters and auspicious signs manifested themselves in connection with ministers. Although both books were composed primarily concerning sacrificial affairs, examination of their broad principles and essential meaning—the phrase concerning instruction issuing from the imperial mind is uncertain [?]—reveals earnest concern for the principles linking Heaven and humanity and profound attention to the responses manifested in disasters and auspicious signs. The sole purpose was to make rulers throughout the realm and in later ages understand the benevolence of Heaven’s heart. Whenever they encounter eclipses of the sun or moon, encroachments among the stars, collapsing mountains and drying rivers, surging waters and earthquakes, or persistent rain or sunshine, persistent warmth or cold—in every case where human affairs go awry below and Heaven responds with anomalies above—they must concentrate their minds and steel their resolve, examine affairs and seek the source, and reflect upon what has elicited these responses…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
由求所以消復之道誠知夫吉凶不僭在
人而天降災祥在德禍福無不自己求者
必六事自責如成湯必遇災而懼如周宣
應之以實不以文感之以誠不以言敬天
之怒無敢戲豫其必曰未有不召而自至
之祥亦未有已至而不應之變一以天之
心為心所以變災而為祥轉禍而為福者
無所不用其極而為之臣者亦莫不以君
之心為心四方災異郡未及上也而輒以
===
聞如魏相之於漢諸路水旱衆以為無徵
也而輒以奏如李沆之於宋必不敢以湯
旱歸之桀如公孫弘也必不敢以天變為
不足畏如王安石也所以輔君以事天者
亦無所不用其極焉此則
聖祖垂訓之深意豈徒致謹於祀事之間而已
哉然竊嘗伏而窺之二書之為災祥作也
則一而其命名也則不同於警乎君者則
以存心言非緩於身也心者身之主言心

亦無所不用其極焉此則
聖祖垂訓之深意豈徒致謹於祀事之間而已
哉然竊嘗伏而窺之二書之為災祥作也
則一而其命名也則不同於警乎君者則
以存心言非緩於身也心者身之主言心
punctuated:
由，求所以消復之道。誠知夫吉凶不僭在人，而天降災祥在德，禍福無不自己求者，必六事自責如成湯，必遇災而懼如周宣，應之以實，不以文；感之以誠，不以言。敬天之怒，無敢戲豫。其必曰：「未有不召而自至之祥，亦未有已至而不應之變。」一以天之心為心，所以變災而為祥、轉禍而為福者，無所不用其極。而為之臣者，亦莫不以君之心為心。四方災異，郡未及上也，而輒以聞，如魏相之於漢；諸路水旱，衆以為無徵也，而輒以奏，如李沆之於宋。必不敢以湯旱歸之桀，如公孫弘也；必不敢以天變為不足畏，如王安石也。所以輔君以事天者，亦無所不用其極焉。此則聖祖垂訓之深意，豈徒致謹於祀事之間而已哉？
然竊嘗伏而窺之，二書之為災祥作也則一，而其命名也則不同。於警乎君者，則以存心言，非緩於身也。心者身之主，言心
translation_en:
…the cause, and seek the way to dispel calamities and restore normal conditions. Truly understanding that good and ill fortune never go astray and depend upon human conduct, that Heaven’s sending of calamities and auspicious signs depends upon virtue, and that misfortune and blessing are invariably brought upon oneself, a ruler will surely reproach himself on six counts, as Cheng Tang did, and feel fear when calamity strikes, as King Xuan of Zhou did. He will respond with substance rather than outward forms, and move Heaven through sincerity rather than words. Revering Heaven’s anger, he will not dare indulge in play or pleasure. He will surely say: “No auspicious sign arrives of itself without having been called forth; nor does any anomaly, once it has appeared, lack something to which it corresponds.” Taking Heaven’s heart wholly as his own, he will spare no effort to transform calamity into auspiciousness and turn misfortune into blessing. Those who serve as his ministers will likewise take their ruler’s heart as their own. When calamities and anomalies occur throughout the realm, they will report them even before the commanderies have submitted their reports, as Wei Xiang did under the Han. When floods and droughts occur in the various circuits, they will memorialize them even though others consider them unsubstantiated, as Li Hang did under the Song. They will certainly not dare attribute the drought in Tang’s reign to Jie, as Gongsun Hong did, or claim that Heaven’s anomalies need not be feared, as Wang Anshi did. Thus they too will spare no effort in assisting their ruler to serve Heaven. This is the profound intention behind the sagely founding emperor’s bequeathed instructions. Could it merely be to encourage care in sacrificial observances?
Yet, as I have humbly pondered the matter, the two books share the purpose of addressing calamities and auspicious signs, but their titles differ. The one that admonishes the ruler speaks of preserving the heart, without thereby neglecting the person. The heart is the master of the person; to speak of the heart…

見正殿減膳停樂矣而尤詔内外無間極

播告之脩蠲逋負賑饑饉寬獄囚理冤抑蓋

translation_en:
…then the person is included within it. In admonishing ministers [?], he speaks of examining the person, without neglecting the mind. The person is the mind in operation; to speak of the person thus includes the mind within it. Was not the subtle intention of the Sagely Ancestor also to have later rulers and ministers reflect upon and grasp this, so that both would exert their efforts together? The Three Dynasties and earlier ages surely need no discussion. Emperor Guangwu of the Han, for example, was alarmed by admonitory portents appearing in the sun and moon and withdrew from the main hall. He further commanded all officials to submit sealed memorials, withholding nothing. Thus, those who reported disasters and anomalies at that time were not confined to the ministers who assisted the sovereign. Emperor Taizong of the Tang, upon the appearance of a comet, took measures concerning the main hall [?], reduced his meals, and suspended music. He further commanded officials both within and outside the capital, without distinction, to speak fully about the successes and failings of government. Thus, those permitted to speak about disasters and anomalies at that time were likewise not confined to ministers at court. This is why both rulers were able to avert disasters and bring about auspicious signs. Although we cannot fully know their achievements in preserving the mind and examining the person, the concord in virtue between ruler and ministers and their pursuit of good government cannot be denied.
In our dynasty, successive sage sovereigns have shared the same vigilance and reverence. Our present Emperor has been especially devoted to carrying forward their work. Recently, in response to the warning of disasters and anomalies, he issued a special command proclaiming reforms [?], remitted arrears, relieved famine, extended leniency to prisoners, and redressed injustices and oppression. His measures have indeed left nothing unattended. Now, wishing to consider how further to alleviate…

無不脩所謂奉天之敬在是矣為上為德

其國而不知有其家如是則身以脩而心

translation_en:
…the anxiety over □□, thereby helping to bring about harmony: in my humble opinion, there is no need to seek elsewhere. One need only reverently follow the instructions of the Sagely Progenitor, with those above and below united in virtue, preserving the mind as he preserved his mind and examining oneself as he examined himself. That is all. The ruler’s single mind is exceedingly subtle, yet the things that assail it are exceedingly numerous. Only when every thought is pure can one speak of preserving it. Otherwise, even one impure thought is enough to contravene Heaven and distort government. Can one therefore experience alarm and fear once and then stop? The many affairs administered by the assembled ministers are exceedingly numerous; they cannot necessarily all be free from error. Only when every affair has been put in order can one speak of self-examination. Otherwise, even one affair left unattended is enough to harm the people and afflict the world. Can one therefore experience reverent fear once and then stop?
Thus one must exercise care in matters of governing principles, laws, and institutions, and scrutiny in dispensing rewards and punishments, granting and withholding. One must exalt reverence and awe, and guard against ease and desire. In this way the mind is preserved, and one’s conduct is fully cultivated: herein lies what is called reverence in serving Heaven. Know only that one has a ruler, without regard for oneself; know only that one has a state, without regard for one’s family. text:
既親之誠則輔之雖有可畏之實未嘗無
可親之理焉畏威易役民若無可畏矣然
順之則服逆之則去非但有可畏之理固
自有可畏之勢焉天之可畏人孰不知之
而民之可畏則溺於世主崇高富貴之情
而知之者鮮矣此我
聖祖所以闡其微旨而懇懇於可愛非君可畏
非民之戒也大哉
皇言其與舜之所以授禹者夫豈異致哉方
===
今承平既久天下之民無一不涵泳鼓舞於
深仁厚澤之中較之
國初干戈甫定之秋宜若無足畏者然
國初之民此心也今日之民亦此心也豈前
日之民可畏而今日之民獨不可畏乎
聖祖所謂畏民者豈徒以干戈甫定之際謂民
有可畏之勢哉蓋民心之向背係天命之
去留謂為可畏者實以其理之可畏矣然
今日之當畏者亦豈特以安養既久□繇謂

punctuated:
既親之，誠則輔之，雖有可畏之實，未嘗無可親之理焉。畏威易役，民若無可畏矣；然順之則服，逆之則去，非但有可畏之理，固自有可畏之勢焉。天之可畏，人孰不知之？而民之可畏，則溺於世主崇高富貴之情，而知之者鮮矣。此我聖祖所以闡其微旨，而懇懇於「可愛非君，可畏非民」之戒也。大哉，皇言！其與舜之所以授禹者，夫豈異致哉？
方今承平既久，天下之民無一不涵泳鼓舞於深仁厚澤之中，較之國初干戈甫定之秋，宜若無足畏者。然國初之民，此心也；今日之民，亦此心也。豈前日之民可畏，而今日之民獨不可畏乎？聖祖所謂畏民者，豈徒以干戈甫定之際，謂民有可畏之勢哉？蓋民心之向背，係天命之去留，謂為可畏者，實以其理之可畏矣。然今日之當畏者，亦豈特以安養既久，□繇謂
translation_en:
…Heaven draws near to the reverent [?] and assists the sincere. Though there is indeed cause to fear it, there is also reason to draw close to it. The people fear authority and are easily put to service, so they might seem to offer no cause for fear. Yet if one accords with them, they submit; if one goes against them, they depart. There is not merely reason in principle to fear them: their power itself gives cause for fear. Who does not know that Heaven is to be feared? But worldly rulers are so immersed in their feelings of exalted rank, wealth, and honor that few recognize that the people are to be feared. This is why our Sagely Progenitor elucidated this subtle meaning and so earnestly offered the admonition, “Who is to be cherished if not the ruler? Who is to be feared if not the people?” How great are these imperial words! How could their purport differ from what Shun imparted to Yu?
Now that peace has long prevailed, every person under Heaven is steeped in profound benevolence and abundant favor, rejoicing in them. Compared with the time at the dynasty’s founding, when warfare had only just been quelled, there would seem to be nothing to fear. Yet the people at the dynasty’s founding had these same hearts, and the people today have these same hearts as well. Could the people of former days have been fearsome, while those of today alone are not? When the Sagely Progenitor spoke of fearing the people, was it merely because, just after warfare had been quelled, he considered their power fearsome? Whether the people’s hearts turn toward or away from the ruler determines whether Heaven’s Mandate remains or departs. To call them fearsome is thus truly to recognize a principle that warrants fear. Yet ought we today to fear them merely because they have long enjoyed peace and nurture, [illegible; wording uncertain] to say …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
民將有可畏之機哉盖防微杜漸之念實
致治保邦之要所以畏之者非過慮也亦
以其理有可畏焉耳此我
皇上所以仰繩
祖武而夙夜惓惓不遑寧處誠有在于是也故
一聞四方寇盜之警輒下所司俾圖其弭
盜之方其畏民可謂勤矣然而楚蜀之間
民之淪於盜賊者尚未聞其有還定閭里
之期是盖非有他故也良由下無畏民之
===
吏饑饉荐臻恬不加意縱使無顆粒之儲
而虛張斂散之數胥徒以點視為名而因
行漁獵之計民安得不淪於盜賊乎為今
之計莫若求其人如龔遂之在渤海而寬
以亂繩之治張綱之在廣陵而服以單車
之誠則可化刀劔為犁鋤矣豈不足以紓
皇上憂盜賊之心哉一聞四方水旱之虞輒下
所司俾議其穰災之策其畏民可謂切矣
然而蘇松之境民之傷於水潦者尚未聞

之計莫若求其人如龔遂之在渤海而寬

之誠則可化刀劒爲犂鋤矣豈不足以紓

所司俾議其懺災之策其畏民可謂切矣
然而蘇松之境民之傷於水潦者尚未聞
punctuated: 民將有可畏之機哉？盖防微杜漸之念，實致治保邦之要。所以畏之者，非過慮也，亦以其理有可畏焉耳。此我皇上所以仰繩祖武，而夙夜惓惓、不遑寧處，誠有在于是也。故一聞四方寇盜之警，輒下所司，俾圖其弭盜之方，其畏民可謂勤矣。然而楚蜀之間，民之淪於盜賊者，尚未聞其有還定閭里之期。是盖非有他故也，良由下無畏民之吏，饑饉荐臻，恬不加意，縱使無顆粒之儲，而虛張斂散之數；胥徒以點視為名，而因行漁獵之計，民安得不淪於盜賊乎？為今之計，莫若求其人，如龔遂之在渤海，而寬以亂繩之治；張綱之在廣陵，而服以單車之誠，則可化刀劔為犁鋤矣。豈不足以紓皇上憂盜賊之心哉？一聞四方水旱之虞，輒下所司，俾議其穰災之策，其畏民可謂切矣。然而蘇松之境，民之傷於水潦者，尚未聞
translation_en:
…that circumstances might arise in which the people become formidable? Indeed, the resolve to guard against troubles while they are still slight and prevent their gradual growth is essential to achieving good government and preserving the realm. To stand in awe of the people is no excessive anxiety: it is simply that the underlying principle warrants such awe. Here truly lies the reason why our Emperor looks up to his ancestor’s example and follows in his footsteps, tirelessly solicitous morning and night, with no leisure to rest at ease.

Thus, whenever he hears reports of banditry anywhere in the realm, he immediately issues instructions to the responsible offices, directing them to devise ways to suppress it. His diligence in standing in awe of the people may well be praised. Yet among the people of Chu and Shu who have fallen into banditry, we have still heard of no prospect of their returning to settle peacefully in their home communities. This surely has no other cause than the absence, among subordinate officials, of men who stand in awe of the people. Famines follow one upon another, yet these officials remain complacent and pay no heed. Even when there is not a single grain in reserve, they inflate the figures for grain collected and distributed. Clerks and runners use inspections as a pretext to pursue schemes of predatory exploitation. How can the people avoid falling into banditry?

The best course now is to seek suitable men: men like Gong Sui in Bohai, who treated the people leniently, governing as one would untangle knotted threads; or Zhang Gang in Guangling, who won their submission through the sincerity he demonstrated by going among them in a lone carriage. Then swords could be turned into ploughs and hoes. Would this not suffice to relieve the Emperor’s anxiety over banditry?

Whenever he hears of the threat of flood or drought anywhere in the realm, he immediately issues instructions to the responsible offices, directing them to deliberate on measures to avert disaster. His earnestness in standing in awe of the people may well be praised. Yet concerning the people in the Suzhou and Songjiang region who have suffered from flooding, we have still not heard …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
其無凍餒田野之憂是亦非有他故也良
由下無畏民之吏變異屢見漫不知省禱
神祈請應行故事而初無感格之誠徵科
輸發仍行督責而初無矜恤之意民安得
不傷於水潦乎為今之計莫若求其人如
富弼之在京東勸民出粟以活飢民洪皓
之在秀州鎖截綱運以濟流冗則可變災
沴為豐穰矣豈不足以紓
皇上憂水旱之念哉雖然此非其本也若論其
本則又在於
君民一體上下交孚澤必下究情必上通寬恤
之令行矣不視之為虛文蠲貸之
詔頒矣不應之以故事實心必存於中實政
必達於外如此則即古所謂養民如子蓋
之如天容之如地而民之愛戴亦將如赤
子之於慈母戀戀然而不忍去惟見其可
愛不見其可畏矣雖時有盜賊水旱之警
亦奚足為吾慮哉謹對

punctuated: 其無凍餒田野之憂。是亦非有他故也，良由下無畏民之吏，變異屢見，漫不知省；禱神祈請，應行故事，而初無感格之誠；徵科輸發，仍行督責，而初無矜恤之意。民安得不傷於水潦乎？為今之計，莫若求其人，如富弼之在京東，勸民出粟以活飢民；洪皓之在秀州，鎖截綱運以濟流冗，則可變災沴為豐穰矣。豈不足以紓皇上憂水旱之念哉？雖然，此非其本也。若論其本，則又在於君民一體，上下交孚，澤必下究，情必上通。寬恤之令行矣，不視之為虛文；蠲貸之詔頒矣，不應之以故事。實心必存於中，實政必達於外。如此，則即古所謂養民如子，蓋之如天，容之如地，而民之愛戴亦將如赤子之於慈母，戀戀然而不忍去，惟見其可愛，不見其可畏矣。雖時有盜賊水旱之警，亦奚足為吾慮哉？謹對。
translation_en:
…that they are free from the fear of freezing and starving in the fields. This, too, has no other cause: it is precisely because there are no officials below who stand in awe of the people. Anomalies repeatedly appear, yet they carelessly fail to examine themselves. In praying and making supplications to the spirits, they merely perform the customary observances, without any sincerity capable of moving the divine powers. In levying taxes and exacting deliveries, they continue to press their demands, without any intention of showing compassion or providing relief. How, then, could the people escape suffering from floods? The best course now would be to seek suitable men: men like Fu Bi in Jingdong, who urged the people to contribute grain to keep the hungry alive, or Hong Hao in Xiuzhou, who intercepted grain convoys to aid displaced and destitute people. Then calamity could be turned into abundance. Would this not suffice to ease Your Majesty’s concern over floods and droughts?

Even so, this is not the foundation. If we consider the foundation, it lies in ruler and people forming one body, with mutual trust between those above and those below. Beneficence must reach down to the people, and their circumstances and feelings must be communicated upward. When orders for leniency and relief are put into effect, they must not be treated as empty words; when edicts granting remissions and relief loans are promulgated, they must not be met with mere routine observances. A sincere heart must reside within, and substantive measures of government must be carried out in practice. This would realize what the ancients called nurturing the people as one’s children, sheltering them as Heaven does, and embracing them as Earth does. The people’s love and allegiance would likewise resemble an infant’s attachment to its loving mother: so deeply attached that they could not bear to leave. We would see only how lovable they are, not how fearsome. Though alarms over bandits, floods, and droughts might arise from time to time, how could these give us cause for anxiety? Respectfully submitted in reply.

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第三問
紫太
同考試官教諭王批據程朱之言辨諸子之
是非得失至於論兼愛一事又能發儒先未言之蘊
其亦所謂善學者矣
同考試官教諭蔡批文中子之僭經及韓昌
黎之孔墨並論作者皆知議其失至其所論孔墨同處
則鮮有辨者此作獨能舉其言而折之然後曉然明其
所以爲異而朱紫之辨不容混矣豈孟子所謂聖人之
===
徒者與
考試官侍讀李批墨子之道與孔子不相爲謀若
文中子則慕聖人而失之僭者此篇既各議其失而抑
揚輕重行乎其間可謂審於權度者矣
考試官侍讀學士蔣批河汾墨翟事據先儒定說斷之
況文勢嚴整讀之可敬非博學高識者安能有是哉
據淺見以擬聖學者君子斥其僭肆橫議
以背聖道者君子正其非斥其爲僭則不
可比而同也正其爲非則不可推而附也

punctuated:
第三問

紫太

同考試官教諭王批：據程朱之言，辨諸子之是非得失。至於論兼愛一事，又能發儒先未言之蘊，其亦所謂善學者矣。

同考試官教諭蔡批：文中子之僭經及韓昌黎之孔墨並論，作者皆知議其失。至其所論孔墨同處，則鮮有辨者。此作獨能舉其言而折之，然後曉然明其所以爲異，而朱紫之辨不容混矣。豈孟子所謂聖人之徒者與？

考試官侍讀李批：墨子之道與孔子不相爲謀。若文中子，則慕聖人而失之僭者。此篇既各議其失，而抑揚輕重行乎其間，可謂審於權度者矣。

考試官侍讀學士蔣批：河汾、墨翟事，據先儒定說斷之。況文勢嚴整，讀之可敬，非博學高識者安能有是哉？

據淺見以擬聖學者，君子斥其僭；肆橫議以背聖道者，君子正其非。斥其爲僭，則不可比而同也；正其爲非，則不可推而附也。
translation_en:
Third Question

Zi Tai [?; the name or heading appears garbled]

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: Drawing on the words of Cheng and Zhu, this essay distinguishes the rights and wrongs, strengths and failings of the various masters. In discussing impartial love, it also brings out implications that earlier Confucian scholars had not articulated. Its author may indeed be called one who knows how to learn.

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: Writers all know to criticize Master Wenzhong’s presumptuous imitation of the Classics and Han Changli’s treatment of Confucius and Mozi together. Yet few distinguish the errors in his assertions about what Confucius and Mozi shared. This essay alone can cite his words and refute them, then clearly explain how the two differ, so that vermilion and purple—the orthodox and the spurious—cannot be confused. Might its author be what Mencius called a follower of the sage?

Comment by Examiner Li, Reader-in-Waiting: Mozi’s Way and that of Confucius admit of no common counsel. Master Wenzhong, by contrast, admired the sage but erred through presumption. This essay discusses the failings of each, while judiciously apportioning praise and blame and weighing their gravity. Its author may be said to exercise careful judgment in weighing and measuring.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Reader-in-Waiting Academician: The matters concerning the master of He and Fen [Wang Tong] and Mo Di are judged according to the established conclusions of earlier Confucian scholars. Moreover, the writing is disciplined and orderly, commanding respect as one reads it. How could anyone without broad learning and lofty discernment achieve this?

When someone relies on shallow insights to emulate the learning of the sage, the gentleman condemns his presumption; when someone indulges in reckless arguments that contravene the Way of the sage, the gentleman corrects his errors. To condemn the former’s presumption means that he cannot be compared with the sage and treated as his equal; to correct the latter’s errors means that he cannot be commended and associated with the sage.

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
此墨子之橫議所以得罪於名教而文中
子之僭擬孔子其不知量亦甚矣哉大哉
孔子之聖開闢以來所未有也夷尹不敢
比其德堯舜不能擬其功而况於他人乎
夫何隋之王通講學河汾偃然有自擬之
意一時學者翕然以聖人歸之故其自言
曰紹宣尼之事業吾不得讓而董常之尊
其師也則曰仲尼没而文在兹其師弟子
之間僭妄極矣噫通之學非無可觀也然
===
其於聖人之道僅識其用而未嘗深探其
本由孔門視之殆未能升其堂者而敢以
之自擬乎彼見夫子之述六經也以為後
之六經舍我其誰於是乎續書以存漢晉
之實續詩以辨六代之俗脩元經以斷南
北之疑賛周易以申先師之旨正禮樂以
旌後王之失凡以擬諸孔子之制作云爾
今其遺編雖不可見然考之中說而可知
其槩也其謂續詩之化猶先王之有□□

此墨子之橫議所以得罪於名教而文中
子之僭擬孔子其不知量亦甚矣哉夫哉
孔子之聖開闢以來所未有也夷尹不敢
比其德堯舜不能擬其功而況於他人乎
夫何隋之王通講學河汾偃然有自儗之
意一時學者翕然以聖人歸之故其自言
曰紹宣尼之事業吾不得讓而董常之尊
其師也則曰仲尼沒而文在茲其師弟子
之間僭妄極矣噫通之學非無可觀也然
===
其於聖人之道僅識其用而未嘗深探其
本由孔門視之殆未能升其堂者而敢以
之自擬乎彼見夫子之述六經也以為後
之六經舍我其誰於是乎續書以存漢晉
之實續詩以辨六代之俗脩元經以斷南
北之疑贊周易以申先師之旨正禮樂以
旌後王之失凡以擬諸孔子之制作云爾
今其遺編雖不可見然考之中說而可知
其槩也其謂續詩之化猶先王之□□
punctuated: 此墨子之橫議所以得罪於名教，而文中子之僭擬孔子，其不知量亦甚矣哉！大哉，孔子之聖！開闢以來所未有也。夷尹不敢比其德，堯舜不能擬其功，而况於他人乎？夫何隋之王通講學河汾，偃然有自擬之意，一時學者翕然以聖人歸之？故其自言曰：「紹宣尼之事業，吾不得讓。」而董常之尊其師也，則曰：「仲尼没而文在兹。」其師弟子之間僭妄極矣！噫！通之學非無可觀也，然其於聖人之道僅識其用，而未嘗深探其本。由孔門視之，殆未能升其堂者，而敢以之自擬乎？彼見夫子之述六經也，以為後之六經，舍我其誰？於是乎續書以存漢晉之實，續詩以辨六代之俗，脩元經以斷南北之疑，賛周易以申先師之旨，正禮樂以旌後王之失，凡以擬諸孔子之制作云爾。今其遺編雖不可見，然考之中說而可知其槩也。其謂續詩之化猶先王之有□□
translation_en:
…This is why Mozi’s unrestrained arguments offended the moral teaching upheld by the established social order; as for Wenzhongzi’s presumptuous comparison of himself to Kongzi, how utterly he failed to know his own limits! Great indeed was Kongzi’s sagehood! Since the beginning of the world, there had been nothing like it. Bo Yi and Yi Yin dared not compare their virtue with his; Yao and Shun could not match his achievements. How much less could anyone else? Why, then, did Wang Tong of the Sui dynasty, lecturing in the He and Fen region, complacently entertain the idea of equating himself with him, while scholars of the time unanimously acclaimed him as a sage? He himself therefore said, “In carrying on the work of Xuanni [Kongzi], I cannot yield to anyone.” Dong Chang, in honoring his teacher, said, “Zhongni [Kongzi] is gone, but his cultural legacy is here.” The presumption and delusion shared by this teacher and his disciples had reached an extreme!

Alas! Tong’s learning was not without merit. Yet of the Way of the sage, he recognized only its practical applications and had never deeply explored its foundation. Viewed from the school of Kongzi, he had scarcely even ascended its hall; how could he dare compare himself with the sage? Seeing that the Master had transmitted the Six Classics, he thought, “Who but I can produce the Six Classics for later ages?” Accordingly, he continued the Book of Documents to preserve the historical realities of the Han and Jin; continued the Book of Odes to distinguish the customs of the Six Dynasties; compiled the Classic of the Primal Principle (Yuanjing) to settle disputed questions concerning the Northern and Southern dynasties; elucidated the Changes of Zhou to expound the intentions of the former teacher; and rectified rites and music to expose the failings of later rulers. All this was simply intended to emulate Kongzi’s literary and institutional work. Although his surviving writings can no longer be seen, their general outlines can be understood by examining the Central Discourses (Zhongshuo). He says that the transforming influence of his Continuation of the Odes is like the former kings’ possession of [two illegible characters]…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
詩之政猶列國之有風則其自比於夫□
之刪詩明矣又曰春秋作而典誥絕元經
興而帝制亡則其自比於夫子之春秋而
書亦在其中矣然高文武宣之制豈有精
一執中之傳書何為而續也曹劉沈謝之
詩豈有物則秉彛之訓詩何為而續也其
所賛之易於先天後天體用之妙何在其
所述之禮樂視伯夷后夔周公之懿何如
至於宋魏而下南北並峙校功度德未有
===
以相君臣也則其天命人心之向背統緒
繼承之偏正亦何足論而必欲奪彼予此
以自列於孔子之春秋哉此通之僭妄所
以見闢於朱子而直謂其不足以供兒童
之一戲則其斥之也深矣若夫孟子之於
墨翟一則責其無父二則惡其賊道距之
何嚴也而昌黎韓子乃有孔墨相用之說
謂孔子畏大人不非其邦之大夫春秋譏
□□之尚同汎愛親仁以博施濟衆□

繼承之倫正亦何足論而必欲奪彼予此
以自列於孔子之春秋哉此通之僭妄所
以見闢於朱子而直謂其不足以供兒童
之一戲則其斥之也深矣若夫荀子之於
墨翟一則責其無父二則惡其賊道距之
何嚴也而昌黎韓子乃有孔墨相用之說
謂孔子畏大人不非其邦之大夫春秋譏
□之尚同汎愛親仁以博施濟衆
punctuated:
詩之政猶列國之有風，則其自比於夫□之刪詩明矣。又曰：「春秋作而典誥絕，元經興而帝制亡。」則其自比於夫子之春秋，而書亦在其中矣。然高文武宣之制，豈有精一執中之傳？書何為而續也？曹劉沈謝之詩，豈有物則秉彛之訓？詩何為而續也？其所賛之易，於先天後天體用之妙何在？其所述之禮樂，視伯夷后夔周公之懿何如？至於宋魏而下，南北並峙，校功度德，未有以相君臣也。則其天命人心之向背、統緒繼承之偏正，亦何足論，而必欲奪彼予此，以自列於孔子之春秋哉？此通之僭妄所以見闢於朱子，而直謂其不足以供兒童之一戲，則其斥之也深矣。
若夫孟子之於墨翟，一則責其無父，二則惡其賊道，距之何嚴也！而昌黎韓子乃有孔墨相用之說，謂孔子畏大人，不非其邦之大夫，春秋譏□□之尚同；汎愛親仁，以博施濟衆□
translation_en:
…the governance expressed in the poems was like the Airs of the various states. Thus it is clear that he compared himself to the Master's [?] editing of the Book of Odes. He also said: “When the Spring and Autumn Annals was composed, the Canonical Documents and Announcements ceased; when the Fundamental Classic (Yuan jing) arose, imperial institutions perished.” Thus he compared his work to the Master's Spring and Autumn Annals, and the Book of Documents was also implicated in this comparison.
Yet did the institutions of Emperors Gao, Wen, Wu, and Xuan contain the transmission of being refined and single-minded and holding fast to the mean? Why, then, continue the Book of Documents? Did the poems of Cao, Liu, Shen, and Xie contain the teaching that things have their governing norms and that people hold to their constant nature? Why, then, continue the Book of Odes? In his elucidation of the Book of Changes, where are the subtleties of what precedes Heaven and what follows Heaven, of substance and function? How do his writings on rites and music compare with the excellence of Bo Yi, Hou Kui, and the Duke of Zhou? From the Song and Wei onward, the southern and northern regimes stood opposed. Judging their achievements and weighing their virtue, there was no basis for making one sovereign and the other subject. What grounds, then, were there to discuss which enjoyed or lost Heaven's mandate and the people's allegiance, or which succession was partial or legitimate? Why insist on denying legitimacy to one and granting it to the other, thereby placing oneself alongside Confucius's Spring and Autumn Annals? This presumptuousness and recklessness of Tong was why Master Zhu repudiated him. Indeed, he declared that Tong's work was not sufficient to furnish even a single amusement for children: his condemnation was severe indeed.
As for Mengzi's treatment of Mo Di, on the one hand he reproached him for denying the claims of fatherhood, and on the other he detested him for harming the Way. How sternly he opposed him! Yet Master Han of Changli advanced the claim that Confucius and Mo Di drew upon one another. He said that Confucius stood in awe of great men and did not criticize the great officers of his own state; that the Spring and Autumn Annals censured [two illegible characters] in connection with “exalting conformity” [?]; and that Confucius loved all broadly and drew close to the humane, and took extending benefits widely and aiding the multitude [illegible character] …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
為聖猶墨之兼愛以四科進褒弟子疾沒
世而名不稱猶墨之尚賢有祭如在之誠
有祭則受福之語猶墨之明鬼韓子之所
以推墨而附於孔子者其說如此然謂墨
之尚賢明鬼有合於孔子者猶之可也謂
孔子尚同兼愛與墨子同則謬甚矣自今
觀之孔子之畏大人不非其邦之大夫乃
用下敬上之義而其所以譏專臣者則至
公之道存焉夫豈同乎流俗者哉孔子之
===
汎愛博濟乃一視同仁之心而其所謂親
仁者則親疎之别在焉夫豈愛無差等者
哉盖聖人之道匪立異也而不主於苟同
聖人之愛無不周也而不容以混施乃槩
以尚同兼愛目之不亦謬乎程子謂退之
斯言有樂取人善之心而失之持教不嚴
誠哉是言也使韓子之說行得無立異端
之赤幟乎夫孔墨之殊固不待辨而言出
於退之則有可疑者退之嘗作原道以闢

有祭則受福之語猶墨之明鬼韓子之所

===
汎愛博濟乃一視同仁之心而其所謂親
仁者則親疎之別在焉夫豈愛無差等者
哉蓋聖人之道雖並立異也而不主於苟同
聖人之愛無不周也而不容以混施乃槩
以尚同兼愛目之不亦謬乎程子謂退之
斯言有樂取人善之心而失之持敎不嚴
誠哉是言也使韓子之說行得無立異端
之亦懺乎夫孔墨之殊固不待辨而言出
於退之則有可疑者退之嘗作原道以抑
punctuated: 為聖，猶墨之兼愛；以四科進褒弟子，疾沒世而名不稱，猶墨之尚賢；有祭如在之誠，有祭則受福之語，猶墨之明鬼。韓子之所以推墨而附於孔子者，其說如此。然謂墨之尚賢、明鬼有合於孔子者，猶之可也；謂孔子尚同、兼愛與墨子同，則謬甚矣。自今觀之，孔子之畏大人、不非其邦之大夫，乃用下敬上之義，而其所以譏專臣者，則至公之道存焉。夫豈同乎流俗者哉？孔子之汎愛博濟，乃一視同仁之心，而其所謂親仁者，則親疎之别在焉。夫豈愛無差等者哉？盖聖人之道匪立異也，而不主於苟同；聖人之愛無不周也，而不容以混施。乃槩以尚同、兼愛目之，不亦謬乎？程子謂退之斯言有樂取人善之心，而失之持教不嚴。誠哉，是言也！使韓子之說行，得無立異端之赤幟乎？夫孔墨之殊，固不待辨，而言出於退之，則有可疑者。退之嘗作《原道》，以闢
translation_en:
…constitutes sagehood, resembling Mozi’s impartial care; his advancing and commending disciples under four categories, and his concern that one’s name might go unrecognized after death, resemble Mozi’s exalting the worthy; his sincerity in sacrificing as though the spirits were present, and his statement that sacrifice brings blessings, resemble Mozi’s elucidation of ghosts. Such were Master Han’s arguments for commending Mozi and aligning him with Confucius. Yet to say that Mozi’s exalting the worthy and elucidating ghosts accord in some respects with Confucius is still permissible; to say that Confucius upheld conformity and impartial care in the same way as Mozi is profoundly mistaken.

Viewed from our present standpoint, Confucius’s awe of great men and his refusal to criticize the grandees of his own state embody the principle that those below should respect those above. His criticism of ministers who monopolized power, however, preserves the Way of utmost impartiality. How could this amount to conforming to vulgar custom? Confucius’s universal care and extensive assistance express a heart that regards all with equal benevolence; yet his injunction to draw close to the benevolent preserves distinctions between the close and the distant. How could this be love without gradations? The sage’s Way does not seek to establish differences, but neither does it advocate indiscriminate agreement. The sage’s love encompasses everyone, but neither does it permit affection to be bestowed without distinction. Is it not mistaken to characterize these wholesale as conformity and impartial care?

Master Cheng said that these words of Tuizhi [Han Yu] showed a willingness to recognize goodness in others, but erred in failing to uphold the teaching rigorously. How true these words are! Were Master Han’s account to gain currency, would it not raise the red banner of heterodoxy? The distinction between Confucius and Mozi certainly needs no argument to establish it; yet because these words came from Tuizhi, they give grounds for perplexity. Tuizhi once wrote An Inquiry into the Way (Yuan dao) in order to refute…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
邪崇正為已任又嘗推尊孟氏闢楊墨之
功以為不在禹下矣今乃儕墨於孔子何
其言之自相牴牾若是邪蓋由其因文以
見道而無身體力行之學故其論道也或
明於此而不明於彼其語聖也或知其一
而不知其二無惑乎其言之失也意者讀
墨之篇乃其少作而原道之著尊孟之言
則其晚年所自得乎不然何一人之身而
向背之頓殊也今夫學不可不慎也墨子
===
蓋學為仁者而毫釐之差其流遂至於無
父不有孟子起而攻之則世之墮其術者
將接迹於後矣若文中子則庶乎知道者
也程子固嘗稱其極有格言矣採其言之
善者而用之則亦豈不足為身心之助顧
不可安於小成而以之自處耳管見如斯
未知是否惟與其進也而教之幸甚
第四問
王遵

則其晚年所自得乎不然何一人之身而

不可安於小成而以之自處耳管見如斯
未知是否惟與其進也而教之幸甚
王遵
第四問
punctuated:
邪、崇正為已任，又嘗推尊孟氏闢楊墨之功，以為不在禹下矣。今乃儕墨於孔子，何其言之自相牴牾若是邪？蓋由其因文以見道，而無身體力行之學，故其論道也，或明於此而不明於彼；其語聖也，或知其一而不知其二，無惑乎其言之失也。意者《讀墨》之篇乃其少作，而《原道》之著、尊孟之言，則其晚年所自得乎？不然，何一人之身而向背之頓殊也？今夫學不可不慎也。墨子蓋學為仁者，而毫釐之差，其流遂至於無父。不有孟子起而攻之，則世之墮其術者將接迹於後矣。若文中子，則庶乎知道者也。程子固嘗稱其極有格言矣。採其言之善者而用之，則亦豈不足為身心之助？顧不可安於小成而以之自處耳。管見如斯，未知是否，惟與其進也而教之，幸甚。

第四問
王遵
translation_en:
…refuting heterodoxy and upholding orthodoxy as his own responsibility. He also exalted Mengzi’s achievement in refuting Yang Zhu and Mozi, judging it no less than that of Yu. Yet now he places Mozi alongside Kongzi. How can his words contradict one another so greatly? This is because he sought to perceive the Way through literary composition, without the learning that comes from personally embodying it and vigorously putting it into practice. Thus, when discussing the Way, he sometimes understood one aspect but not another; when speaking of the sages, he sometimes knew one part but not the other. It is no wonder that his statements went astray. Perhaps his essay Reading Mozi (Du Mo) was a youthful composition, while his Inquiry into the Way (Yuan Dao) and his words honoring Mengzi expressed insights he attained in his later years? Otherwise, how could one person’s allegiances differ so abruptly?

Now, one cannot be too careful in learning. Mozi presumably sought through learning to become benevolent, yet a deviation of the slightest degree ultimately led his teaching to the denial of fathers. Had Mengzi not risen to attack it, those in the world who fell under its sway would have followed one another in an unbroken succession. As for Wenzhongzi, he came close to understanding the Way. Master Cheng indeed once praised him as having some excellent maxims. If one selects the good among his sayings and puts them to use, could they fail to aid the cultivation of body and mind? One must simply avoid resting content with a small achievement and making it the limit of one’s aspirations. Such is my narrow view; I do not know whether it is correct. I would be most fortunate if you would approve my efforts to advance and instruct me.

Fourth Question
Wang Zun

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導陸批治道一策能悉東萊之
說以訂隋漢宋諸君反覆辯論意尤懇至其識蓋加於
人一等矣
同考試官教諭耿批此策於民財民力民情
盡不盡處敷演詳悉斷制明白蓋士之積學而有識者
考試官侍讀朱批策有考慮有斟酌有議論非識
學兼備者不能及此
考試官侍講學士蔣批東萊所以論漢事者具有成說
此策能悉之且又引而論宋事尤得東萊不盡之意其
殆善於讀書而能推類者乎
===
有天下者欲建萬世不拔之業必為萬世
可繼之政使行之於我而不可以繼之於
人行之於今而不可以繼之於後則雖足
以取快於目前而終不免貽患於身後治
天下者能不去彼取此而顧以一時之快
貽無窮之患哉是故不能不用民之財也
使經費不虧足矣不敢盡其財也不能不
役民之力也使工役不乏足矣不敢盡其

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
力也不能不求民之情也使奸隱不滋矣
美不敢盡其情也是三者非不可盡也可
盡也而不可繼故不忍於盡也使可盡也
而又可繼焉則盡之可也然既盡矣必不
可以繼可一而不可再也是徇目前者之
計也非長顧却慮以為其子孫之計也彼
治天下者豈苟為目前之計而已哉固將
為子孫千萬世之計也欲為子孫千萬世
之計而於財於力於情皆使之不可繼焉
===

繼以供吾子孫無窮之用乎此東萊呂氏
所以有慨於宋之神宗而因追慕乎仁宗
故因論漢之文帝而深致憾於武帝豈不
以文帝仁宗之所為為有合於此乎觀夫

謂不敢輕用天下之財矣若夫帷帝衾裯

然恐民財之或匱也匈奴三入而三拒之

translation_en:
…their strength. Nor can one refrain from inquiring into the people's circumstances: it is enough to prevent concealed wrongdoing from proliferating; one dare not probe their circumstances exhaustively [the character 美 here is doubtful]. These three things are not incapable of being exhausted. They can be exhausted, but then cannot be sustained; thus one cannot bear to exhaust them. If they could be exhausted and yet sustained, then exhausting them would be permissible. Once exhausted, however, they necessarily cannot be sustained: it can be done once, but not again. This is a scheme that serves the immediate moment, not one that looks far ahead and deliberates deeply on behalf of one's descendants. How could those who govern the realm merely plan for the immediate moment? Surely they intend to plan for their descendants through countless generations. If they wish to plan for their descendants through countless generations, yet render wealth, strength, and the inquiry into people's circumstances alike unsustainable, would it not be better to leave what remains with the people, allowing it to flow forth in an unbroken succession to supply the endless needs of our descendants?
This is why Master Lü of Donglai lamented the conduct of Emperor Shenzong of the Song and consequently looked back with admiration upon Emperor Renzong; hence, in discussing Emperor Wen of the Han, he expressed profound regret over Emperor Wu. Was this not because he considered the actions of Emperor Wen and Emperor Renzong to accord with this principle? Consider how Emperor Wen begrudged the expenditure of a hundred units of gold on the Dew Terrace, and how the women of his inner palace wore no robes that trailed upon the ground. Surely he could be said not to have dared spend the wealth of the realm lightly. As for Emperor Renzong, his curtains [?] and bedcovers were mostly made of ordinary silks; he did not demand roast lamb, being concerned lest living creatures be killed. He was ever apprehensive that the people's wealth might run short. The Xiongnu invaded three times, and Emperor Wen repelled them three times…

…he refused to exhaust his troops by sending them beyond the frontier passes. He may indeed be said not to have dared lightly to expend the strength of the realm. Likewise, when the people of Xia invaded the frontier, Renzong repelled them beyond the border; when the Khitan broke their covenant, he increased the annual tribute payments. He was ever apprehensive lest the people’s strength be exhausted. When the Prince of Wu failed to attend court, Wendi bestowed an armrest and staff upon him; when Zhang Wu accepted bribes, he bestowed further gifts to shame him. He certainly did not dare make excessive demands upon the goodwill of the realm. Likewise, Renzong denied promotion for life to those responsible for wrongly convicting someone of a capital crime, and ordered all doubtful capital cases submitted to higher authority for review. He was ever fearful lest the people be driven to extremity and their lives destroyed. In all such actions, was the intention not to leave whatever could be spared with the people, as an inexhaustible resource for his descendants?

Thus, although Wendi reigned for only twenty-three years, the tradition of magnanimity and benevolence he established could extend into the four hundred years of the Han; although Renzong reigned for only forty-two years, the tradition of benevolence and generosity he established could extend into the three hundred years of the Song. Had Wendi been followed by successors like himself, the Han might well have survived even to the present day. Had Renzong been followed by successors like himself, the Song too might well have survived even to the present day. text:
財於力於情皆無不盡焉者矣以武帝之
雄才使不雜於多慾則亦何至是哉仁宗
再傳而為神宗散青苗錢立手實法而利
路開以王韶經略熈河以章惇經略荆湖
而邊釁啓置大理獄置京城邏卒而法網
密則於財於力於情亦無不盡焉者矣以
神宗之勵精使不誤於安石則亦何至此
哉此文帝仁宗所以為漢宋守成之賢君
而非武帝神宗之所能及也然則後之有
===
天下者可不以文帝仁宗為法而以武帝
神宗為戒乎方今
聖明在上節用愛人省刑薄斂方將法堯舜三
王以為治彼漢宋二君固不足為
今日道然
聖不自聖則在二君者寧能無一二足以上契
聖心者乎有以契之則必思有以行之草茅微
賤之臣又何足以知之哉執事幸恕其狂
瞽而進之

財、於力、於情，皆無不盡焉者矣。以武帝之雄才，使不雜於多慾，則亦何至是哉？仁宗再傳而為神宗，散青苗錢，立手實法，而利路開；以王韶經略熈河，以章惇經略荆湖，而邊釁啓；置大理獄，置京城邏卒，而法網密。則於財、於力、於情，亦無不盡焉者矣。以神宗之勵精，使不誤於安石，則亦何至此哉？此文帝、仁宗所以為漢、宋守成之賢君，而非武帝、神宗之所能及也。然則後之有天下者，可不以文帝、仁宗為法，而以武帝、神宗為戒乎？
方今聖明在上，節用愛人，省刑薄斂，方將法堯、舜、三王以為治。彼漢、宋二君，固不足為今日道。然聖不自聖，則在二君者，寧能無一二足以上契聖心者乎？有以契之，則必思有以行之。草茅微賤之臣，又何足以知之哉？執事幸恕其狂瞽而進之。
translation_en:
…in wealth, in strength, and in feeling, the people were utterly exhausted. With Emperor Wu’s extraordinary talents, had he not mingled them with excessive desires, how could matters have reached this point? Two successions after Emperor Renzong came Emperor Shenzong. He distributed Green Sprouts loan funds and instituted the Personal Declaration Law for reporting property, opening avenues for profit-seeking. He employed Wang Shao to conduct frontier operations in Xihe and Zhang Dun to conduct frontier operations in Jinghu, provoking border hostilities. He established a prison under the Court of Judicial Review and patrol troops in the capital, tightening the net of the law. Thus, in wealth, in strength, and in feeling, the people were likewise utterly exhausted. Given Emperor Shenzong’s determined efforts, had he not been misled by Anshi, how could matters have reached this point? This is why Emperor Wen and Emperor Renzong were worthy rulers who preserved the achievements of the Han and Song dynasties, and why Emperor Wu and Emperor Shenzong could not equal them. Should not those who subsequently rule the realm take Emperor Wen and Emperor Renzong as their models, and Emperor Wu and Emperor Shenzong as their warnings?
Today our sage and enlightened sovereign reigns above, exercising economy and cherishing the people, reducing punishments and lightening taxation. He is now taking Yao, Shun, and the Three Kings as models for his government. Those two rulers of Han and Song are certainly unworthy of mention in speaking of the present day. Yet a sage does not regard himself as a sage: could there not be one or two things about those two rulers worthy of finding accord with the imperial mind? If something does find such accord, he will surely consider putting it into practice. But how could a humble and lowly servant from the countryside presume to know this? May you, sir, kindly pardon my rashness and blindness and advance this submission.

text:
第五問
孫繼先
同考試官教諭姚批此策正欲觀士子格物
窮理之學是卷條荅不遺而評品是非確有定見且篇
末數語特為三君子詳辨尤見待人之恕與善之公其
亦知言之士乎
考試官侍讀朱批論古昔人物賢否事理得失瞭
然如指諸掌可以見窮理之學矣
考試官侍讀學士蔣批品評人物一一切當策手也
===
觀人者不可以一事而盖其平生論事者
不可以平生而略其一事盖君子雖有一
眚不能揜其德然論事者亦不以其人之
賢而文之也小人雖有片善不能救其惡
然論事者亦不以其人之惡而泯之也執
此以論則人之賢否事之是非皆可得而
識矣請因明問所及而條陳之三代而下
所謂忠賢者若張子房之為人程子嘗稱
其有儒者氣象矣夫何滅項之謀背鴻溝

觀人者，不可以一事而盖其平生；論事者，不可以平生而略其一事。盖君子雖有一眚，不能揜其德，然論事者亦不以其人之賢而文之也；小人雖有片善，不能救其惡，然論事者亦不以其人之惡而泯之也。執此以論，則人之賢否、事之是非，皆可得而識矣。請因明問所及而條陳之。三代而下，所謂忠賢者，若張子房之為人，程子嘗稱其有儒者氣象矣。夫何滅項之謀，背鴻溝
translation_en:
Fifth Question
Sun Jixian

Comment by Associate Examiner Yao, Instructor: This policy question was intended precisely to examine the candidates’ learning in investigating things and fathoming principles. This paper answers every point without omission, and its judgments of right and wrong show firm convictions. Moreover, the few words at its close offer a particularly detailed defense of the three gentlemen, especially revealing the writer’s forbearance toward others and impartiality in acknowledging goodness. Surely he is a scholar who understands words!

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-Waiting: His discussion of the worthiness or otherwise of figures of antiquity, and of the merits and faults of actions and their underlying principles, is as clear as pointing to something in his own palm. Here one can see his learning in fathoming principles.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: His assessments of individuals are apt in every case. He is an accomplished writer of policy essays.

Those who judge a person must not let a single deed overshadow his entire life; those who discuss a deed must not let his entire life cause them to overlook that particular deed. Although a gentleman may have a single fault, it cannot obscure his virtue; nevertheless, those who discuss the deed must not gloss over it on account of the man’s worthiness. Although a petty man may possess some small measure of goodness, it cannot redeem his wickedness; nevertheless, those who discuss the deed must not efface it on account of the man’s wickedness. If we hold to this in our judgments, we can discern both the worthiness or otherwise of people and the right or wrong of deeds. Allow me to set these matters out point by point, following the subjects touched upon in your illuminating question.

Among those called loyal and worthy since the Three Dynasties, take Zhang Zifang as an example. Master Cheng once praised him as possessing the bearing of a Confucian scholar. Why, then, in his plan to destroy Xiang, did he betray the Honggou …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之約而不顧於理直乎斯謀也陳平寔共
之然平非子房比也故君子獨於子房而
責備焉諸葛孔明之為人程子嘗許其有
王佐之心矣夫何取蜀之事棄劉璋之好
而不恤於義得乎斯謀也法正寔倡之然
正非孔明比也故君子獨於孔明而責備
焉相業如崔祐甫善矣顧乃薦楊炎為同
列當時可相者不有李泌顏真卿乎而何
取於忮害用私之楊炎也相業如李泌偉
===
矣顧乃舉竇參以自代當時可相者不有
陸贄乎而何取於峭刻任數之竇參也郭
子儀之至公無我其心廓然也惜乎信吳
曜之讒而殺張曇過矣又逐高郢而箝口
焉寧免為盛德之累乎張浚之忠義自奮
其節凛然也惜乎聽吳玠之譖而誣曲端
冤矣又使康隨而甘心焉寧不致軍士之
憤乎之數公者立身之大節卓乎其可尚
而窮理之學或有未精謀國之大猷炳然

punctuated: 之約，而不顧於理直乎？斯謀也，陳平寔共之，然平非子房比也，故君子獨於子房而責備焉。諸葛孔明之為人，程子嘗許其有王佐之心矣。夫何取蜀之事，棄劉璋之好，而不恤於義得乎？斯謀也，法正寔倡之，然正非孔明比也，故君子獨於孔明而責備焉。相業如崔祐甫善矣，顧乃薦楊炎為同列。當時可相者，不有李泌、顏真卿乎？而何取於忮害用私之楊炎也？相業如李泌偉矣，顧乃舉竇參以自代。當時可相者，不有陸贄乎？而何取於峭刻任數之竇參也？郭子儀之至公無我，其心廓然也。惜乎信吳曜之讒而殺張曇，過矣！又逐高郢而箝口焉，寧免為盛德之累乎？張浚之忠義自奮，其節凛然也。惜乎聽吳玠之譖而誣曲端，冤矣！又使康隨而甘心焉，寧不致軍士之憤乎？之數公者，立身之大節，卓乎其可尚，而窮理之學或有未精；謀國之大猷，炳然
translation_en:
…the agreement at Honggou, without regard for whether his cause was right? Chen Ping indeed shared in this plan, but Ping was no equal of Zifang; thus the gentleman demands perfection of Zifang alone. As for Zhuge Kongming’s character, Master Cheng once credited him with the aspiration to assist a true king. Why, then, in taking Shu did he abandon his friendship with Liu Zhang, without concern for whether the acquisition accorded with righteousness? Fa Zheng indeed initiated this plan, but Zheng was no equal of Kongming; thus the gentleman demands perfection of Kongming alone.

Cui Youfu’s achievements as chief councilor were admirable, yet he recommended Yang Yan to serve as his colleague. Among those then fit to be chief councilor, were there not Li Mi and Yan Zhenqing? Why choose the malicious Yang Yan, who acted from private interests? Li Mi’s achievements as chief councilor were great, yet he recommended Dou Can to succeed him. Among those then fit to be chief councilor, was there not Lu Zhi? Why choose the harsh and cruel Dou Can, who relied on manipulation?

Guo Ziyi was utterly impartial and selfless, his heart broad and open. Regrettably, he believed Wu Yao’s slander and killed Zhang Tan: this was a fault! He also expelled Gao Ying and silenced him. How could this fail to blemish his abundant virtue? Zhang Jun exerted himself out of loyalty and righteousness, and his integrity inspired awe. Regrettably, he listened to Wu Jie’s slander and falsely accused Qu Duan: this was an injustice! He further employed Kang Sui to sate his resentment. How could this fail to arouse the soldiers’ indignation?

These several gentlemen [?] were outstanding and worthy of esteem in the great principles by which they conducted their lives, yet their study of the investigation of principle may not have attained full refinement; their grand plans for governing the state shone forth …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
其所觀而克已之功或有未盡故一念之
差或不協於公道一事之誤或不愜乎輿
情固不能以是而累其人也然即其一事
而論之亦安得不謂之過哉所謂小人者
若裴矩以諛佞誤隋煬罪莫大焉及其事
唐也乃能諫贓吏之誅而直以陷人於法
為不可孰謂諛佞如矩而能持此論哉盧
杞以奸邪誤德宗惡莫甚焉然其守虢也
乃能論乳豕之害而又以移患同州為不
===
可孰謂奸邪如杞而能建此議哉李義甫
之事太子獻承華之箴而以絕邪佞為言
知養正之義矣然義甫之諂得非所謂邪
佞者與王叔文之事太子因宫市之論而
以預外事為戒知為子之道矣然叔文之
譎夫豈真能輔導者與王欽若何如人也
而有蠲負釋囚之請異乎剥民奉上者矣
使其每事皆然亦何訾焉豈謂政府一入
而遂縱其惡哉丁謂何如人也而建罷兵

使其每事皆然亦何嘗焉豈謂叹府一入
而遂縱其惡哉丁謂何如人也而建罷兵
punctuated: 其所觀，而克已之功或有未盡，故一念之差，或不協於公道；一事之誤，或不愜乎輿情。固不能以是而累其人也，然即其一事而論之，亦安得不謂之過哉？所謂小人者，若裴矩以諛佞誤隋煬，罪莫大焉。及其事唐也，乃能諫贓吏之誅，而直以陷人於法為不可。孰謂諛佞如矩，而能持此論哉？盧杞以奸邪誤德宗，惡莫甚焉。然其守虢也，乃能論乳豕之害，而又以移患同州為不可。孰謂奸邪如杞，而能建此議哉？李義甫之事太子，獻承華之箴，而以絕邪佞為言，知養正之義矣。然義甫之諂，得非所謂邪佞者與？王叔文之事太子，因宫市之論，而以預外事為戒，知為子之道矣。然叔文之譎，夫豈真能輔導者與？王欽若何如人也，而有蠲負釋囚之請，異乎剥民奉上者矣。使其每事皆然，亦何訾焉？豈謂政府一入，而遂縱其惡哉？丁謂何如人也，而建罷兵
translation_en:
…in what they displayed [?], yet their efforts at self-mastery may not have been complete. Thus a single mistaken thought might fail to accord with public justice, and an error in a single undertaking might fail to satisfy public sentiment. Certainly these things alone cannot discredit the men themselves. Yet, judging that particular undertaking, how could one avoid calling it a fault?
As for those called petty men, take Pei Ju: through flattery and sycophancy he led Emperor Yang of Sui astray—no crime could be greater. Yet when he served the Tang, he could remonstrate against the execution of a corrupt official, declaring outright that entrapping someone into breaking the law was unacceptable. Who would have thought that someone as sycophantic as Ju could advance such an argument? Lu Qi led Emperor Dezong astray through treachery and wickedness—no evil could be worse. Yet when he governed Guo, he could discuss the harm caused by a sow with young [?], and further held that transferring the trouble to Tongzhou was unacceptable. Who would have thought that someone as treacherous as Qi could offer such counsel?
When Li Yifu served the crown prince, he presented the Admonition for the Crown Prince (Chenghua), speaking of cutting off wicked sycophants: he understood the principle of nurturing rectitude. Yet was not Yifu, with his own flattery, precisely one of those wicked sycophants? When Wang Shuwen served the crown prince, discussion of palace purchases led him to warn against involvement in affairs outside the palace: he understood the proper conduct of a son. Yet, deceitful as Shuwen was, could he truly have been capable of providing guidance?
What sort of man was Wang Qinruo? Yet he petitioned to remit debts and release prisoners, differing in this from those who stripped the people to supply their superiors. Had he acted thus in every undertaking, what would there have been to criticize? Who would have expected that, once admitted to the chief council, he would give free rein to his wickedness? What sort of man was Ding Wei? Yet he proposed withdrawing the troops…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
撫蠻之議異乎開邊起釁者矣使其終身
若此亦何責焉孰知相位一得而遂肆其
奸哉之數人者雖立心之頗僻也而其才
則有可用雖制行之汗下也而其識則有
可取故一言之善或合乎天理之公一行
之美或得乎君子之道固不能以是而許
其人也然即其一事而論之亦安得不謂
之善哉抑小人之善固無足深論矣而明
問所指諸賢之過則其中蓋有不可盡非
===
者何則子房之出本以為韓項羽不滅則
韓成之讐不可復蓋自間行歸漢之日固
已蓄是念矣至是而始快其忿耳孔明之
出將以扶漢益州不取則興復之業無所
資蓋自昭烈枉駕之時固已定斯計矣至
是而始成其謀耳二公之過其孔子所謂
觀過知仁者乎郭子儀之為人其責己也
厚其待人也恕惟張曇高郢之事乃其終
身之一失耳然其因僚佐之求去而悉薦

韓成之讐不可復蓋自間行歸漢之日固
已蓄是念矣至是而始快其忿耳孔明之
出將以扶漢益州不取則興復之業無所
資蓋自昭烈枉駕之時固已定斯計矣至
是而始成其謀耳二公之過其孔子所謂
觀過知仁者乎郭子儀之爲人其責已也
厚其待人也恕惟張曇高郢之事乃莫終
身之一失耳然其因僚佐之求去而悉薦
punctuated:
撫蠻之議，異乎開邊起釁者矣。使其終身若此，亦何責焉？孰知相位一得，而遂肆其奸哉！之數人者，雖立心之頗僻也，而其才則有可用；雖制行之汗下也，而其識則有可取。故一言之善，或合乎天理之公；一行之美，或得乎君子之道。固不能以是而許其人也，然即其一事而論之，亦安得不謂之善哉？抑小人之善，固無足深論矣，而明問所指諸賢之過，則其中蓋有不可盡非者。何則？

子房之出，本以為韓，項羽不滅，則韓成之讐不可復。蓋自間行歸漢之日，固已蓄是念矣，至是而始快其忿耳。孔明之出，將以扶漢，益州不取，則興復之業無所資。蓋自昭烈枉駕之時，固已定斯計矣，至是而始成其謀耳。二公之過，其孔子所謂觀過知仁者乎？

郭子儀之為人，其責己也厚，其待人也恕，惟張曇、高郢之事，乃其終身之一失耳。然其因僚佐之求去而悉薦
translation_en:
…the proposal to pacify the non-Han peoples differed from the conduct of those who expanded the frontiers and provoked hostilities. Had he acted thus throughout his life, what grounds would there have been to reproach him? Who could have known that, once he secured the position of chief councilor, he would give free rein to his treachery? These several men, although perverse in their intentions, possessed talents that could be put to use; although their conduct was base [?], their judgment had something to recommend it. Thus a good utterance might accord with the impartiality of Heaven’s principle, and an admirable deed might conform to the Way of the gentleman. Certainly one cannot endorse the man on this basis; yet, judging that particular deed alone, how could one deny that it was good? Still, the good deeds of petty men scarcely merit extended discussion. As for the faults of the worthy men identified in your discerning question, some cannot be condemned outright. Why is this?

When Zifang entered public life, his original purpose was to serve Han: unless Xiang Yu were destroyed, the wrong done to Han Cheng could not be avenged. From the day he traveled by a secret route to join the Han side, he had already harbored this intention; only at this point did he finally satisfy his indignation. When Kongming entered public life, his purpose was to support the Han dynasty: unless Yizhou were taken, the undertaking of restoring the dynasty would have no resources on which to draw. From the time Zhaolie condescended to visit him, he had already settled upon this plan; only at this point did he finally accomplish it. Might the faults of these two men exemplify what Confucius meant by discerning a person’s humaneness through observing his faults?

As a man, Guo Ziyi was exacting toward himself and forgiving toward others. Only the affair involving Zhang Tan and Gao Ying constituted a single lapse in his entire life. Yet, when his staff members requested leave to depart, he recommended them all…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之悟吳曜之誤已而遽逐之不旋踵而反
其所為何其改之易也郭公之過其孟子
所謂如日月之食者乎程子有言君子當
於有過中求無過仁夫大賢之用心也愚
也敢誦斯言而為三君子折焉
alt_text:
之悟吳曜之誤已而遽逐之不旋踵而反
其所爲何其改之易也郭公之過其孟子
所謂如日月之食者乎程子有言君子當
於有過中求無過仁夫大賢之用心也愚

punctuated: 之，悟吳曜之誤已而遽逐之，不旋踵而反其所為，何其改之易也！郭公之過，其孟子所謂「如日月之食」者乎？程子有言：「君子當於有過中求無過。」仁夫，大賢之用心也！愚也敢誦斯言，而為三君子折焉。
translation_en: …them all for recommendation; when he realized that Wu Yao had misled him [?], he promptly dismissed him. Without so much as turning on his heel, he reversed what he had done. How readily he corrected himself! Were Lord Guo’s faults not what Mencius described as “like eclipses of the sun and moon”? Master Cheng said: “A gentleman should seek freedom from faults amid his faults.” How humane is the intention of a great worthy! In my humble ignorance, I venture to recite these words and thereby render a judgment on the three gentlemen.

punctuated:
應天府鄉試錄後序

我太祖高皇帝定鼎金陵，以江之南北為畿甸，聲教所被，獨先天下。士生於斯者，其漸摩培養之功有自来矣。

列聖相承，至我皇上，文明之化，萬方攸同。而南畿之内，由漸摩培養之最久者，其化之浹也滋甚，故人才莫盛焉。乃正德庚午，式當鄉試之期，臣冕暨臣希周寔欽承
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Our Emperor Taizu Gao established his capital at Jinling, making the lands north and south of the Yangzi the metropolitan domain. In receiving his civilizing influence and instruction, this region preceded all others under Heaven. The work of gradually educating and nurturing scholars born here thus has a long history.

Successive sage emperors carried on this legacy down to our present emperor, whose civilizing influence extends alike to every region. Within the Southern Metropolitan Region, however, where this gradual education and cultivation have continued longest, that influence has penetrated all the more deeply. Hence nowhere are men of talent more abundant. Now, in the gengwu year of Zhengde [1510], the appointed time for the Provincial Examination arrived. Your servants Mian and Xizhou reverently received …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
上命職應天試事竊念臣昔嘗就
試于兹目覩人才之盛若駑
駘之處于冀北之羣未嘗不
自歎也乃今謬膺校選之任
視今之人才則又盛於昔所
見者顧臣之愚何足以甄别
之哉則惟夙夜戰兢竭力從
===
事必求無遺才以為慊然才
之可取者何限而
制額弗敢過也故不難於取而
難於去其有欲取而不能欲
去而不忍者必為之校閲數
四不得已而置焉試事既竣
然後列中式者氏名及其文

上命職應天試事竊念臣昔嘗親
試于茲目覩人才之盛若駑
駘之處于冀北之羣未嘗不
自歎也乃今謬膺校選之任
視今之人才則又盛於昔所
見者顧臣之愚何足以甄別
之哉則惟夙夜戰兢竭力從

四不得已而置焉試事既竣

punctuated: 上命，職應天試事。竊念臣昔嘗就試于兹，目覩人才之盛，若駑駘之處于冀北之羣，未嘗不自歎也。乃今謬膺校選之任，視今之人才，則又盛於昔所見者。顧臣之愚，何足以甄别之哉？則惟夙夜戰兢，竭力從事，必求無遺才，以為慊。然才之可取者何限，而制額弗敢過也，故不難於取，而難於去。其有欲取而不能、欲去而不忍者，必為之校閲數四，不得已而置焉。試事既竣，然後列中式者氏名及其文
translation_en: …the imperial command to take charge of the examination at Yingtian. I humbly reflect that when I, your servant, formerly sat the examination here and witnessed the abundance of talent, I felt like an inferior horse among the herds of northern Ji, renowned for their fine steeds, and could never help lamenting my own inadequacy. Now, undeservedly entrusted with the responsibility of evaluating and selecting candidates, I find that the talent of today is still more abundant than what I saw in the past. Yet how could someone as dull as your servant be equal to distinguishing among them? I could only proceed in fear and trembling, morning and night, devoting all my strength to the task, seeking to leave no worthy talent overlooked before I could feel satisfied. Yet how numerous were those whose talents merited selection, while I dared not exceed the imperially prescribed quota! Thus the difficulty lay not in selecting candidates but in rejecting them. Whenever there were candidates whom I wished to select but could not, and whom I contemplated rejecting but could not bear to, I invariably reviewed their papers three or four times, setting them aside only when there was no alternative. Once the examination was completed, we then listed the names of the successful candidates and their essays…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之尤者彙次成編曰鄉試錄
凡就試之士登名兹錄者率
三十而得一其間以文錄者
又不過十之一焉文之錄者
何如粹乎理而蔚乎其辭者
也曷為錄之少也舉其尤以
例其餘凡中式之士雖文有
===
等差固皆辭理兼備者耳竊
嘗論人之為文工於辭而背
於理者往往有之理到而辭
不工者未之有也盖惟精於
理則所見必瑩所得必深故
其發為文章有明暢者有雄
健者有方嚴縝密者有汪洋
alt_text:
之尤者彙次成編曰鄉試錄
凡就試之士登名茲錄者卒
三十而得一其間以文錄者
又不過十之一焉文之錄者
何如粹乎理而蔚乎其辭者
也曷為錄之少也舉其尤以
例其餘凡中式之士雖文有
===
等差固皆辭理兼備者耳竊
嘗論人之為文工於辭而背
於理者往往有之理到而辭
不工者未之有也蓋惟精於
理則所見必瑩所得必深故
其發為文章有明暢者有沉
健者有方嚴縝密者有汪洋
punctuated:
之尤者，彙次成編，曰《鄉試錄》。凡就試之士，登名兹錄者，率三十而得一；其間以文錄者，又不過十之一焉。文之錄者何如？粹乎理而蔚乎其辭者也。曷為錄之少也？舉其尤以例其餘。凡中式之士，雖文有等差，固皆辭理兼備者耳。
竊嘗論人之為文，工於辭而背於理者，往往有之；理到而辭不工者，未之有也。盖惟精於理，則所見必瑩，所得必深，故其發為文章，有明暢者，有雄健者，有方嚴縝密者，有汪洋
translation_en:
…the finest among their writings, gathering and arranging them into a compilation entitled Record of the Provincial Examination. Of all the candidates who sat the examination, approximately one in thirty has his name entered in this record; among these, no more than one in ten also has his writing included. What distinguishes the writings selected? They are pure in principle and rich in expression. Why are so few included? The finest are presented as examples of the rest. Although the writings of successful candidates differ in quality, all are assuredly accomplished in both expression and principle.
I have reflected on how people compose: writings that are skillful in expression yet depart from principle are often encountered; writings that fully grasp principle yet lack skill in expression have never been found. For only through a refined understanding of principle can one’s perceptions be clear and one’s attainments profound. Thus, when these find expression in writing, some compositions are lucid and fluent, some vigorous and forceful, some disciplined, grave, meticulous, and closely reasoned, and some vast and flowing…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
浩蕩者不患乎辭之不工也
其或淺陋粗畧不達於辭者
則其於理必無所得焉耳理
到者辭固足以發之寧有是
病哉故取士於辭未必其合
乎理也取士於理辭在其中
矣夫浮華之辭非不足膾炙
===
人口而君子病之為其無實
也由今所取之士而觀乎其
言其於道德仁義之實固皆
的然有所見矣其平居之所
以脩身及其出而有位所以
措諸事業者果能皆踐其言
否乎苟或行與言戾而徒以

否乎苟或行與言戾而徒以
punctuated: 浩蕩者，不患乎辭之不工也。其或淺陋粗畧、不達於辭者，則其於理必無所得焉耳。理到者，辭固足以發之，寧有是病哉？故取士於辭，未必其合乎理也；取士於理，辭在其中矣。夫浮華之辭，非不足膾炙人口，而君子病之，為其無實也。由今所取之士而觀乎其言，其於道德仁義之實，固皆的然有所見矣。其平居之所以脩身，及其出而有位所以措諸事業者，果能皆踐其言否乎？苟或行與言戾，而徒以
translation_en: …vast and expansive: there is no need to worry that their expression will lack skill. Those whose writing is shallow, crude, and deficient in expression must have gained no understanding of principle. For those who have attained an understanding of principle, words are surely adequate to convey it; how could they suffer from this defect? Thus, selecting men by their expression does not ensure that they accord with principle; selecting men by their understanding of principle encompasses expression as well. Florid language can certainly win popular acclaim, yet the gentleman finds fault with it because it lacks substance. Judging the men selected on this occasion by their words, all have indeed attained a clear understanding of the substance of the Way, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness. But in cultivating themselves in everyday life, and in putting their understanding into practice in public affairs once they take office, can they truly live up to all their words? If their conduct should contradict their words, and they merely use this as…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
是為青紫之媒則其弊與浮
辭等爾而何理之足云豈惟
有負於
聖明求賢之意抑亦有玷於茲錄
矣今夫試必有錄錄必梓行
固將昭示於無窮也然歷年
既久則世罕有見者而宋紹
===
興戊辰進士之錄迄今幾四
百年乃盛行於世一時名第
後先及其家世邑里之詳歷
歷可考豈不以登名錄中者
有朱晦菴其人乎鄉舉之視
甲科雖試有小大錄有詳畧
而其傳一也苟有接朱子之

是爲青紫之媒則其弊與浮
辭等爾而何理之足云豈惟
有負於
聖明求賢之意抑亦有玷於茲録
矣今夫試必有録録必梓行
固將昭示於無窮也然歷年
既久則世世爲有身者而宋紹
興戊辰進士之録迄今幾四
===
百年乃盛行於世一時名第
後先及其家世邑里之詳歷
歷可考豈不以登名録中者
有朱晦菴其人乎鄉舉之視
甲科雖試有小大録有詳畧
而其傳一也苟有接朱子之
punctuated:
是為青紫之媒，則其弊與浮辭等爾，而何理之足云？豈惟有負於聖明求賢之意，抑亦有玷於茲錄矣。
今夫試必有錄，錄必梓行，固將昭示於無窮也。然歷年既久，則世罕有見者。而宋紹興戊辰進士之錄，迄今幾四百年，乃盛行於世。一時名第後先，及其家世邑里之詳，歷歷可考。豈不以登名錄中者有朱晦菴其人乎？鄉舉之視甲科，雖試有小大，錄有詳畧，而其傳一也。苟有接朱子之
translation_en:
…this as a means of obtaining high office, then the harm is no different from that of empty rhetoric. What principle could there be to speak of? This would not only betray His enlightened Majesty’s intention to seek worthy men, but also bring discredit upon this record.
Now every examination must have a record, and every record must be printed from woodblocks, certainly with the intention of making it known for all time. Yet after many years have passed, such records are seldom seen in the world. Nevertheless, the record of metropolitan graduates (jinshi) for the wuchen year of the Song dynasty’s Shaoxing reign remains widely circulated today, nearly four hundred years later. The candidates’ names and relative rankings, together with details of their family backgrounds and native places, can all be examined clearly. Is this not because among those whose names appear in that record was Zhu Hui’an [Zhu Xi]? Although the Provincial Examination and the examination for the jinshi degree differ in scale, and their records in fullness of detail, the principle governing their transmission is the same. If among those recorded there should be someone who follows in Master Zhu’s…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
武者登名錄中則斯錄之傳
雖百世可也諸士子生長
畿甸涵育
聖化既深且久宜必有若人焉出
乎其間寧獨文之盛而已哉
晦菴新安人也新安為今
南畿之地故於應天試錄之
===
成特舉以為諸士勗而兼以
自厲焉
翰林院侍讀朱希周謹序
alt_text:
武者登名錄中則斯錄之傳
雖百世可也諸士子生長
畿甸涵育
聖化既深且久宜必有若人焉出
手其間寧獨文之盛而已哉
晦菴新安人也新安爲今
南畿之地故於應天試錄之
成特舉以爲諸士勗而兼以
自厲焉
翰林院侍讀朱希周謹序
punctuated:
武者登名錄中，則斯錄之傳，雖百世可也。諸士子生長畿甸，涵育聖化，既深且久，宜必有若人焉出乎其間，寧獨文之盛而已哉！晦菴，新安人也。新安為今南畿之地，故於應天試錄之成，特舉以為諸士勗，而兼以自厲焉。
翰林院侍讀朱希周謹序。
translation_en:
…should someone following in Master Zhu’s footsteps have his name entered in this record, then this record could be transmitted even for a hundred generations. These scholars have grown up in the metropolitan region and have been nurtured by the sage sovereign’s transforming influence, both deeply and for a long time. Surely someone of this kind ought to emerge among them. Could their distinction lie solely in literary accomplishment?
Hui’an was a native of Xin’an. Xin’an lies within what is now the Southern Metropolitan Region. Thus, upon the completion of the Yingtian examination record, I have singled out his example to encourage these scholars and also to spur myself onward.
Preface respectfully composed by Zhu Xizhou, Reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy.

text:
暨諸執事更相戒誓而後就
列乃窮日夜精校閱慎去取
之於四千一百四十卷中拔
其文之優者得百三十有五
人其卷若是乎其多也而所
拔乃僅止此非士之可取者
止於此也遵
===
制額而不敢過也文則錄而刻
者二十篇亦間舉其一二以
例之錄何能盡也然即其所
已錄者而觀之雖一出於風
簷短晷倉卒督迫所成率皆
明於理而達於辭蔚然鏘然
有可誦而傳者則其平日從

明於理而達於辭蔚蔚然鏘然

punctuated:
暨諸執事更相戒誓而後就列，乃窮日夜精校閱，慎去取之。於四千一百四十卷中，拔其文之優者，得百三十有五人。其卷若是乎其多也，而所拔乃僅止此，非士之可取者止於此也，遵制額而不敢過也。
文則錄而刻者二十篇，亦間舉其一二以例之，錄何能盡也？然即其所已錄者而觀之，雖一出於風簷短晷、倉卒督迫所成，率皆明於理而達於辭，蔚然鏘然，有可誦而傳者，則其平日從
translation_en:
…and, together with all the functionaries, admonished one another and exchanged pledges before taking their places. Then, working day and night, they carefully examined the scripts and made their selections with caution. From 4,140 scripts, they selected those whose writing was superior, obtaining 135 successful candidates. The scripts were so numerous, yet those selected amounted to only this number. This was not because the worthy candidates numbered only so many, but because they observed the imperially prescribed quota and dared not exceed it.
As for the compositions, twenty pieces were transcribed and printed. These, too, were merely a selection of a few examples to illustrate the whole: how could the record include them all? Yet, judging from those already included, although they were all produced beneath wind-swept eaves, with little time, amid haste and pressure, they are generally lucid in principle and fluent in expression, rich and resonant, worthy of recitation and transmission. Then their writings composed in their ordinary days at leisure…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
容展布之作將不有大且深
於此焉者乎即其在錄中者
而推其遺於錄外者使非限
於
制額則人之見取文之見錄雖
或倍蓰於此亦無不可然而
有所不敢者法之所在不容
===
以己意參乎其間也仰惟
皇上嗣大歷服以來無一政一事
不遵
祖宗成法至於試事尤切
惓惓屢
渙大號戒飭所司申條格謹防
範於凡徇情干正假公售私

===
皇上嗣大歷服以來無一政一事
以己意參乎其間也仰惟
不遵
祖宗成法至於試事尤切
惓惓屢
渙大號戒飭所司申條格謹防
範於凡徇情干正假公售私
punctuated:
容展布之作，將不有大且深於此焉者乎？即其在錄中者，而推其遺於錄外者，使非限於制額，則人之見取、文之見錄，雖或倍蓰於此，亦無不可。然而有所不敢者，法之所在，不容以己意參乎其間也。
仰惟皇上嗣大歷服以來，無一政一事不遵祖宗成法。至於試事，尤切惓惓，屢渙大號，戒飭所司，申條格，謹防範，於凡徇情干正、假公售私
translation_en:
…works composed at leisure, with room to develop their ideas—would these not possess still greater breadth and depth? If we infer from those included in this record the quality of those omitted, then, were it not for the prescribed quota, there would be nothing objectionable in selecting twice or five times as many men and recording twice or five times as many compositions. Yet there are things we dare not do: where the law applies, we may not interpose our own preferences.
We reverently consider that, since His Majesty succeeded to the great imperial mandate, there has been no policy or undertaking in which he has not followed the established laws of his ancestors. He has shown especially earnest concern for examination affairs, repeatedly issuing imperial proclamations to admonish the responsible authorities, reaffirm the regulations, and maintain strict safeguards against all who indulge personal attachments to the detriment of impartiality or use public authority to advance private interests…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄

情如造化至公如權衡者而
後已焉皆法之為也若乃解
額之在鄉試者則間增於北
卷額之在會試者則去中數

===

祖宗之法本之於身以達之家國

下之心處之萬世守之萬世

哉然姑即試事求之則凡法
之所在雖

translation_en:
…those who do so are punished with particular severity. Nothing short of what the ancients called being “without partiality like the workings of creation, utterly impartial like a balance” will suffice. All this is the operation of established law. As for the quotas for provincial graduates in the Provincial Examination, these have occasionally been increased in the north; as for the quotas for examination papers in the Metropolitan Examination, the central allocation has been removed and divided between the north and south. Although these measures reflect intentions beyond the established law, they nevertheless represent adjustments made in response to changing circumstances.
For the laws of our imperial ancestors take the person as their foundation and extend to the family, the state, and all under Heaven. There is no administrative measure or affair that they do not address with a concern for impartiality toward all under Heaven. These laws are to be upheld for ten thousand generations and cannot be altered in ten thousand generations. How could this apply only to examinations? Yet, if we confine our inquiry for the moment to examinations, wherever established law applies, even…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
朝廷之上亦未嘗輒以已意參
之也况有司乎有司之奉法
雖遠而藩服猶凜然如在
朝廷也况
畿甸乎法以嚴於
畿甸以率乎天下務期所取
之士無不得焉以取重於天
===
下以無負乎
朝廷所尤重之意此臣之志也
而士之所以自重則又係乎
士之所自立者何如是豈臣
之所能與哉士之所自立凡
處已待物事君治民之道亦
豈無成法哉自昔聖賢具載

punctuated: 朝廷之上，亦未嘗輒以已意參之也，况有司乎？有司之奉法，雖遠而藩服，猶凜然如在朝廷也，况畿甸乎？法以嚴於畿甸，以率乎天下，務期所取之士無不得焉，以取重於天下，以無負乎朝廷所尤重之意，此臣之志也。而士之所以自重，則又係乎士之所自立者何如，是豈臣之所能與哉？士之所自立，凡處已待物、事君治民之道，亦豈無成法哉？自昔聖賢具載
translation_en: …even at the imperial court, no one has ever presumed to introduce his own ideas into them; how much less should the responsible officials do so? In upholding the laws, officials even in distant frontier territories remain as solemnly vigilant as though they were at court; how much more should this be so in the metropolitan region? The laws are to be rigorously enforced in the metropolitan region, to set an example for all under Heaven. Every effort must be made to ensure that all the scholars selected are worthy, thereby winning esteem throughout the realm and fulfilling the court’s intention in attaching particular importance to this matter. This is your servant’s aspiration. Yet how scholars uphold their own dignity depends in turn on how they establish their own character. How could this lie within your servant’s power to influence? As for establishing their character—in all the ways of conducting themselves, dealing with others, serving the ruler, and governing the people—are there not established standards for these as well? The sages and worthies of old fully set these down …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
於經其本末次第可考而知
者士當敬以守之隨其職守
才力所至而皆求以不悖不
以利害為趨舎不以毀譽為
前却如此而始如此而終如
此而貧賤如此而富貴其有
所當為也如水之必寒如火
===
之必熱其有所不為也如騶
虞之不殺如竊脂之不穀有
斷斷乎其不可易者非可視
時高下而為之損益者也使
或悖乎此則非士之所以為
士者矣凡天下之士皆然而
況

punctuated: 於經，其本末次第可考而知者，士當敬以守之，隨其職守才力所至，而皆求以不悖。不以利害為趨舎，不以毀譽為前却。如此而始，如此而終；如此而貧賤，如此而富貴。其有所當為也，如水之必寒，如火之必熱；其有所不為也，如騶虞之不殺，如竊脂之不穀。有斷斷乎其不可易者，非可視時高下而為之損益者也。使或悖乎此，則非士之所以為士者矣。凡天下之士皆然，而況
translation_en: …in the Classics. Where their fundamentals, particulars, and proper sequence can be ascertained through study, scholars should reverently abide by them. Within the reach of their official responsibilities, abilities, and strength, they should always seek to avoid contravening them. They should not let advantage or harm determine what they pursue or abandon, nor let criticism or praise determine whether they advance or retreat. They should proceed thus at the beginning and at the end, in poverty and low station as in wealth and high rank. When there is something they ought to do, they should be as certain to do it as water is to be cold or fire to be hot; when there is something they should not do, they should be like the zouyu, which does not kill, or the qiezhi bird, which does not eat grain. There are things firmly settled that cannot be altered; they cannot be diminished or augmented to suit the changing circumstances of the times. Should scholars contravene this, they would no longer possess that which makes a scholar a scholar. This holds for all scholars under Heaven, and how much more for…

First Session

Four Books
When those above cherish ritual propriety, the people are easy to direct.
To make oneself sincere is to choose what is good and hold firmly to it.
Shun rose from among the fields; Fu Yue was raised to office from among those building rammed-earth walls; Jiao Ge was raised from the fish and salt trade; Guan Yiwu was raised from the custody of a prison officer; Sun Shu’ao was raised from the seacoast; and Baili Xi was raised from the marketplace.

Book of Changes (Yijing)
Beauty resides within, extends through the four limbs, and manifests itself in undertakings: this is beauty at its utmost.
The noble man thereby rectifies his position and consolidates the mandate.
Thus, four operations complete a change, and eighteen changes complete a hexagram.
Heaven and earth establish their positions; mountains and marshes exchange their vital energies; thunder and wind impel one another; water and fire do not oppose one another; the eight trigrams interweave.

Book of Documents (Shujing)
Those who daily manifest three virtues, discerning them deeply morning and night, may govern a household; those who daily and reverently honor six virtues may govern a state, faithfully conducting its affairs.

translation_en:
…you must examine whether it accords with what is contrary to the Way.
One should not look into water for a mirror; one should look to the people for a mirror.
Distinguish the good from the wicked, mark their dwellings and villages, make goodness manifest and punish evil, and thereby establish a guiding moral influence. For those who do not follow the prescribed teachings, set apart their fields and boundaries, so that they may learn fear and emulation. Clearly demarcate the outer districts and frontiers, carefully strengthen the borders and their defenses, and thereby bring peace to all within the Four Seas.

Book of Odes
Ascend that lordly hall; raise that rhinoceros-horn cup: may you live ten thousand years without end!
The people's substance lies in their daily food and drink. All the common people everywhere depend upon your virtue.
The descendants of King Wen, the main line and its branches, shall endure for a hundred generations. All the officers of Zhou—are they not illustrious, generation after generation?
Vigorously break up your private fields throughout the full thirty li. Attend also to your plowing: ten thousand work in pairs.

Spring and Autumn Annals
The duke and Yifu of Zhu made a covenant at Mie. First year of Duke Yin.
The armies of Qi, Song, and Cao encamped at Niebei to relieve Xing. First year of Duke Xi.
They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. Fourth year of Duke Xi.
Men of Jin, Song, Wei, and Chen invaded Zheng. Second year of Duke Xuan.
For the first time, a tax was levied by the mu of land. Fifteenth year of Duke Xuan. A levy for military equipment was instituted by the qiu land unit. First year of Duke Cheng.
A military levy based on farmland was imposed. Twelfth year of Duke Ai.

Fifth Question

Question: Our Emperor Taizu Gao once commanded Confucian officials to compile two records, Preserving the Mind (Cunxin) and Examining Oneself (Xinggong). They recorded all instances in which emperors and kings of successive ages, in conducting sacrifices, were moved by disasters or auspicious signs, as well as instances of disasters and auspicious signs manifesting themselves in relation to ministers from the Han, Tang, and Song onward. The direction for these compilations came entirely from His Majesty’s sagely mind, and their titles issued wholly from his imperial words. Their circulation at the time and transmission to later generations were intended solely to make rulers and ministers, superiors and subordinates, share the same vigilance and reverence, applying themselves to the cultivation of their persons and minds so as to transform disaster into good fortune. Could the purpose have been merely to exercise care in sacrificial observances?

Yet I have ventured respectfully to consider the meaning of the two books’ titles. In admonishing the ruler, the title speaks of the mind and urges him to preserve it; in admonishing ministers, it speaks of the person and urges them to examine themselves. Can it be that the ruler has no concern with his person, and ministers no concern with their minds? Or are there also ways in which rulers and ministers can assist one another in these efforts? translation_en:
…those who understand it. This is because they regard themselves as exalted and important, while treating the people as insignificant. Only when they understand that the people and they themselves depend upon one another will they surely avoid the fault of slighting the people. Thus it is said: “Who is to be cherished, if not the ruler [?]; who is to be feared, if not the people?” How great are these imperial words! In the thousands of years since Shun and Yu personally transmitted rule to one another, such words have scarcely been heard.

Let us discuss this with you candidates. When our sagely founder spoke of fearing the people, did he truly consider the people fearsome? Or was he merely explaining the principle in these terms? Compared with those at the founding of the dynasty, are the people of the realm today likewise to be feared, or is there nothing about them to fear? At the dynasty’s founding, warfare had only just been brought to an end, and there might perhaps have been something fearsome about the people then. Now that peace has endured so long, everyone throughout the realm bathes in profound benevolence and abundant favor, rejoicing and taking heart. What can there still be to fear?

Yet our Emperor remains solicitous day and night, with no leisure to rest at ease. Whenever he hears reports of floods, droughts, brigandage, or theft in any quarter, he immediately refers the matter to the responsible authorities, directing them to devote their full attention to devising measures. The imperial edicts expressing this concern are too numerous to recount. Unless he took as his own the ancient emperors’ and kings’ fear of the people, and aspired reverently to follow his ancestor’s footsteps, how could he attain such a degree of concern? Why, then, have we still heard of no prospect that those among the people of Chu and Shu who have fallen into banditry will return and settle peacefully in their home communities? 姦慝何由而詰乎？雖使堯舜三王，亦無以治天下矣。然宋儒之論，顧以不盡人之財、不盡人之力、不盡人之情者為賢，而以歸於漢世之君，且嘅其繼治者之不能然，何也？然則治天下者，於斯三者果可以盡歟？果不可以盡歟？抑宋儒之論，雖曰論漢，其實又借漢以論宋也？宋世之君，於斯三者亦固有盡不盡焉者矣。果孰賢而孰非賢歟？夫治道莫要於斯三者，漢宋諸君同以之治天下也，而其所行之得失乃不同如此，庸可不求其故歟？諸士子皆明於古今之故者，是固不容默矣。
一問：士之窮理，於古昔人物臧否皆所當知。然欲知其臧否者，亦惟考其行事之實焉耳。大抵君子之所為必當於理者也，小人之所為必背於理者也。然或忠貞鯁亮，勳德著聞，而其所行亦有不愜於
translation_en:
…How could wickedness and wrongdoing be brought to account? Even Yao, Shun, and the Three Kings would then have no means of governing the realm. Yet the Song Confucian scholars, in their discussions, instead considered worthy those who did not exhaust the people's wealth, did not exhaust their strength, and did not press their feelings to the utmost. They attributed these qualities to rulers of the Han, and lamented that their successors could not do likewise. Why was this? In governing the realm, may one indeed go to the utmost in these three matters, or may one not? Or, although the Song scholars ostensibly discussed the Han, were they in fact using the Han to discuss the Song? Among Song rulers, too, there were certainly those who went to the utmost in these three matters and those who did not. Which, then, were worthy, and which were not? Nothing is more essential to the way of governing than these three matters. The rulers of the Han and Song alike governed the realm through them, yet the merits and failings of their actions differed so greatly. Can we fail to seek the reasons? You candidates all understand the circumstances of past and present; on this you surely cannot remain silent.

translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“When those above cherish ritual propriety, the people are easy to direct.”
Shen Gui 沈櫃

Comment by Associate Examiner Tian, Instructor: The topic itself is grand and dignified, and most candidates in the examination could develop it. Yet closer scrutiny showed that merits and flaws [?] were inevitably present in equal measure. Late in the reading I found this essay. Its wording is apt, its resonance enduring; it truly surpasses the others. I have therefore selected it to serve as a model for future students.

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: Topics from the Analects seem easy but are actually difficult. Over successive days of reading scripts, very few have satisfied me. This essay expresses its meaning directly through the topic; its language is economical, yet its grasp of principle is distinctive. I have therefore selected it.

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-Waiting: It clearly apprehends the meaning of the two characters “easy to direct.”

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: Fluent in expression and clear in principle, it surpasses the other compositions.

If those who govern others can esteem what is natural to principle, those who serve others will rest content in what their allotted stations properly require. Ritual propriety arises from natural principle, and nothing in it is more important than the distinctions of station. When those above cherish ritual propriety, it reaches those below and their stations become settled. How, then, could there be people who are difficult to direct? The meaning of our Master’s words of old was as though he said: For securing those above and governing the people, nothing excels ritual propriety. When the gentleman occupies a superior position and presides over those below, can he fail to esteem it? In his going out and coming in, rising and resting, he must act entirely within the bounds of established standards, cherishing ritual propriety alone, thereby putting it into practice in …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
一身俾民有所式焉設施措置不出乎儀則之
外而所好惟禮于以綱維乎庶政俾民有所守
焉蒞之以莊未也而所以動斯民者必於禮乎
是崇道之以德未也而所以齊斯民者必於禮
乎是尚上之好禮也如此則禮教達於下矣焉
有禮達而分不定分定而民不服者乎故凡民
之在所統者是惟無使也一有以使之則莫不
曰上之所以使我者分也分所當為吾何敢愛
其力邪民之在所治者是惟無役也一有以役
===
之則莫不曰我之所以為上役者職也職所當
盡吾何敢顧其私邪使之興作也則趨事赴功
之恐後而勞非所辭不徒貌之從也而實安於
心焉使之攻守也則折衝禦侮之爭先而危非
所避不徒法之畏也而實勇於義焉是則為人
上者不患民之難使而患禮之不達盍亦知所
務哉雖然上之好禮豈以欲民易使而然亦惟

punctuated: 一身，俾民有所式焉；設施措置不出乎儀則之外，而所好惟禮，于以綱維乎庶政，俾民有所守焉。蒞之以莊，未也，而所以動斯民者，必於禮乎是崇；道之以德，未也，而所以齊斯民者，必於禮乎是尚。上之好禮也如此，則禮教達於下矣。焉有禮達而分不定，分定而民不服者乎？故凡民之在所統者，是惟無使也，一有以使之，則莫不曰：「上之所以使我者，分也。分所當為，吾何敢愛其力邪？」民之在所治者，是惟無役也，一有以役之，則莫不曰：「我之所以為上役者，職也。職所當盡，吾何敢顧其私邪？」使之興作也，則趨事赴功之恐後，而勞非所辭；不徒貌之從也，而實安於心焉。使之攻守也，則折衝禦侮之爭先，而危非所避；不徒法之畏也，而實勇於義焉。是則為人上者，不患民之難使，而患禮之不達，盍亦知所務哉？雖然，上之好禮，豈以欲民易使而然？亦惟盡其道之當為，而其應有必至耳。若子犯之告晉文公，則曰：「民未知禮，未生其共。」於是乎大蒐
translation_en: …in his own person, giving the people an example to follow; in his arrangements and measures, he never steps beyond the rules of proper conduct, and delights only in ritual propriety. Through this he orders the manifold affairs of government, giving the people standards to uphold. Presiding over them with dignity is not enough: to move these people, he must exalt ritual propriety. Guiding them with virtue is not enough: to bring these people into accord, he must esteem ritual propriety. When those above delight in ritual propriety in this way, its teachings reach those below. How could ritual propriety prevail without the duties of each station becoming settled, or those duties become settled without the people submitting? Thus, among all the people under his authority, it is only a matter of whether he calls upon their service. Once he does, they all say: “Those above call upon my service in accordance with the duties of my station. Where those duties require action, how could I dare spare my strength?” Among the people under his governance, it is only a matter of whether he calls upon their labor. Once he does, they all say: “It is my duty to labor for those above. Where that duty must be fulfilled, how could I dare attend to my private interests?” When he calls upon them to undertake works, they hasten to their tasks and strive for accomplishment, fearing only that they will lag behind; they do not shrink from toil. Their obedience is not merely outward: in their hearts they are truly at ease with it. When he calls upon them to attack or defend, they vie to be first in repelling the enemy and resisting aggression; they do not avoid danger. They are not merely afraid of the law: they are truly courageous in the cause of righteousness. Thus, those who stand above others should worry not that the people are difficult to employ, but that ritual propriety has failed to reach them. Should they not recognize where to direct their efforts? Nevertheless, do those above delight in ritual propriety because they wish to make the people easy to employ? They simply fulfill what the Way requires of them, and the corresponding response is certain to follow. As for Zifan’s advice to Duke Wen of Jin, he said: “The people do not yet understand ritual propriety, and reverence has not yet arisen in them.” Thereupon the duke held a great hunt…
