title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
理之實於已也不亦難哉中庸引孔子答哀公
之問政言誠者誠之者有天道人道之分而此
則釋誠之之事何則誠之原於天也本無不同
而其在乎人也不能無異誠之者知理之閒以
欲也欲變其異求與誠者同歸知理之雜以人
也欲反其同求與天道一致是果何如其用力
哉以為擇之不精則天下之理必將錯雜於是
非之間而心體終於昏昧矣何以知其善之所
在而詣之哉於是辨真偽於疑似之間務求何
===
者為是何者為非不底於至當之歸不已也審
取舍於隱微之際務求何者為真何者為妄不
造於至善之地不已也今日格一物明日格一
物凡天下之理皆有以究析其幾微今日致一
知明日致一知凡天下之理皆有以窮極其蘊
奧夫然則有以真知善之所在而有誠之地矣
以為執之不固則所擇之理必將得失於苟且
之餘而表裏終於扞格矣何以得其善於吾心
而安之哉于是擇之於始者執之於後而持守

理之實於己也不亦難哉中庸載孔子答哀公
之問政言誠者誠之者有天道人道之分而此
則釋誠之之事何則誠之原於天也本無不同
而其在乎人也不能無異誠之者知理之間以

也欲反其同求與天道一致是果何如其用力
哉以爲擇之不精則天下之理必將錯雜於是
非之間而心體終於昏昧矣何以知其善之所
在而詣之哉於是辨眞僞於疑似之間務求何
===
者爲是何者爲非不底於至當之歸不已也審
取舍於隱微之際務求何者爲眞何者爲妄不
造於至善之地不已也今日格一物明日格一
物凡天下之理皆有以究析其幾微今日致一
知明日致一知凡天下之理皆有以窮極其蘊
奥夫然則有以眞知善之所在而有誠之地矣
以爲執之不固則所擇之理必將得失於茍且
之餘而表裏終於扞格矣何以得其善於吾心
而安之哉于是擇之於始者執之於後而持守
punctuated: 理之實於已也，不亦難哉？《中庸》引孔子答哀公之問政，言誠者、誠之者，有天道、人道之分，而此則釋誠之之事。何則？誠之原於天也，本無不同，而其在乎人也，不能無異。誠之者，知理之閒以欲也，欲變其異，求與誠者同歸；知理之雜以人也，欲反其同，求與天道一致。是果何如其用力哉？以為擇之不精，則天下之理必將錯雜於是非之間，而心體終於昏昧矣，何以知其善之所在而詣之哉？於是辨真偽於疑似之間，務求何者為是、何者為非，不底於至當之歸不已也；審取舍於隱微之際，務求何者為真、何者為妄，不造於至善之地不已也。今日格一物，明日格一物，凡天下之理，皆有以究析其幾微；今日致一知，明日致一知，凡天下之理，皆有以窮極其蘊奧。夫然，則有以真知善之所在，而有誠之地矣。以為執之不固，則所擇之理必將得失於苟且之餘，而表裏終於扞格矣，何以得其善於吾心而安之哉？于是擇之於始者，執之於後，而持守
translation_en:
…for principle to become fully realized in oneself—is this not difficult? The Doctrine of the Mean quotes Confucius’s reply to Duke Ai’s question about government, distinguishing between the Way of Heaven and the Way of humanity in speaking of sincerity and making oneself sincere. This passage explains the work of making oneself sincere. Why is this so? Sincerity originates in Heaven and is fundamentally the same in all; yet as it exists in human beings, differences inevitably arise. Those who make themselves sincere recognize that desires intrude upon principle. They wish to transform what differs and attain the same end as those who are sincere. They recognize that principle is mixed with human interference. They wish to restore its original sameness and become one with the Way of Heaven. How, then, do they apply their efforts?

They consider that, unless their discernment is exact, the principles of all under Heaven will become confused amid right and wrong, and the substance of the mind will remain obscure. How could they then know where goodness lies and attain it? Thus they distinguish the genuine from the false amid doubtful appearances, striving to determine what is right and what is wrong, and never stopping until they arrive at what is perfectly appropriate. They scrutinize what to accept and what to reject at the subtlest beginnings, striving to determine what is true and what is delusive, and never stopping until they reach the highest goodness. Today they investigate one thing; tomorrow they investigate another. In this way they can examine and distinguish the subtlest workings of all the principles under Heaven. Today they extend their knowledge in one respect; tomorrow they extend it in another. In this way they can thoroughly fathom the hidden depths of all the principles under Heaven. Only then can they truly know where goodness lies and establish a foundation for sincerity.

They consider that, unless their grasp is firm, the principles they have discerned will be gained and lost through careless expediency, and their outward conduct and inner life will ultimately remain at odds. How could they then possess goodness within their own minds and rest securely in it? Thus what they discerned at the outset they hold fast to afterward, maintaining their grasp…

於昔者執之於今而操持之也篤務俾理與心
契不或在而或亡也時有久暫而執之之功不
以久暫而或殊事有常變而守之之力不以常
變而或異夫然則有以造詣乎善之所歸而入
誠之域矣誠之者而能至是焉則與誠者同其
歸而與天道無二致矣反其異以歸於同擇善
固執之功焉可誣哉大抵聖賢之學未有不以
知行為要者虞書之惟精惟一大易之學問寬
===
仁顏子之博文約禮曾子之格致誠正孟子之
盡知存養皆是物也然則吾夫子擇善固執之
說豈獨哀公之所當知哉宜乎子思引之以明道
之費隱也歟

punctuated:
之也堅，務使心與理融，不隨得而隨失也。擇之於昔者，執之於今，而操持之也篤，務俾理與心契，不或在而或亡也。時有久暫，而執之之功不以久暫而或殊；事有常變，而守之之力不以常變而或異。夫然，則有以造詣乎善之所歸，而入誠之域矣。誠之者而能至是焉，則與誠者同其歸，而與天道無二致矣。反其異以歸於同，擇善固執之功焉可誣哉！大抵聖賢之學，未有不以知行為要者。《虞書》之惟精惟一，《大易》之學問寬仁，顏子之博文約禮，曾子之格致誠正，孟子之盡知存養，皆是物也。然則吾夫子擇善固執之說，豈獨哀公之所當知哉！宜乎子思引之以明道之費隱也歟！

translation_en:
…and holds to it firmly, striving to bring the mind and principle into harmony, so that what is gained is not immediately lost. What one chose in the past one holds to in the present, maintaining it steadfastly and striving to make principle accord with the mind, so that it is not sometimes present and sometimes absent. Periods of time may be long or short, but the effort of holding fast does not vary with their length; circumstances may be ordinary or exceptional, but the strength with which one maintains one's commitment does not vary accordingly. Only then can one reach the ultimate destination of goodness and enter the realm of sincerity. If those who strive to become sincere can attain this, they reach the same destination as those who are naturally sincere, and their attainment is no different from the Way of Heaven. By overcoming their difference, they arrive at the same end: how could the efficacy of choosing goodness and holding firmly to it be denied!

Broadly speaking, the learning of sages and worthies has always taken knowing and acting as essential. The injunction to be discerning and single-minded in the Documents of Yu; learning, inquiry, capaciousness, and benevolence in the Great Book of Changes; Master Yan's broadening of learning through cultural study and restraint through ritual; Master Zeng's investigation of things, extension of knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectification of the mind; and Master Meng's full realization of the mind, understanding of one's nature, preservation of the mind, and nourishment of one's nature—all concern this same matter. Thus, was our Master's teaching of choosing goodness and holding firmly to it something that Duke Ai alone ought to understand? How fitting that Zisi quoted it to illuminate both the all-pervading reach and the hidden subtlety of the Way!

“Shun rose from the fields; Fu Yue was raised up from work building rammed-earth walls; Jiao Ge was raised up from the fish and salt trades; Guan Yiwu was raised up from the custody of a judicial officer; Sunshu Ao was raised up from the seacoast; Baili Xi was raised up from the marketplace.”

Integrated and vigorous.

大賢述古人之亨於困有統治於上者有輔治
===
於下者蓋舜以聖人治天下而傅說諸賢則皆
隨時輔治之臣也其亨皆未始不由於困何莫
而非天意之所在哉孟子之意如此誠以富貴
福澤固天所以厚乎人而困窮拂鬱天亦何嘗
薄於人邪是故舜聖人也受堯禪而膺歷數之
歸之中國而踐天子之位人知舜之登庸也而
不知四岳之舉實始於歷山之耕側陋之揚實
由於往日之日舜蓋發於畎畝之中焉傅說身
居版築其晦陋矣高宗則舉之以作相舟楫資
punctuated:
宛若親接其人，詳其事而為之記述焉。佳哉，作也！

同考試官學正徐批：於聖賢亨困事，發揮明盡，一語丸有學識，其殆尚論古人而能自得師者乎？

同考試官學正韓批：此題「發」「舉」二字，本文甚明，但作者一槩混説，殊為可厭。能融會題意而措詞雅馴，若此篇者，可多得耶？

考試官侍讀朱批：孟子義詳雅整潔，當是作手。

考試官侍讀學士蔣批：説得孟子意出□□□。

大賢述古人之亨於困，有統治於上者，有輔治於下者。蓋舜以聖人治天下，而傅説諸賢則皆隨時輔治之臣也。其亨皆未始不由於困，何莫而非天意之所在哉？孟子之意如此。誠以富貴福澤，固天所以厚乎人，而困窮拂鬱，天亦何嘗薄於人邪？是故舜，聖人也，受堯禪而膺歷數之歸，之中國而踐天子之位。人知舜之登庸也，而不知四岳之舉，實始於歷山之耕；側陋之揚，實由於往田之日。舜蓋發於畎畝之中焉。傅説身居版築，其地陋矣，高宗則舉之以作相，舟楫資
translation_en:
…as though he had personally met these men, learned the details of their affairs, and recorded them. An excellent composition!

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor: The discussion of the sages’ and worthies’ advancement and adversity is clear and exhaustive; every phrase displays learning and understanding [?]. Is this perhaps someone who, in discussing the men of antiquity, can find teachers for himself among them?

Comment by Associate Examiner Han, Instructor: The two words in this topic, “rose” and “was raised,” are perfectly clear in the original text. Yet writers invariably confuse them in their discussions, which is exceedingly tiresome. Can many essays be found that integrate the meaning of the topic and express it with such elegance and propriety as this one?

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-waiting: The exposition of Mencius’s meaning is detailed, elegant, orderly, and clean. This must be an accomplished writer.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: It brings out Mencius’s meaning □□□ [three illegible characters].

The great worthy recounted how men of antiquity attained success through adversity: some exercised overall rule from above, while others assisted in governing from below. Shun governed All under Heaven as a sage, while Fu Yue and the other worthies were all ministers who assisted in government as their times required. Their success invariably arose from adversity. In which of these cases was Heaven’s intention not at work? Such was Mencius’s meaning. Wealth, rank, blessings, and favor are indeed means by which Heaven treats people generously; yet in hardship, poverty, frustration, and distress, when has Heaven ever treated people ungenerously?

Thus Shun was a sage. He received Yao’s abdication and assumed the succession ordained by Heaven; he went to the central realm and ascended the throne of the Son of Heaven. People know of Shun’s elevation to office, but do not know that his recommendation by the Four Peaks originated in his plowing at Lishan, or that his promotion from humble obscurity began in the days when he went out to the fields. Shun indeed rose from among the furrows and fields. Fu Yue was engaged in building rammed-earth walls—a humble station indeed. Yet Gaozong raised him up to serve as chief minister, relying on him as a boat and oars…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之以作也鹽梅資之以和也則捄度之處非其
夢弼之地乎膠鬲身鬻魚鹽其事汙矣文王則
舉之以為政或藉之以先後也或藉之以疏附
也則貿易之塲非其奮跡之所乎齊桓公以管
夷吾為相國舉之果何所自邪則拘於士師之
官而縲紲方且困繫也楚莊王以孫叔敖為令
尹舉之抑何所從邪則困於隱處之地而海濱
且將終身也以至百里奚之賢而為秦穆公之
舉得非混跡於商賈之區屈志於懋遷之市而
===
始出哉是則亨不遽於亨也而必始於困困不
終於困也而卒至於亨古之聖賢大率類此謂
非天意可乎雖然舜大聖人也以傅說膠鬲擬
之固已非其倫矣况夷吾輩區區霸者之佐哉
而孟子乃一律言之何也盖雜舉小大之成就
皆出於困窮憂患中用以示學者堅志熟仁之
一助耳然則有志之士其可以憂患而自沮哉
易
君子以正位凝命

punctuated:
之以作也，鹽梅資之以和也，則捄度之處，非其夢弼之地乎？膠鬲身鬻魚鹽，其事汙矣，文王則舉之以為政，或藉之以先後也，或藉之以疏附也，則貿易之塲，非其奮跡之所乎？齊桓公以管夷吾為相國，舉之果何所自邪？則拘於士師之官，而縲紲方且困繫也。楚莊王以孫叔敖為令尹，舉之抑何所從邪？則困於隱處之地，而海濱且將終身也。以至百里奚之賢，而為秦穆公之舉，得非混跡於商賈之區，屈志於懋遷之市，而始出哉？是則亨不遽於亨也，而必始於困；困不終於困也，而卒至於亨。古之聖賢，大率類此，謂非天意可乎？雖然，舜大聖人也，以傅說、膠鬲擬之，固已非其倫矣，况夷吾輩區區霸者之佐哉！而孟子乃一律言之，何也？盖雜舉小大之成就，皆出於困窮憂患中，用以示學者堅志熟仁之一助耳。然則有志之士，其可以憂患而自沮哉？

《易》
君子以正位凝命。
translation_en:
…relied on him to serve as boat and oars, and relied on him as salt and plums to bring harmony. Was not the place of his labor [?] the very place where the assisting minister seen in the king’s dream was found? Jiao Ge personally sold fish and salt, a lowly occupation; yet King Wen raised him up to administer government, relying on him either to guide and assist or to draw the distant into allegiance. Was not the marketplace the place from which he rose to distinction? Duke Huan of Qi made Guan Yiwu his Chancellor of State. From what circumstances did he raise him? He was detained by the judicial authorities, still bound and confined in fetters. King Zhuang of Chu made Sunshu Ao his Chief Minister. From what circumstances did he raise him? He was languishing in seclusion and was about to spend his entire life by the seashore. Even the worthy Baili Xi was raised up by Duke Mu of Qin: was it not only after mingling among merchants and subordinating his aspirations to trade in the marketplace that he emerged?

Thus success does not come immediately as success, but must begin in adversity; adversity does not end in adversity, but ultimately leads to success. The sages and worthies of antiquity were, for the most part, like this. Can one say that this was not Heaven’s intent? Nevertheless, Shun was a great sage. To compare Fu Yue and Jiao Ge with him already places together men of different orders; how much more so with Yiwu and his like, mere assistants to hegemonic rulers! Why, then, does Mencius speak of them all in the same terms? He brings together achievements both small and great, all arising amid hardship and distress, simply to offer students an aid to strengthening their resolve and bringing their benevolence to maturity. How, then, could a man of aspiration allow distress to discourage him?

Book of Changes
The noble man thereby rectifies his position and makes firm his mandate.

華金

同考試官教諭蔡批命乃君子所已受於天

考試官侍讀朱批明贍可取

君子體鼎之象必端其身之所履以承乎天之
===
所祐蓋位者身之所履而命則天之所祐也天
位正則天命有歸矣豈不足以凝之哉且下巽
上離卦名曰鼎吾夫子係之以象蓋謂木上有
火鼎象也鼎之為物非安重而不動者乎有天
下之君子觀斯象而體之必也齊莊中正端居
乎五位之尊嚴肅整齊高拱乎九重之上大寶
至貴也正以持之而不敢慢所以為天下之大
觀者屹乎其鎮重而有威之可畏焉神器至重
也正以守之而不敢忽所以為萬物之利見者

同考試官教諭田批：詞理精微，深得夫子《象傳》之旨，可嘉。
同考試官教諭蔡批：命乃君子所已受於天者，但欲其凝之耳。作者多體貼欠明，此篇獨能發揮本旨，宜在所錄。
考試官侍讀朱批：明贍可取。
考試官侍讀學士蔣批：講正位凝命處，非他卷可及。

君子體鼎之象，必端其身之所履，以承乎天之所祐。蓋位者，身之所履，而命則天之所祐也。天位正，則天命有歸矣，豈不足以凝之哉？且下巽上離，卦名曰鼎。吾夫子係之以象，蓋謂木上有火，鼎象也。鼎之為物，非安重而不動者乎？有天下之君子觀斯象而體之，必也齊莊中正，端居乎五位之尊；嚴肅整齊，高拱乎九重之上。大寶至貴也，正以持之而不敢慢，所以為天下之大觀者，屹乎其鎮重，而有威之可畏焉。神器至重也，正以守之而不敢忽，所以為萬物之利見者……
translation_en:
Hua Jin.

Comment by Associate Examiner Tian, Instructor: The language and reasoning are subtle and refined, capturing profoundly the Master's meaning in the Commentary on the Images. Commendable.
Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: The mandate is what the noble man has already received from Heaven; he need only make it firm. Most writers lack clarity in their interpretation. This essay alone develops the original meaning and deserves inclusion among the selected answers.
Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-Waiting: Clear and ample; worthy of selection.
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: Its exposition of rectifying one's position and consolidating the mandate is beyond the reach of the other papers.

The noble man, embodying the image of the Cauldron, must rectify the position he occupies in order to receive Heaven's blessing. For position is what one occupies, while the mandate is Heaven's blessing. When the heavenly position is rectified, Heaven's mandate has a proper resting place. Is this not sufficient to consolidate it? With Xun below and Li above, the hexagram is named the Cauldron. Our Master appended an explanation of its image, saying, in effect: “Above wood there is fire: the image of the Cauldron.” Is the cauldron not an object that stands securely and weightily, without moving? The noble man who possesses all under Heaven observes this image and embodies it. He must be reverent, dignified, centered, and correct, occupying uprightly the honored fifth position; solemn and orderly, he sits with hands folded on high within the ninefold palace precincts. The great treasure of the throne is supremely precious: he maintains it through rectitude, never daring to be remiss. Thus, as the grand exemplar for all under Heaven, he stands firm in his gravity and possesses an awe-inspiring majesty. The sacred vessel of sovereignty is supremely weighty: he guards it through rectitude, never daring to be neglectful. Thus, as the one whom it benefits all beings to behold …

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
儼乎其恪恭而有儀之可象焉夫位之所存命
之所存也正其位非所以凝其命乎蓋命本不
易也惟鎮重足以勝之而凝集於穆清之地命
本靡常也惟恪恭足以膺之而萃聚於淵默之
中大寶之貴實天所眷佑者于以承之而安於
磐石豐亨之治可常保也神器之重實天所付
托者于以受之而固於苞桑豫大之慶可常享
也夫位之正也猶鼎之正其器也命之凝也猶
鼎之凝其實也君子其善於體易者與抑又論
===
之君子之正位非以致飾也蓋其敬德之容發
於外者然耳夫子於大舜嘗以恭己正南面贊
之是恭己者即舜之所以正位也然而禄位名
壽咸萃于厥躬則凝命之驗信不誣矣為人君
者其可不以舜為法乎
是故四營而成易十有八變而成卦
童楷

punctuated:
儼乎其恪恭，而有儀之可象焉。夫位之所存，命之所存也。正其位，非所以凝其命乎？蓋命本不易也，惟鎮重足以勝之，而凝集於穆清之地；命本靡常也，惟恪恭足以膺之，而萃聚於淵默之中。大寶之貴，實天所眷佑者，于以承之而安於磐石，豐亨之治可常保也；神器之重，實天所付托者，于以受之而固於苞桑，豫大之慶可常享也。夫位之正也，猶鼎之正其器也；命之凝也，猶鼎之凝其實也。君子其善於體易者與！抑又論之，君子之正位，非以致飾也，蓋其敬德之容發於外者然耳。夫子於大舜，嘗以恭己正南面贊之，是恭己者即舜之所以正位也。然而禄位名壽咸萃于厥躬，則凝命之驗信不誣矣。為人君者，其可不以舜為法乎？

是故四營而成易，十有八變而成卦。
童楷

translation_en:
…solemn in his reverent comportment, with a bearing worthy of emulation. Where the sovereign’s position resides, there also resides the Mandate. Is setting his position aright not the means of consolidating his Mandate? The Mandate is indeed not easily sustained: only dignified gravity suffices to bear it, bringing it firmly together in the place of august purity. The Mandate is indeed inconstant: only reverent respect suffices to receive it, gathering it amid profound stillness. The exalted dignity of the throne is truly what Heaven cherishes and protects. By thus upholding it and making it secure as a great rock, one can preserve forever a flourishing and prosperous reign. The weighty sacred vessel of sovereignty is truly what Heaven has entrusted to the ruler. By thus receiving it and making it firm as a clump of mulberry roots, one can enjoy forever the blessings of joyous greatness. Setting one’s position aright is like setting the vessel of the cauldron upright; consolidating the Mandate is like bringing the cauldron’s contents to firmness. How well the gentleman embodies the Book of Changes!

To consider this further: when the gentleman sets his position aright, he does not do so for outward embellishment. It is simply the outward manifestation of his reverence for virtue. The Master once praised the great Shun for reverently composing himself and taking his proper place facing south. Thus, reverently composing himself was precisely how Shun set his position aright. Moreover, emolument, rank, fame, and longevity all gathered in his person: this surely provides genuine proof of the consolidation of the Mandate. Can a ruler fail to take Shun as his model?

“Thus, four operations complete a change, and eighteen transformations complete a hexagram.”
Tong Kai 童楷

The Great Commentary discusses the method of counting yarrow stalks, tracing how changes arise and bringing together the means by which the lines are completed. Counting yarrow stalks is the means of obtaining a hexagram. Yet unless one investigates the initial process by which a change is completed, how can a hexagram be formed? Now, the number of the Great Expansion is fifty, of which forty-nine are used. What, then, should be the sequence for using them? The procedure begins with dividing them into two groups; next, one stalk is set apart; then they are counted off in fours, making three operations. Finally, the remainders are gathered, making four operations. In this way, the method of comparing and checking the numbers has a basis, and their actual quantities can be verified. A total of five or four produces the odd value of a single change; a total of nine or eight produces the even value of a single change. At this point the counting of yarrow stalks reaches a fresh beginning, and its component steps are complete. If even one operation were missing, how could a change be completed?

From the first line to the topmost, root and culmination are fully displayed; from beginning to end, the successive stages [?] are ordered. Nor is this all. By extending the process and developing it through analogous cases, a single hexagram can be transformed into all sixty-four hexagrams. One who can maintain constancy in the virtues he has already attained will surely prove effective in the duties for which he is subsequently employed. This concerns discerning men’s worth. For attained virtue must be manifest and constant. If it is not, how can it serve the needs of noble houses and states, and bring about government that is profoundly enlightened and faithfully discharges its duties? Gao Yao presented his counsels to Shun, and here he speaks of discerning men’s worth. Is his meaning not this: men of accomplished virtue are certainly capable of pursuing good government, but in the manifestation of their virtue, constancy is especially precious?
Among the nine virtues, there are those who possess three. If these three virtues are not manifested daily, then those who have attained them will simply remain at that level. If such a man is employed as a grand master, how can he bring profound enlightenment to the affairs of his noble house? Surely he must renew himself daily and flourish monthly, so that his efforts at self-cultivation increase without cease; he must advance daily and grow monthly, so that his efforts to extend and develop his virtues strengthen without declining. What he has acquired within himself, he makes manifest and ever more radiant; what appears in his conduct, he expands and makes ever greater. If such a person is made a regional lord, how can he effectively discharge the duties of governing a state? Surely he must exercise restraint and dare not indulge himself: he must tirelessly preserve what he already possesses and constantly strive for what he has yet to attain. He must maintain self-command and dare not grow lax: he must hold fast without slackening to what he has already achieved and remain deeply concerned about his deficiencies. In this way, the six virtues become manifest in his person and enduring.

If such a person is appointed a regional lord, I envisage moral instruction spreading resplendently within his state's boundaries and the transforming influence of good government abundantly permeating its territory. Thus it is said: “Daily make them manifest and daily attend to them with reverence”; then they become evident and enduring. It is said: “Greatly illuminate them and faithfully discharge one's duties”; then one is excellent and fit for service. If a ruler wishes fully to accomplish the task of knowing men, how can he neglect this?

賢王命大臣，既欲明勸懲之政以化殷民，尤欲嚴根本之地以安天下。蓋勸懲既明，則民之區別者未必皆能自安也。使非嚴根本之地，亦何以防未然之釁，以安天下哉？康王命畢公保釐東郊而勉之以此，若謂予命公以周公之事者，豈有他哉？亦惟望公盡保釐之責耳。彼商民之中，不有淑者乎？則旌之而不沒其善；不有慝者乎？則別之而不宥其惡。旌淑何如？蓋率汝訓典而不違，民之淑者也，則表其宅里，于焉顯其善

…the suburban boundaries; carefully secure the territorial defenses, thereby bringing peace to all within the Four Seas.

Yu Yi

Associate Examiner Lu, an Assistant Instructor, comments: The topic itself is stately and dignified. Writers generally treat the passages on distinguishing the good from the wicked and commending goodness and censuring evil only cursorily [two illegible characters; sense uncertain]. This essay analyzes them clearly and thoroughly, capturing King Kang’s intention to transform the people of Yin and secure the foundations of his rule. It is therefore included as a model for students of the Classics.

Associate Examiner Geng, an Instructor, comments: Concise in expression and complete in meaning, it fully captures the proper manner of charging a minister. Admirable, admirable!

Examiner Zhu, a Reader-in-waiting, comments: It skillfully develops the meaning of King Kang’s address to the Duke of Bi.

Examiner Jiang, a Reader-in-waiting Academician, comments: The composition has openings and “locks” [?].

When a worthy king charges a great minister, he wishes both to make clear the policies of encouragement and punishment in order to transform the people of Yin, and, above all, to secure the region that forms the foundation of his rule in order to bring peace to the realm. For once encouragement and punishment have been made clear, those among the people who have been distinguished from one another may not all remain content with their lot. Without securing this foundational region, how could he forestall trouble before it arises and bring peace to the realm? King Kang charged the Duke of Bi with safeguarding and administering the eastern suburbs and exhorted him in these terms, as though saying: “In entrusting you, my lord, with the work of the Duke of Zhou, could I have any other purpose? I merely hope that you will fully discharge your responsibility to safeguard and administer the region. Among those people of Shang, are there not good people? Honor them, so that their goodness is not obscured. Are there not wicked people? Distinguish them, and do not pardon their wickedness. How should the good be honored? Those who follow your instructions and established rules without contravening them are the good among the people. Mark their dwellings and neighborhoods, thereby making their goodness manifest…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以病其惡使為善之風聲聳然而樹挺然而立
有以播今而傳後也別慝何如盖違汝訓典而
弗率民之慝者也則殊其井疆乎以區其惡不
雜於善使為惡之頑民畏禍於已慕福於人莫
不警悚而悔悟也然既兼舉夫旌別之政則當
潛消其覬覦之心故郊圻之制昔固規畫矣公
必思其歲乆則易湮而申明之有章封域之險
昔固有守矣公必念其時平則易玩而戒嚴之
有備王畿既尊則居重以馭輕而四海之遠可
===
康乂也況商民之見旌者寧不益勉於善乎京
邑既嚴則宅中以制外而天下之大可寧謐也
況商民之見別者安敢復肆其惡乎吁既明勸
懲以化殷民又嚴根本以防殷民保釐之政尚
有要於此哉大抵旌別不明則善惡必至於混
殽根本不固則姦宄必至於窺伺果爾古之人
君未有不以勸善懲惡脩內攘外為治道之要
者康王生重熙累洽之後能不以宴安自怠保
釐之命拳拳以是望之畢公盖非徒以監畢公

punctuated: 以病其惡，使為善之風聲聳然而樹，挺然而立，有以播今而傳後也。別慝何如？盖違汝訓典而弗率，民之慝者也，則殊其井疆乎，以區其惡，不雜於善，使為惡之頑民畏禍於已，慕福於人，莫不警悚而悔悟也。然既兼舉夫旌別之政，則當潛消其覬覦之心。故郊圻之制，昔固規畫矣，公必思其歲乆則易湮，而申明之有章；封域之險，昔固有守矣，公必念其時平則易玩，而戒嚴之有備。王畿既尊，則居重以馭輕，而四海之遠可康乂也，況商民之見旌者，寧不益勉於善乎？京邑既嚴，則宅中以制外，而天下之大可寧謐也，況商民之見別者，安敢復肆其惡乎？吁！既明勸懲以化殷民，又嚴根本以防殷民，保釐之政尚有要於此哉？大抵旌別不明，則善惡必至於混殽；根本不固，則姦宄必至於窺伺。果爾，古之人君未有不以勸善懲惡、脩內攘外為治道之要者。康王生重熙累洽之後，能不以宴安自怠，保釐之命拳拳以是望之畢公，盖非徒以監畢公
translation_en:
…thereby to rebuke their evil, so that the influence and reputation of doing good rise conspicuously and stand firmly established, spreading in the present and passing down to posterity. What does it mean to distinguish the wicked? Those who violate your instructions and statutes and refuse to follow them are the wicked among the people. Set apart the boundaries of their well-field allotments, thereby separating the wicked so that they do not mingle with the good. This will make the stubborn people who do evil fear calamity for themselves and covet the blessings enjoyed by others, so that all become alarmed, repent, and awaken to their errors.

Yet once both policies—honoring the good and distinguishing the wicked—have been implemented, their covetous ambitions must also be quietly extinguished. The arrangements for the capital’s outskirts and borderlands were certainly planned long ago; you, my lord, must consider how easily they may fall into oblivion as the years pass, and reaffirm them through clear regulations. The strategic positions within the territory certainly had defenses long ago; you must remember how readily these may be neglected in peaceful times, and enforce vigilance with adequate preparations. Once the royal domain commands respect, its central weight can govern the less weighty regions, and even the distant lands within the Four Seas can enjoy peace and order. How much more, then, will those among the Shang people who have been honored strive to do good! Once the capital is strictly secured, the center can control the outer regions, and the whole vast realm can enjoy tranquility. How, then, would those among the Shang people who have been singled out dare again to indulge in evil?

Ah! Having made encouragement and punishment clear in order to transform the Yin people, and having also secured the realm’s foundations in order to guard against them, could anything be more essential to the work of protecting and governing? In general, if honoring the good and distinguishing the wicked are not clearly carried out, good and evil will inevitably become confused; if the foundations are not secure, evildoers within and without will inevitably watch for an opportunity. This being so, rulers of antiquity invariably regarded encouraging good and punishing evil, ordering affairs within and warding off threats from without, as essential to the way of government. Born after successive generations of prosperity and settled rule, King Kang nevertheless did not allow ease and comfort to make him remiss. In his charge to protect and govern, he earnestly placed these expectations upon Bi Gong, surely not merely to admonish Bi Gong…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
命而代商者皆由於此以戒成王此則言大命
福周之遠其意謂夫我文王以亹亹之德膺天
心之眷豈徒尊榮其身而已哉是故麟趾振振
衍瑞慶於無窮何者非我文王之孫子瓜瓞綿
綿垂休禎於不竭何者非我文王之子孫有宗
子焉莫不出震繼離而統馭乎萬方將使歷百
世之遠永傳帝王之曆數也有支庶焉莫不分
茅胙土而君臨乎一國將使歷千載之久永為
王室之藩衛也豈但已哉彼疏附先後我文王
===
有一代之臣也濟濟乎其多矣奔走禦侮我文
王有一代之士也藹藹乎其眾矣今皆自天佑
之使周士之後昆亦顯顯乎世脩其德上有是
君下有是臣將永保至治之休而與周家媲美
於無疆焉自天申之使周士之後嗣亦昭昭乎
世濟其美君明於上臣良於下將永綏太平之
盛而與我周匹休於無窮焉是則本支百世固
福周也不顯亦世亦福周也文王盛德格天之
至有如是哉大抵帝王大業未有不由於祖宗

punctuated: 命而代商者，皆由於此，以戒成王。此則言大命福周之遠，其意謂：夫我文王以亹亹之德，膺天心之眷，豈徒尊榮其身而已哉？是故麟趾振振，衍瑞慶於無窮，何者非我文王之孫子？瓜瓞綿綿，垂休禎於不竭，何者非我文王之子孫？有宗子焉，莫不出震繼離而統馭乎萬方，將使歷百世之遠，永傳帝王之曆數也。有支庶焉，莫不分茅胙土而君臨乎一國，將使歷千載之久，永為王室之藩衛也。豈但已哉？彼疏附先後，我文王有一代之臣也，濟濟乎其多矣；奔走禦侮，我文王有一代之士也，藹藹乎其眾矣。今皆自天佑之，使周士之後昆亦顯顯乎世脩其德，上有是君，下有是臣，將永保至治之休，而與周家媲美於無疆焉。自天申之，使周士之後嗣亦昭昭乎世濟其美，君明於上，臣良於下，將永綏太平之盛，而與我周匹休於無窮焉。是則本支百世，固福周也；不顯亦世，亦福周也。文王盛德格天之至，有如是哉！大抵帝王大業，未有不由於祖宗
translation_en:
…that its receiving the Mandate and supplanting Shang all arose from this, thereby admonishing King Cheng. This passage speaks of the far-reaching blessings bestowed upon Zhou by the great Mandate. Its meaning is this: our King Wen, through his unremitting virtue, received Heaven’s favor. Could this have served merely to honor and exalt his own person?

Thus, like the auspicious qilin’s feet, his descendants were virtuous and flourishing, extending auspicious blessings without end. Which of them was not a descendant of our King Wen? Like an unbroken succession of large and small melons upon the vine, they perpetuated good fortune inexhaustibly. Which of them was not an offspring of our King Wen? Those of the principal line all emerged in Zhen and succeeded in Li—the images of sovereign succession in the Changes—to rule the myriad regions, so that through a hundred generations they might transmit forever the succession ordained for emperors and kings. Those of the collateral lines all received grants of thatch and territory and ruled over individual states, so that for a thousand years they might remain forever the royal house’s protecting bulwarks.

Was this all? Those who drew the distant near, attached the people to him, and assisted him before and behind were our King Wen’s ministers of that age: how numerous and distinguished they were! Those who hastened in his service and resisted aggression were our King Wen’s officers of that age: how abundant their ranks! Now Heaven protects them all, causing the descendants of Zhou’s officers likewise to cultivate their virtue conspicuously from generation to generation. With such rulers above and such ministers below, they will preserve forever the blessings of consummate government and rival the house of Zhou in excellence without limit. Heaven renews its favor toward them, causing the heirs of Zhou’s officers likewise to carry forward their excellence illustriously from generation to generation. With enlightened rulers above and worthy ministers below, they will secure forever the flourishing of great peace and match our Zhou in glory without end.

Thus, that ‘the main line and its branches endure for a hundred generations’ is assuredly a blessing upon Zhou; that ‘they are illustrious from generation to generation’ is also a blessing upon Zhou. Such was the utmost power of King Wen’s abundant virtue to reach Heaven! In general, the great enterprise of emperors and kings has never failed to derive from their ancestors…

translation_en:
…in encamping, he failed to observe the propriety of relieving distress; subsequently, in encamping during his campaign against Chu, he attained the benevolence of caring for the people. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to censure the one and praise the other? Alas, when Xing suffered an attack by the Di, Duke Huan of Qi led the armies of three states to its rescue, and there was an encampment at Niebei. The Spring and Autumn Annals praised the encampment in the later campaign at Xingting; why, then, did it censure this one? Because the danger facing the people of Xing was so imminent that they might not last until evening. If Duke Huan wished to rescue them, he had to act swiftly. Had the duke, once the alarm sounded on the frontier, marched with redoubled speed, what would the Spring and Autumn Annals have censured? Why did he merely proclaim his concern for those in distress while actually harboring the intention of letting disorder grow? With Song and Cao alongside him, his strength was certainly sufficient, yet he hesitated and would not advance. Repelling external enemies and securing internal peace was an undertaking admitting of no doubt, yet he treated the enemy lightly and waited for Xing to perish. Only when Xing’s situation grew more desperate by the day, until it could scarcely survive, did he slowly bestir himself and build walls for it. Such was his lack of resolve in relieving distress! In compiling the Classic, the Sage considered rescuing those in distress and sharing the burden of calamity urgent duties under ritual propriety. Yet in rescuing Xing, Duke Huan deliberately delayed when he ought to have acted swiftly. Could the Sage refrain from censuring him? Thus the encampment is recorded first and the rescue afterward. As the Commentary says, “When a rescue is recorded with an encampment, the encampment conveys censure.” This is precisely the point.

As for Chu’s becoming a menace to the Central States, Duke Huan of Qi led his state’s army to attack it, and there was an encampment at Xingting. Because the people of Chu could not readily be won over by force. Duke Huan wished to [four illegible characters] and could not act without caution [?]. title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
春秋奚美焉幸而謀欲出于萬全志不快于一
逞嚴兵固圉非畏縮也將以慎用乎民脩詞問
罪非迂緩也將以柔服乎遠逮夫楚人震恐遣
使如師即退舍以禮之非有志於愛民者能如
是哉聖人脩經以為好攻樂殺於罪為大而桓
之伐楚能全師愛民如此欲不美之可乎故先
書伐而後書次者傳曰伐而書次以次為美是
矣是則救邢不譏則凡怠恤患之義者無所懲
伐楚不美則凡存愛民之仁者無所勸褒貶在
===
一人而無窮之勸懲以寓然則聖人之義其可
以一端求之哉抑救邢之後始之次也固可罪
矣而終之城也亦可罪乎伐楚之役終之次也
固可美矣而始之專也亦可美乎故觀夷儀之
後而繼有三師之城侵蔡之下一而敢專八國之
伐則桓公之功過得失當相準矣噫功不足以
掩過得不足以救失伯者之事大抵皆然吾於
桓公乎何尤

punctuated:
《春秋》奚美焉？幸而謀欲出于萬全，志不快于一逞。嚴兵固圉，非畏縮也，將以慎用乎民；脩詞問罪，非迂緩也，將以柔服乎遠。逮夫楚人震恐，遣使如師，即退舍以禮之。非有志於愛民者，能如是哉？聖人脩經，以為好攻樂殺，於罪為大，而桓之伐楚，能全師愛民如此，欲不美之可乎？故先書伐而後書次者，傳曰：「伐而書次，以次為美。」是矣。是則救邢不譏，則凡怠恤患之義者無所懲；伐楚不美，則凡存愛民之仁者無所勸。褒貶在一人，而無窮之勸懲以寓。然則聖人之義，其可以一端求之哉？抑救邢之後，始之次也固可罪矣，而終之城也亦可罪乎？伐楚之役，終之次也固可美矣，而始之專也亦可美乎？故觀夷儀之後，而繼有三師之城；侵蔡之下，一而敢專八國之伐，則桓公之功過得失當相準矣。噫！功不足以掩過，得不足以救失，伯者之事大抵皆然。吾於桓公乎何尤？

translation_en:
…what would the Spring and Autumn Annals praise in this? Fortunately, his plans sought complete security, and his ambition was not gratified by a single display of force. He readied his troops and secured his defenses, not out of timidity, but to exercise care in employing the people. He framed his words carefully and called Chu to account, not out of dilatoriness, but to win the submission of those afar through conciliation. When the people of Chu became terrified and sent an envoy to his army, he withdrew his camp to receive the envoy with due courtesy. Could anyone without a determination to cherish the people have acted thus? In compiling the Classic, the Sage considered a fondness for aggression and a delight in killing among the gravest offenses. Yet Duke Huan’s campaign against Chu so preserved his army and cherished the people: how could it go unpraised? Thus, concerning the recording of the attack first and the encampment afterward, the Commentary says: “When an attack is recorded followed by an encampment, the encampment is grounds for praise.” This is precisely the point.

If the relief of Xing were not censured, those who neglected the duty to relieve distress would receive no admonition. If the campaign against Chu were not praised, those who maintained a benevolent concern for the people would receive no encouragement. Praise and blame concern a single man, yet embody encouragement and admonition without end. Can the Sage’s moral judgment, then, be sought in just one aspect? Moreover, in the relief of Xing, the initial encampment certainly deserved blame; but did the eventual building of city walls also deserve blame? In the campaign against Chu, the final encampment certainly deserved praise; but did the initial assumption of unauthorized power also deserve praise? Thus, when we observe that the reference to Yiyi is followed by the three armies’ building of its walls, and that the incursion into Cai is followed by his daring, alone [?], to assume authority over the eight states’ campaign, Duke Huan’s achievements and faults, successes and failures, should be weighed against one another. Alas! Achievements cannot conceal faults, nor can successes make good failures. Such, on the whole, are the affairs of hegemons. Why should I single out Duke Huan for reproach?

Men of Jin, Song, Wei, and Chen made an incursion into Zheng. 〔Third year of Duke Xuan〕

This essay alone develops them as an integrated whole, allowing the commentary’s meaning to emerge naturally. It is assuredly an essay that contributes to understanding.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, an Academician Expositor-in-waiting: It displays great decisiveness of judgment.

When a hegemonic state chastises a wavering ally but lacks moral justification, the Spring and Autumn Annals records the facts directly to convey its criticism. Here we see that Zheng had a valid case for attacking Song on Chu’s behalf, whereas Jin lacked justification for siding with Song and oppressing Zheng. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals refrain from sternly censuring Jin? Why is this so? When Zheng defeated Song at Daji, Zheng was indeed aligned with Chu. Jin, wishing to retaliate against Chu, assembled allied forces to attack Zheng. Thus Guisheng’s defeat of Song amounted to following the barbarians, while Zhao Dun’s chastisement of Zheng amounted to preserving the Chinese states. Once Jin’s army marched out, three states followed it. Why, then, in recording this campaign, does the Spring and Autumn Annals designate the ministers merely as “men” and describe the military action as an “incursion”? Righteousness is the impartial moral principle shared by all under Heaven; profit is the selfish impulse of human desire. The wickedness of Bao of Song was beyond pardon under royal law. Why did Jin’s ruler and ministers undertake no expedition to punish the traitor, but instead negotiate a covenant that consolidated the disorder? They had thereby already abandoned the great moral obligation owed to all under Heaven. Of Guisheng’s attack on Song at Chu’s command, one might say that he led barbarians to ravage the Chinese states. Yet this overlooks the fact that anyone may punish a traitor guilty of high treason—and Chu did punish him. … righteousness did not permit siding with it, yet Jin did so. An army’s cause must be just before its spirit can be strong; an undertaking must begin cautiously if it is to end well. At the outset, Jin, greedy for gain, set aside the punishment ordained by Heaven. What caution was there in this? Subsequently, it sided with evildoers and dispatched troops to bully the weak. What justice was there in this? Its cause was crooked rather than upright, and thus, although its army was powerful, it was dispirited. Hence, in the incursion at Fenmin [?], it failed to take up arms to punish wrongdoing; when Dou Jiao arrived, it hastily packed up its armor and withdrew. Had the covenant at Hu been free of the fault of greed for bribes, why would Jin’s army, then at the height of its strength, have come to fear Chu? Had the incursion into Zheng not been an act of siding with evildoers, why, with all the allied states present, could it not bring Zheng to submission? When the gentleman undertakes something, he plans its beginning; planning the beginning is how he takes thought for the end. What trace of this was there in the ruler of Jin? Thus, in this passage, the Spring and Autumn Annals refers to the ministers merely as “men” and records the punitive expedition against Zheng as an “incursion.” Because its foundation was unsound, the text censures it severely, as a warning against the consequences that follow. Ah! Within this single instance of its manner of recording events are embodied the duty to punish traitors, the warning against greed for gain, the injunction to be cautious at the outset, and the way of rectifying the foundation. How true the saying that none but a sage could compile the Spring and Autumn Annals!

Yet although Jin’s guilt certainly cannot be excused, Zheng’s conduct was, after all, not entirely good either. Duke Ling of Jin was greedy and corrupt, and certainly unworthy of alliance; but King Zhuang of Chu was a barbarian from the periphery—was he someone whom Zheng ought to follow? Moreover, mobilizing its forces today to ravage Chen and wearing out its troops tomorrow to plunder Song, Zheng could neither escape the offense of bringing turmoil upon the Chinese states nor fulfill the righteous duty of punishing traitors. What, indeed, was Zheng trying to accomplish? The Spring and Autumn Annals censures Jin over the incursion into Zheng specifically because Jin sided with evildoers. 夫禮雖有一定之制，而亦有變通之宜也。義無害於可為，則禮不妨於創矣，奚必嫌於古制之未有哉？記《禮運》者謂夫先王以治情為急，治情以脩禮為先。彼經禮三百，固所以防範乎人情者也；然經制一定，孰得而踰其規程？曲禮三千，固所以綱維乎人情者也；然法制一定，孰得而

…was without fault and Jin ought not to have punished it. This, too, is something readers of the Classic should understand.

Book of Rites (Liji)
“Thus ritual is the concrete embodiment of rightness. If a practice is measured against rightness and accords with it, then even though the former kings had no such ritual, it may be instituted on the basis of rightness.”

越其矩度曰親曰疎隨事順理人知其為義矣
而不知親疎之禮實確乎其有定則焉曰貴曰
賤因時制宜人知其為義矣而不知貴賤之禮
實卓乎其有定制焉是果何自而見之哉以禮

translation_en:
…overstep their prescribed bounds? In distinguishing close from distant kin, one follows the circumstances and accords with principle. People recognize this as righteousness, yet do not recognize that the rites governing close and distant kin have firmly established rules. In distinguishing the noble from the lowly, one adapts measures to the times. People recognize this as righteousness, yet do not recognize that the rites governing noble and lowly have clearly established institutions. How, then, can this be seen? Rites cannot simply be initiated at will. Yet if, after deliberation and assessment, the circumstances accord with righteousness, then even a rite unknown to the former kings may be newly instituted through consideration of righteousness. What constraint need there be? Rites cannot simply be devised at will. Yet if, after careful consideration, righteousness is brought into accord with circumstances, then even a rite not established by the former kings may be newly made into a rule by weighing it against righteousness. What objection need there be? For example, the ritual emphasis on substance had not existed under the Xia; the Shang initiated it in accordance with righteousness and were never constrained by the Xia emphasis on loyalty. The ritual emphasis on refinement had not existed under the Shang; the Zhou initiated it in accordance with righteousness and likewise never clung to substance. Rites arise through righteousness, and righteousness is put into practice through rites. Thus we can see that rites are the concrete embodiment of righteousness. Could the former kings have had no reason for making the cultivation of rites their first priority in regulating human feelings? Generally speaking, rites and righteousness must accompany one another; neither can dispense with the other. Without rites, righteousness has no means of embodying its constant principles; without righteousness, rites have no means of accommodating change. This is why the former kings, in regulating human feelings, necessarily took rites and righteousness as their guiding framework and never departed from them. Let those intent on instituting rites examine this.

To fathom the root and understand change is the essential nature of music; to manifest sincerity and eliminate falsity is the constant principle of rites.

治情而情無不同者樂化之自然治情而情無

===

不同同則本一也自其氣而言不能無異異則
變多也樂以統同故能窮其本之同而使理之
原於心者皆全其降衷之初知其變之異而使

則情無不同矣此豈強之使然哉蓋統同者樂
之用也情不與樂期而樂自妙於情之中樂不

To regulate the feelings so that all are brought into harmony is the natural effect of music’s transforming influence; to regulate the feelings so that all become good is the proper effect of ritual’s ordering power. Ritual and music bear profoundly upon human feelings. When feelings are regulated and none remain unregulated, could this be anything other than the operation of ritual and music? The gentleman speaking in the Record of Music means: People know that ritual and music encompass human feelings, but who understands how ritual and music regulate them? Consider human feelings: in terms of their principle, they are originally alike. Being alike, their root is one. In terms of their vital force, however, they cannot be without differences. Being different, their variations are many. Music unifies what is alike. Thus it can fathom the common root of feelings, allowing the principle originating in the heart to preserve fully its original, Heaven-endowed integrity. It can comprehend their differing variations, allowing human nature, when led astray amid feelings, to recover the goodness of its original substance. When the root is fathomed and the variations understood, all feelings are brought into harmony. How could this be achieved through compulsion? Unifying what is alike is the function of music. title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
與情會而情自得於樂之化凡所以安久天神
一皆感通之自然者耳謂非樂之情而何人之
情理存於中而甚微微則誠隱也欲動於物而
甚危危則偽生也禮以辨異故能著其理之誠
而使微者以顯純乎天理之流行去其欲之偽
而使危者以安絕無物欲之留滯夫著誠去偽
則情無不善矣此豈事之可已哉盖辨異者禮
之用也禮必達於情而後情之發始著其誠則
著誠之功何可無情必治於禮而後情之用始
===
去其偽則去偽之功何可少凡所以莊敬嚴威
一皆脩為之當然者耳謂非禮之經而何是則
禮樂之能治乎人情如此此其所以不可斯須
去身也歟雖然禮樂一道也而以為有情有經
若不同焉何也盖自天地之髙下散殊周流合
同而禮主於收斂樂主於發達固已有不同者
此禮所以能脩外而樂所以能脩內也至其交
錯於中而發形於外恭敬而温文焉則又何可
以異視哉學者析其異而會其同則得之矣

translation_en:
…meet with the feelings, yet the feelings find fulfillment through music’s transforming influence. Whatever brings about peace, endurance, conformity with Heaven, and spiritual efficacy arises entirely from the spontaneous workings of sympathetic response and communion. What could this be but the essential nature of music? Within human feelings, principle resides inwardly and is exceedingly subtle; because it is subtle, sincerity remains hidden. Desire is stirred by external things and is exceedingly precarious; because it is precarious, falsity arises. Ritual distinguishes differences. It can therefore manifest the sincerity of principle, making what is subtle apparent, so that there is nothing but the flow of heavenly principle. It removes the falsity of desire, bringing what is precarious to peace, so that no material desires remain lodged within. When sincerity is manifested and falsity removed, all feelings become good. How could this work ever be abandoned? Distinguishing differences is the function of ritual. Only when ritual reaches the feelings does their expression begin to manifest sincerity. How, then, could the work of manifesting sincerity be dispensed with? Only when the feelings are regulated by ritual does their operation begin to shed falsity. How, then, could the work of removing falsity be neglected? Whatever produces solemnity, reverence, dignity, and authority belongs entirely to what cultivation properly requires. What could this be but the constant principles of ritual? Such is the capacity of ritual and music to regulate human feelings. Is this not why one must never depart from them, even for an instant?

Nevertheless, ritual and music constitute a single Way. Why, then, speak of an essential nature for the one and constant principles for the other, as though they differed? The distinction is already present in the height of Heaven and the lowliness of Earth, in the differentiation and dispersal of things and in their circulating movement and harmonious union: ritual chiefly gathers and restrains, while music chiefly unfolds and gives expression. This is why ritual can cultivate the outward person and music the inward person. Yet when they interweave within and take visible form without, producing reverence and gentle refinement, how can they be regarded as separate? If learners distinguish their differences and comprehend their unity, they will grasp their meaning.

Discourse

The Sages’ Great Principles for Ordering the World

Hua Jin

Comment by Associate Examiner Tian, Instructor: The conception is lofty and imbued with antiquity; the phrasing is refined and elegant. This is surely among the outstanding discourses of this session.

It is like the unseasoned broth and plain water of ritual offerings, yet its harmonization has a distinction of its own. It differs from works that indulge in superficial ornament. This is what constitutes the proper form of a discourse.

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-Waiting: On this session’s topic, writers readily produce more than a thousand words, but their language is often vague and fails to address the point. This piece restrains ornament and concentrates on substance; its understanding is genuine and precise, without a single superfluous phrase. For this reason, I regard it as difficult to achieve.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: It illuminates principles, and its prose contains no empty language. This is an excellent discourse.

text:
法之著於簡冊者則固可考也後之人君如不
欲平治天下則已苟有志於治而舍聖人之大
法亦何足以言治哉子程子論帝王之學而曰
聖人經世大法備在方冊苟得其要舉而行之
無難也美哉言乎請繹其說夫天佑下民必生

從事則其責有不得而辭者矣於是乎裁成天
地之道輔相天地之宜以經綸乎斯世而立之

translation_en:
…the laws recorded on bamboo slips and in books can certainly be examined. If later rulers have no desire to bring peace and order to All under Heaven, there is nothing more to say; but if they aspire to good government yet abandon the sages’ great laws, how can they deserve to speak of governing? Master Cheng, discussing the learning of emperors and kings, said: “The sages’ great laws for ordering the world are fully preserved in books. If one grasps their essentials, putting them into practice presents no difficulty.” How admirable these words are! Allow me to unfold their meaning.

Heaven, in protecting the common people, must bring forth sages to serve as their rulers and teachers, governing and instructing them. When the sages undertake their work in accordance with Heaven’s intent, theirs is a responsibility they cannot decline. Thus they regulate and bring to completion the Way of Heaven and Earth, assist what is fitting to Heaven and Earth, and establish great laws to order this world. Concerned that the world might lack sustenance, they institute the well-field system to provide for it; concerned that it might lack instruction, they establish schools to teach it; concerned that it might lack encouragement, they make the five grades of official dress conspicuous to encourage goodness; concerned that it might lack restraints, they make the five punishments clear to restrain evil. Concerned that people might deceive one another, they provide tallies, seals, weights, and measures to ensure trust; concerned that people might encroach upon one another, they provide inner and outer city walls, armor, and weapons to protect them. They use the astronomical instruments to bring the celestial movements into harmony [?], thereby making the Way of Heaven manifest in the world; they regulate calendrical calculations and celestial observations to announce the seasons, thereby putting human affairs in order throughout the world. They employ the eight handles of authority to govern their ministers, so that all who serve as ministers follow their commands, none daring to dispense favors or wield punitive authority on their own. They employ the eight bonds of governance to govern the myriad people, so that all the people follow their way, none daring to act upon private likes or dislikes. As for the prescribed ceremonies for court audiences, diplomatic visits, and assemblies of rulers, and the established forms for cappings, marriages, funerals, and sacrifices…

text:
輿馬宮室之有等凡所以為經世之大法者何
徃而不備乎夫如是則仁義禮樂四達而不悖
而天下萬物咸囿於大法之中矣柰何世不常
治法不常守而聖人之生或不得其位則其於
天下獨能恝然矣乎於是舉先王經世之大法
托之經以詔後世則法雖不行於時而皆具於
方策之中矣是故賛易自羲軒而下則羲軒之

輿馬宮室之有等，凡所以為經世之大法者，何徃而不備乎？夫如是，則仁義禮樂四達而不悖，而天下萬物咸囿於大法之中矣。柰何世不常治，法不常守，而聖人之生或不得其位，則其於天下獨能恝然矣乎？於是舉先王經世之大法，托之經以詔後世，則法雖不行於時，而皆具於方策之中矣。是故賛《易》，自羲軒而下，則羲軒之經世大法寓於《易》；序《書》，自堯舜而下，則堯舜之經世大法寓於《書》；刪《詩》，自文武而下，則文武之經世大法寓於《詩》；脩《春秋》，自桓文而下，時雖無聖人之治，而吾夫子則假魯史之文，寓經世大法焉。
夫聖人之法，無一而非心之所存，無一而非道之所寓，所謂建諸天地而不悖，質諸鬼神而無疑，百世以俟聖人而不惑者也。後之君天下者，不於此而求之可乎？夫人之一心，廣大無垠，萬善咸備，盛德大業皆由此出。聖人之法所以傳之萬世而無弊者，固此心之推也。然則欲傳聖人之道而行聖人之法者，可不思所以擴
translation_en:
…and distinctions of rank in carriages, horses, palaces, and dwellings: in all that constitutes the great laws for ordering the world, what provision was lacking? Thus benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music extended everywhere without conflict, and all things under Heaven were encompassed within these great laws. Yet the world is not always well governed, the laws are not always observed, and a sage, when born, may fail to attain the proper position. Could he then remain indifferent to the world? He therefore took the former kings’ great laws for ordering the world and entrusted them to the classics to instruct later generations. Although these laws were not put into practice in his time, they were all preserved in written texts. Thus, in elucidating the Book of Changes, he traced matters from Fuxi and Xuanyuan onward, lodging their great laws for ordering the world in the Changes. In arranging the Book of Documents, he traced matters from Yao and Shun onward, lodging their great laws for ordering the world in the Documents. In editing the Book of Odes, he traced matters from Kings Wen and Wu onward, lodging their great laws for ordering the world in the Odes. In compiling the Spring and Autumn Annals, he treated the period from Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin onward. Although that age lacked the government of a sage, our Master used the text of the historical records of Lu to lodge within it the great laws for ordering the world.
There is not one law of the sage that does not embody what resides in his heart, nor one in which the Way does not dwell. These are what is meant by “established before Heaven and Earth without contradiction, tested against ghosts and spirits without doubt, and awaiting a sage a hundred generations hence without misgiving.” Can those who later rule all under Heaven fail to seek their guidance here? The human heart is vast and boundless, containing every goodness; flourishing virtue and great achievements all issue from it. The sage’s laws can be transmitted through ten thousand generations without becoming defective precisely because they are an extension of this heart. Thus, can those who wish to transmit the sage’s Way and put the sage’s laws into practice fail to consider how to expand…

充其心乎？欲充是心，必自學始，而帝王之學，非尋章摘句之為務也，亦在乎得其要耳。茍得其要也，而充是心以行之，則吾之德即聖人之德，吾之業即聖人之業，而二帝三王之治，孰謂其不可復哉？嗟乎！三代而下，人主好學者蓋有之矣。若魏文、隋煬之流，馳騁乎詞章翰墨者，固不足與論聖人之道。至於漢武帝之表章六經、明帝之講經辟雍，若有志乎聖學矣，而其治終不古若者，何哉？由其心之不充，而學之無其要故也。故欲行先王之大法者，其必從事於精一執中之訓而後可。茍無是心，則雖舉是法而行之，亦徒法耳，又安能比隆於唐虞三代哉？程子他日又云：「必有關雎、麟趾之意，然後可以行周官之法度。」其推本之論深矣。

translation_en:
…expand and fully develop their heart? To develop this heart fully, one must begin with learning. Yet the learning of emperors and kings does not consist in searching out passages and picking out phrases; it lies in grasping the essentials. If I grasp those essentials and fully develop this heart so as to put them into practice, then my virtue will be the virtue of the sages, and my achievements will be the achievements of the sages. Who could say that the good government of the Two Emperors and Three Kings cannot be restored?
Alas! Since the Three Dynasties, there have indeed been rulers who loved learning. Men such as Emperor Wen of Wei and Emperor Yang of Sui, who ranged freely through literary composition and brushwork, are certainly unworthy of being included in a discussion of the Way of the sages. As for Emperor Wu of Han’s honoring and promoting the Six Classics, and Emperor Ming’s lecturing on the classics at the Biyong, the imperial ceremonial academy, these seem to show an aspiration toward the learning of the sages. Why, then, did their government ultimately fail to equal that of antiquity? It was because they did not fully develop their hearts, and their learning failed to grasp the essentials. Thus, anyone wishing to implement the great institutions of the former kings must first devote himself to the teaching of refinement, singleness of purpose, and holding fast to the Mean. Without this heart, even if one adopts and implements these institutions, they remain mere institutions. How could one then rival the flourishing rule of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties? Master Cheng also said on another occasion: “Only when one possesses the spirit of ‘Guanju’ [The Calling Ospreys] and ‘Linzhi’ [The Qilin’s Hooves] can one put into practice the laws and institutions of the Offices of Zhou.” Profound indeed is his argument tracing things back to their root.

運歷之靈長，垂光厚被於雲來，流澤涵濡於億兆。發揮昌緒，見大宗小宗之蕃；申載宏綱，示特書屢書之重。奕奕瓊瑶之刻，洋洋軌範之言，繫日繫時，有倫有要。申命纂修於秘閣，有嚴論述於史筵。昭穆派分，咸星羅於紫極；戚疎區別，實日靖於洪圖。振振仁厚之風，皞皞泰和之治。銀潢滉漾，玉版閎嚴。千八百國之封，先乎異姓；五三六經之籍，展也同符。烈祖文孫，一本纘承之懿；皇支帝載，萬年基業之隆。歡洽臣民，光生海宇。
恭惟皇帝陛下，隆恩睦族，
translation_en:
…the numinous longevity of the dynasty’s allotted span, extending its radiance abundantly to distant descendants and letting its beneficence permeate the countless multitudes. Elucidating the glorious succession, it reveals the flourishing of the senior and junior lineage branches; setting forth anew the grand guiding principles, it demonstrates the importance of recording matters expressly and repeatedly. Resplendent are the inscriptions on precious jade; abundant are the words that establish norms. Dates and times are attached, with due order and essential points. Renewed commands order compilation in the Palace Library, and exposition proceeds with solemn care at the historians’席 [?]. The lineage branches are distinguished by alternating generational rank, arrayed like stars about the imperial pole; close and distant kin are differentiated, daily securing the grand dynastic design. Flourishing is the spirit of benevolence and generosity; expansive and joyous is the reign of supreme harmony. The celestial river—the imperial lineage—flows broad and shimmering; the jade tablets are magnificent and solemn. In the enfeoffment of eighteen hundred states, imperial kinsmen took precedence over those of other surnames; with the records of the Five Emperors and Three Kings and the Six Classics [?], this truly accords. Illustrious ancestors and cultured descendants display the excellence of succession from a single root; imperial branches and sovereign undertakings sustain the grandeur of a foundation lasting ten thousand years. Joy suffuses officials and people; radiance fills the realm within the seas.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor, through abundant favor, brings harmony to the imperial clan…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
駿惠紹基
世胄綿延監
枝葉本根之輔
皇猷渾灝思規摸榘矱之遵既蕩蕩以無名
實親親而有序
本宗繼體為
天子一統至于萬年支庶分土為
親藩永命兼乎三代舄越光華之旦昭宣丕
大之彝典冊崇成天人交慶臣等叨官侍
===
從備職編摩才愧柳芳陋唐室新圖之日
錄識慚班固鄙漢家世譜之歲脩幸琬琰
之在陳仰
殿廷而上
進伏願
一人有慶萬方共仰乎休明
四國于蕃九有同躋於嘉靖臣等無任瞻
天仰
聖激切屏營之至謹以所修

駿惠紹基

枝葉本根之輔

本宗繼體爲

親藩永命兼乎三代劉越光華之旦昭宣丕

===
從備職編摩才愧柳芳陋唐室新圖之日
錄識慚班固鄙漢家世譜之歲淆幸琬琰
之在陳仰
殿廷而上
進伏願
一人有慶萬方共仰乎休明
四國于蕃九有同躋於嘉靖臣等無任瞻
天仰
聖激切屛營之至謹以所修
punctuated:
駿惠紹基，世胄綿延，監枝葉本根之輔；皇猷渾灝，思規摸榘矱之遵。既蕩蕩以無名，實親親而有序。本宗繼體為天子，一統至于萬年；支庶分土為親藩，永命兼乎三代。舄越光華之旦，昭宣丕大之彝，典冊崇成，天人交慶。
臣等叨官侍從，備職編摩，才愧柳芳，陋唐室新圖之日錄；識慚班固，鄙漢家世譜之歲脩。幸琬琰之在陳，仰殿廷而上進。伏願一人有慶，萬方共仰乎休明；四國于蕃，九有同躋於嘉靖。臣等無任瞻天仰聖、激切屏營之至，謹以所修
translation_en:
…Grandly following your predecessors and continuing their foundations, you perpetuate the hereditary line, discerning how branches and leaves sustain the root and trunk. Your imperial designs are vast and expansive; you intend to follow the established patterns and standards. Your greatness is indeed beyond naming, yet your affection for your kin observes due order. The principal lineage succeeds to the throne as Son of Heaven, maintaining unified rule for ten thousand years; the collateral branches receive territories as imperial princes, perpetuating the dynastic mandate to rival the Three Dynasties. On this day of resplendent glory [?], you proclaim the grand and enduring institutions. The august compilation is completed, and Heaven and humankind rejoice together.
We, your servants, have undeservedly received appointments in your attendance and discharge the duties of compilation. Our talents fall short of those of Liu Fang; the daily recording of the Tang house’s new genealogical charts seems meager by comparison [?]. Our knowledge falls short of that of Ban Gu; the annual revision of the Han house’s genealogies seems inadequate by comparison. Fortunately, this precious, jade-like work is ready for presentation; looking up toward the palace court, we submit it to you. We humbly wish that the One Man—the sovereign—may enjoy blessings, and that all regions may together look up to your beneficent and enlightened rule; that the lands on every side may serve as protective barriers, and that all the Nine Regions may attain good order and peace together. Gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your Sagely Majesty, we, your servants, cannot contain our fervent emotion and utmost reverent trepidation. We respectfully take what we have compiled…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以道許
聖無虐尤宛曲詳密且忠愛之意溢於言表得士如此良可為賢科慶美
同考試官學正韓批此策於古人弭災之道
條答既悉至論今日
上下恊德脩省之要尤為有見非實才碩學之士而能若是乎
考試官侍讀朱批
皇祖存心省躬二錄誠萬世
君臣之龜鑑場中士子鮮能言之求其源委肯綮如此篇者絕少末復以存
前二事為
===
今日召和之助其意尤切他日有位于
朝必能持此獻忠謨以事
上矣
考試官侍讀學士蔣批此策窺見
聖祖筆酥垂訓之意發而為忠愛之言委曲懇到有有跡不盡之意其可敬
也夫
人君有奉天之道人臣有事君之道奉天
之道在乎敬事君之道在乎忠君焉而不
致力於身心則無以盡其敬臣焉而不致

以益新

□□□□□□□□〔娓娓既懇至論今日〕

君臣之義經場中士子雖能言之求其原究意者如此篇者絶少予復以存
□□□□
===
□□□□□□□
今日爲和之助其意尤切備日有□于
朝必能特嘗當之□以事
上矣
考試官侍讀學士蔣　批〔此篇□見〕
聖祖精勤奉訓之意發而爲忠愛之言是不謬列有有誠不盡之意其可敬
也夫
人君有奉天之道人臣有事君之道奉天
之道在乎敬事君之道在乎忠君焉而不
致力於身心則無以盡其敬臣焉而不致
punctuated:
以道許聖無虐，尤宛曲詳密，且忠愛之意溢於言表。得士如此，良可為賢科慶美。

同考試官學正韓批：此策於古人弭災之道，條答既悉，至論今日上下恊德脩省之要，尤為有見。非實才碩學之士，而能若是乎？

考試官侍讀朱批：皇祖《存心》《省躬》二錄，誠萬世君臣之龜鑑。場中士子鮮能言之，求其源委肯綮如此篇者絕少。末復以存前二事為今日召和之助，其意尤切。他日有位于朝，必能持此獻忠謨以事上矣。

考試官侍讀學士蔣批：此策窺見聖祖筆酥垂訓之意，發而為忠愛之言，委曲懇到，有有跡不盡之意，其可敬也夫！

人君有奉天之道，人臣有事君之道。奉天之道在乎敬，事君之道在乎忠。君焉而不致力於身心，則無以盡其敬；臣焉而不致
translation_en:
…[The opening words, 以道許聖無虐, are unclear: ?] It is especially nuanced, thorough, and precise, and its loyal devotion overflows beyond the words themselves. To obtain a scholar like this is truly cause to celebrate this examination’s worthy selection.

Comment by Associate Examiner Han, Instructor: This policy essay gives a comprehensive, point-by-point account of the ancients’ methods for averting calamities. Its discussion of the essential need today for those above and below to unite in virtue, cultivate themselves, and examine their conduct is particularly perceptive. Could anyone without substantial talent and profound learning achieve this?

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-Waiting: The imperial ancestor’s two records, Preserving the Mind (Cunxin) and Examining Oneself (Shenggong), are truly mirrors for rulers and ministers for all ages. Few candidates in the examination hall can discuss them; exceedingly few investigate their origins, ramifications, and crucial points as this essay does. At the end, it again proposes preserving the preceding two matters [?] as an aid to calling forth harmony today. Its intent is especially earnest. Should this man one day hold office at court, he will surely draw upon this to offer loyal counsel in service to His Majesty.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: This policy essay discerns the sacred ancestor’s intention in leaving written instruction [?; 筆酥 is unclear], expressing it in words of loyal devotion. Its treatment is nuanced, earnest, and thorough, with meaning that is not exhausted by its written traces [?; 有有跡 is unclear]. How worthy of respect!

A ruler has a Way of serving Heaven; a minister has a Way of serving his ruler. The Way of serving Heaven lies in reverence; the Way of serving the ruler lies in loyalty. If a ruler does not devote effort to his person and mind, he has no means of fully realizing his reverence; if a minister does not devote…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
力於身心則無以盡其忠如是而欲望夫
弭災致祥以回天意亦何可得哉此我
太祖高皇帝存心省躬二錄所以不容於不作
而萬世
聖子神孫與夫佐理承化者皆所當深念而不
可忽焉者也仰惟
聖祖在御之時嘗
命儒臣編葺存心錄一書凡歷代帝王祭祀
而有感於災祥者皆載焉既而又
===
命儒臣編葺省躬錄一書凡漢唐宋以來災
祥之應於臣下者皆載焉二書雖皆主於
祀事而作然究其宏綱大義凡指授出於
聖心者則拳拳乎天人之理懇懇乎災祥之應
無非欲天下後世之為人君者知天心之
仁愛也一遇夫日月之薄蝕星辰之凌犯
山崩川竭水湧地震與夫恒雨而恒暘恒
燠而恒寒凡人事乖於下而天變應於上
則必專精礪志察事求端思所以改感之

===
命儒臣編葺省躬錄一書凡漢唐宋以來災

仁愛也一遇夫日月之薄蝕星辰之變犯
山崩川竭水湧地震與夫恒雨恒暘恒
燠而恒寒凡人事乖於下而天變應於上
則必專精礪志察事求端思所以敬感之
punctuated:
力於身心，則無以盡其忠。如是而欲望夫弭災致祥，以回天意，亦何可得哉？此我太祖高皇帝《存心》《省躬》二錄所以不容於不作，而萬世聖子神孫與夫佐理承化者，皆所當深念而不可忽焉者也。
仰惟聖祖在御之時，嘗命儒臣編葺《存心錄》一書，凡歷代帝王祭祀而有感於災祥者，皆載焉。既而又命儒臣編葺《省躬錄》一書，凡漢唐宋以來災祥之應於臣下者，皆載焉。二書雖皆主於祀事而作，然究其宏綱大義，凡指授出於聖心者，則拳拳乎天人之理，懇懇乎災祥之應，無非欲天下後世之為人君者知天心之仁愛也。一遇夫日月之薄蝕、星辰之凌犯、山崩川竭、水湧地震，與夫恒雨而恒暘、恒燠而恒寒，凡人事乖於下而天變應於上，則必專精礪志，察事求端，思所以改感之
translation_en:
…apply himself to cultivating his person and mind, he has no means of fully realizing his loyalty. In such circumstances, how could one hope to avert calamities and bring auspicious signs, thereby turning Heaven’s intentions? This is why our Emperor Taizu Gao could not refrain from having the two records, Preserving the Mind and Examining Oneself, compiled. His sagely and divine descendants through all generations, together with those who assist in government and carry forward his transforming influence, must ponder these deeply and never neglect them.
We reverently recall that, during the reign of the Sagely Ancestor, he once commanded his Confucian officials to compile the Record of Preserving the Mind (Cunxin lu). It recorded all instances in which emperors of successive dynasties, in offering sacrifices, elicited responses in the form of calamities or auspicious signs. Subsequently, he again commanded his Confucian officials to compile the Record of Examining Oneself (Xinggong lu). It recorded all instances, from the Han, Tang, and Song onward, in which calamities or auspicious signs manifested themselves in response to the conduct of officials. Although both books were composed chiefly concerning sacrificial affairs, when we examine their overarching principles and essential meaning, all the instructions issuing from his sagely mind show earnest concern for the principles governing Heaven and humanity and deep solicitude over the responses manifested in calamities and auspicious signs. Their sole purpose was to ensure that rulers throughout the realm in later generations understood the benevolence of Heaven’s mind. Whenever they encountered eclipses of the sun or moon, encroachments among the stars, collapsing mountains and drying rivers, surging waters and earthquakes, or prolonged rain or sunshine, prolonged warmth or cold—in every case where human affairs went awry below and celestial anomalies responded above—they must concentrate their minds and discipline their resolve, examine events and seek their causes, and consider how to amend their conduct and thereby move…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
則身在其中矣於警乎臣者則以省身言
非略乎心也身者心之用言身則心在其
中矣
聖祖之微意豈非又欲使後之君臣思而得之
以交致其力哉三代而上固無容議若漢
之光武因謫見日月而恐懼避殿矣尤詔
百官封事皆無所諱焉蓋其時上言災異
者不獨輔弼之臣為然也唐之太宗以彗
見五車減膳停樂矣而尤詔内外無間極
===
言得失焉蓋其時得言災異者又不獨在
廷之臣為然也此其所以皆能弭災而致
祥也雖其身心存省之功有不可知而上
下之間恊德求治亦自有不可誣者
國家
列聖相承同一警畏至我
皇上尤隆繼述頃因災異之警特勑
播告之脩蠲逋負賑饑饉寬獄囚理冤抑蓋
無所不至矣兹乃欲思所以益舒

===
國家
列聖相承同一警畏至我
皇上尤隆繼述頃因災異之警持勤
播告之脩譴遠負賑饑鍾寬獄曰理冤抑蓋
無所不至矣茲乃欲思所以盡紓
punctuated:
則身在其中矣。於警乎臣者，則以省身言，非略乎心也。身者，心之用；言身，則心在其中矣。聖祖之微意，豈非又欲使後之君臣思而得之，以交致其力哉？三代而上，固無容議。若漢之光武，因謫見日月而恐懼避殿矣，尤詔百官封事，皆無所諱焉。蓋其時上言災異者，不獨輔弼之臣為然也。唐之太宗，以彗見五車，減膳停樂矣，而尤詔内外無間，極言得失焉。蓋其時得言災異者，又不獨在廷之臣為然也。此其所以皆能弭災而致祥也。雖其身心存省之功有不可知，而上下之間恊德求治，亦自有不可誣者。
國家列聖相承，同一警畏。至我皇上，尤隆繼述。頃因災異之警，特勑播告之脩，蠲逋負，賑饑饉，寬獄囚，理冤抑，蓋無所不至矣。兹乃欲思所以益舒
translation_en:
…then the person is encompassed within it. In admonishing ministers, however, he speaks of examining oneself; this does not mean that he neglects the mind. The person is the mind in operation: to speak of the person is therefore to encompass the mind. Was not the subtle intention of the Sagely Progenitor also to have rulers and ministers of later ages reflect upon and grasp this, so that both would exert themselves together? As for the Three Dynasties and earlier ages, there is surely no room for debate. Emperor Guangwu of the Han, alarmed by baleful signs appearing in the sun and moon [?], withdrew from the main hall. Moreover, he commanded all officials to submit sealed memorials, withholding nothing. Thus, those who reported on calamities and anomalies at that time were not confined to the ministers who assisted him in governing. Emperor Taizong of the Tang reduced his meals and suspended music because a comet appeared in the Five Chariots constellation. Thus, those permitted to discuss calamities and anomalies at that time were likewise not confined to ministers at court. title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
則親之誠則輔之雖有可畏之實未嘗無
可親之理焉畏威易役民若無可畏矣然
順之則服逆之則去非但有可畏之理固
自有可畏之勢焉天之可畏人孰不知之
而民之可畏則溺於世主崇高富貴之情
而知之者鮮矣此我
聖祖所以闡其微旨而懇懇於可愛非君可畏

聖祖所謂畏民者豈徒以干戈甫定之際謂民
有可畏之勢哉蓋民心之向背係天命之
去留謂為可畏者實以其理之可畏也然
今日之當畏者亦豈特以安養既久之難调

…then Heaven draws close to him; if he is sincere, Heaven assists him. Although Heaven truly warrants fear, there is also a principle by which it may be approached with affection. The people fear authority and are easily put to service, so they might seem to present nothing to fear. Yet if one accords with them, they submit; if one goes against them, they withdraw. There is not merely a principle that makes them fearsome: their power in itself warrants fear. Who does not know that Heaven is to be feared? Yet rulers become so absorbed in their exalted station, wealth, and honor that few recognize that the people are to be feared. This is why our Sagely Founder elucidated this subtle meaning and so earnestly voiced the admonition: “Is it not the ruler who is to be loved? Is it not the people who are to be feared?” How great these imperial words are! How could their import differ from what Shun imparted to Yu?
Now that peace has long prevailed, all the people under Heaven are steeped in profound benevolence and abundant favor, rejoicing in them. Compared with the beginning of the dynasty, when warfare had only just been quelled, it might seem that there is nothing to fear. Yet the people at the dynasty’s beginning had these same hearts, and the people today have them too. Could the people of former days have been fearsome, while those of today alone are not? When the Sagely Founder spoke of fearing the people, was it merely because, with warfare only just quelled, he considered their power fearsome? Whether the people’s hearts turn toward or away from the ruler determines whether Heaven’s Mandate remains or departs. To call them fearsome is truly to recognize the awesomeness of this principle. Yet ought we to fear them today solely because, after so long being nurtured in peace, they are difficult to govern…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
民將有可畏之機哉盖防微杜漸之念實
致治保邦之要所以畏之者非過慮也亦
以其理有可畏焉耳此我
皇上所以仰繩
祖武而夙夜惓惓不遑寧處誠有在乎是也故
一聞四方寇盜之警輒下所司俾圖其弭
盜之方其畏民可謂勤矣然在楚蜀之間
民之淪於盜賊者尚未聞其有還定閭里
之期是盖非有他故也良由下無畏民之
===

之誠則可化刀劔為犁鋤矣豈不足以紓

所司俾議其攘災之策其畏民可謂切矣
然而蘇松之境民之傷於水潦者尚未聞

…that the people might come to pose a danger? The resolve to guard against the slightest beginnings of trouble and check its gradual growth is essential to achieving good government and preserving the state. To fear the people is no excessive anxiety: the underlying principle itself gives grounds for fear. This is truly why our Emperor follows in his ancestor’s footsteps, remaining earnestly attentive day and night, with no leisure to rest at ease.

Thus, whenever he hears an alarm of banditry anywhere in the realm, he issues instructions to the responsible authorities, directing them to devise means of suppressing it. His diligence in fearing the people may indeed be commended. Yet among the people of Chu and Shu who have fallen into banditry, we have yet to hear of any prospect of their returning to settle peacefully in their villages. There is surely no other reason for this than the absence, at the lower levels, of officials who fear the people. Famines strike repeatedly, yet they remain complacent and pay no heed. Their granaries contain not a single grain in reserve, yet they inflate the figures for grain collected and disbursed. Clerks and runners use inspections as a pretext for schemes of predatory exaction. How can the people avoid falling into banditry?

The best course now is to seek suitable men: men like Gong Sui in Bohai, who governed leniently, as one untangles knotted cords; or Zhang Gang in Guangling, who won submission through the sincerity he showed by going among the rebels in a lone carriage. Then swords could be turned into plows and hoes. Would this not suffice to relieve the Emperor’s anxiety over banditry?

Whenever he hears of a threat of flood or drought anywhere in the realm, he issues instructions to the responsible authorities, directing them to discuss measures for averting disaster. His concern in fearing the people may indeed be called deeply felt. Yet concerning the people harmed by flooding in the territories of Suzhou and Songjiang, we have yet to hear…

之令行矣不視之為虛文蠲代貸之
詔頒矣不應之以故事實心必存於中實政
必達於外如此則即古所謂養民如子蓋
之如天容之如地而民之愛戴亦將如赤
子之於慈母戀戀然而不忍去惟見其可
愛不見其可畏矣雖時有盜賊水旱之警
亦奚足為吾慮哉謹對
punctuated:
其無凍餒，田野亡憂。是亦非有他故也，良由下無畏民之吏，變異屢見，漫不知省；禱神祈請，應行故事，而初無感格之誠；徵科輸發，仍行督責，而初無矜恤之意。民安得不傷於水潦乎？為今之計，莫若求其人，如富弼之在京東，勸民出粟以活飢民；洪皓之在秀州，鎖截綱運以濟流冗。則可變災沴為豐穰矣，豈不足以紓皇上憂水旱之念哉？
雖然，此非其本也。若論其本，則又在於君民一體，上下交孚，澤必下究，情必上通。寬恤之令行矣，不視之為虛文；蠲貸之詔頒矣，不應之以故事。實心必存於中，實政必達於外。如此，則即古所謂養民如子，蓋之如天，容之如地，而民之愛戴，亦將如赤子之於慈母，戀戀然而不忍去，惟見其可愛，不見其可畏矣。雖時有盜賊水旱之警，亦奚足為吾慮哉？謹對。
translation_en:
…that they are free from cold and hunger, and that the countryside is without anxiety. This, too, has no other cause: it is precisely because there are no officials below who hold the people in awe. Anomalies repeatedly appear, yet officials heedlessly fail to examine themselves. In praying and making supplications to the spirits, they follow established formalities, without any sincerity capable of moving the spirits. In levying taxes and requisitions and exacting deliveries and dispatches, they continue their demands and enforcement, without any intention of showing compassion or granting relief. How could the people escape suffering from floods? The best course now is to seek suitable men: men like Fu Bi in Jingdong, who encouraged people to contribute grain to keep the hungry alive, or Hong Hao in Xiuzhou, who detained and intercepted grain convoys to relieve displaced and destitute people. Then calamity could be transformed into abundance. Would this not suffice to ease Your Majesty’s concern over floods and droughts?
Yet this is not the foundation. If we discuss the foundation, it lies in ruler and people forming one body, with mutual trust between those above and below: benevolence must reach all the way down, and the people’s circumstances and sentiments must be communicated upward. When orders for leniency and relief are put into effect, they must not be treated as empty words; when edicts granting remissions and relief loans are promulgated, they must not be answered with mere routine formalities. Sincere intentions must reside within, and substantive measures must take effect without. This would fulfill what the ancients called nurturing the people as one’s children, sheltering them as Heaven does, and embracing them as Earth does. The people’s love and allegiance would likewise resemble an infant’s attachment to its loving mother: so deeply attached that they could not bear to leave. One would see only that the people are lovable, not that they are to be feared. Even if alarms over banditry, floods, and droughts occasionally arose, how could they give us cause for anxiety? Respectfully submitted in reply.

translation_en:
Third Question

Chai Tai

Comment by Associate Examiner Tian, Instructor: 〔Drawing on the words of Cheng and Zhu, he distinguishes right from wrong, and strengths from failings, among the various masters. On the two matters concerning what is called “impartial love,” he further brings out implications that earlier Confucian scholars had not articulated. He may indeed be called one who knows how to learn.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: 〔Regarding Wenzhongzi’s imitation of the Classics and Han Yu’s discussion of Confucius and Mozi together, writers all know to criticize their errors. But as for the claims concerning what Confucius and Mozi shared, and the meritorious contribution of clearly distinguishing these matters, this essay alone can cite those statements and refute them. It thereby makes plain why the two differ, so that vermilion and purple—the genuine and the spurious—cannot be confused. Is he perhaps what Mencius called “a follower of the men of antiquity”?〕

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-waiting: 〔Mozi’s Way and that of Confucius admit of no common undertaking. Wenzhongzi, however, admired the sage but erred through presumption. This essay discusses the failings of each, while apportioning praise and blame with due weight throughout. Its author may be said to exercise sound judgment in weighing and assessing them.〕

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-waiting: 〔On Confucius and Mozi, he censures Han Yu; his exposition is comprehensive, and his judgments on the arguments are manifest [?]. The composition is rigorous and well ordered, commanding respect as one reads it. How could anyone without broad learning and lofty discernment accomplish this?〕

Those who rely on shallow understanding to emulate the learning of the sages are reproached by the gentleman for their presumption; those who indulge in perverse arguments and turn their backs on the Way of the sages have their errors corrected by the gentleman. To reproach the former for presumption means that they cannot be compared with the sages and treated as their equals; to correct the latter’s errors means that they cannot be commended and aligned with the sages.

子之僭擬孔子其不知量亦甚矣哉大哉
孔子之聖開闢以來所未有也夷尹不敢
比其德堯舜不能擬其功而况於他人乎
夫何隋之王通講學河汾偃然有自擬之
意一時學者翕然以聖人歸之故其自言
曰紹宣尼之事業吾不得讓而董常之尊

This is why Mozi’s unrestrained pronouncements offended against the moral teaching founded on proper social relationships; as for Wenzhongzi’s presumptuous imitation of Confucius, how extreme was his failure to know his own limits! Great indeed was the sageliness of Confucius! Since the beginning of heaven and earth, there had been nothing like it. Boyi and Yi Yin dared not compare their virtue with his; Yao and Shun could not match his accomplishments. How much less could anyone else? Why, then, did Wang Tong of the Sui dynasty, teaching in the region of the Yellow and Fen rivers, complacently entertain the intention of likening himself to Confucius, while the scholars of his time unanimously acclaimed him as a sage? Thus he himself said, “In carrying forward the undertaking of Xuanni [Confucius], I cannot yield to another.” And Dong Chang, in exalting his teacher, said, “Zhongni [Confucius] has died, but his cultural legacy is here.” The presumption and delusion shared by this teacher and his disciples had reached an extreme!

Alas! Tong’s learning was not without merit. Yet, concerning the Way of the sage, he recognized only its application and had never deeply investigated its foundation. Viewed from the school of Confucius, he was probably someone who had not even ascended its hall. How could he dare compare himself to Confucius? Seeing that the Master had transmitted the Six Classics, he thought, “Who but me should provide the Six Classics for later ages?” Accordingly, he continued the Documents to preserve the historical realities of the Han and Jin; continued the Odes to distinguish the customs of the Six Dynasties; compiled the Classic of the Primal (Yuan jing) to resolve disputed judgments concerning the Northern and Southern dynasties; elucidated the Changes of Zhou to expound the purport of the former teacher; and rectified rites and music to expose the failings of later rulers. All this was simply intended to emulate the works and institutions of Confucius.

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
詩之政猶列國之有風則其自比於夫子
之刪詩明矣又曰春秋作而典誥絶元經
興而帝制亡則其自比於夫子之春秋而
書亦在其中矣然高文武宣之制豈有精
一執中之傳書何為而續也曹劉沈謝之
詩豈有物則秉彞之訓詩何為而續也其
所贊之易於先天後天體用之妙何在其
所述之禮樂視伯夷后夔周公之懿何如
至於宋魏而下南北並峙校功度德未有
===
以相君臣也則其天命人心之向背統緒
繼承之偏正亦何足論而必欲奪彼予此
以自列於孔子之春秋哉此通之僭妄所
以見闢於朱子而直謂其不足以供兒童
之一戲則其斥之也深矣若夫孟子之於
墨翟一則責其無父二則惡其賊道距之
何嚴也而昌黎韓子乃有孔墨相用之說
謂孔子畏大人不非其邦之大夫春秋譏
