…the governance expressed in its poetry resembles the Airs of the various states. Thus it is clear that he likens himself to the Master in editing the Book of Odes. He also says: “When the Spring and Autumn Annals was composed, the Canons and Counsels ceased; when the Classic of Origins arose, imperial institutions perished.” Thus he likens his work to the Master’s Spring and Autumn Annals, with the Book of Documents also included in the comparison. Yet did the institutions of Emperors Gao, Wen, Wu, and Xuan contain the transmitted teaching of refinement, singleness of purpose, and holding fast to the Mean? Why, then, continue the Book of Documents? Did the poems of Cao, Liu, Shen, and Xie contain the teaching that things have their proper principles and that people hold fast to their constant moral nature? Why, then, continue the Book of Odes? In his elucidation of the Book of Changes, where are the subtleties of the Prior-to-Heaven and Later-than-Heaven arrangements, of substance and function? How do the rites and music he set forth compare with the excellence of Bo Yi, Hou Kui, and the Duke of Zhou? From the Song and Wei onward, the northern and southern regimes stood alongside one another. Judging their achievements and measuring their virtue, there was no basis for making either the sovereign and the other its subject. What, then, was worth debating about which received or lost Heaven’s mandate and the people’s allegiance, or which line of succession was partial or legitimate? Why insist on denying legitimacy to one and granting it to the other, in order to rank his own work alongside Confucius’s Spring and Autumn Annals? It was for this presumptuousness and recklessness that Wang Tong was repudiated by Master Zhu, who went so far as to say that his work was not enough to provide children with even a moment’s amusement. Profound indeed was his condemnation!
As for Mengzi’s treatment of Mo Di, he first reproached him for denying the claims of fathers, and second abhorred him for injuring the Way. How sternly he opposed him! Yet Master Han of Changli advanced the argument that Confucius and Mo Di drew upon one another. He said that Confucius’s reverence for great men, his refusal to disparage the great officers of his own state, and the Spring and Autumn Annals’ criticism of ministers who monopolized power resembled Mo Di’s doctrine of conformity with superiors; that loving all broadly and drawing close to the humane, and taking the broad bestowal of benefits and aid to the multitude as…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
為聖猶墨之兼愛以四科進褒弟子疾沒
世而名不稱猶墨之尚賢有祭如在之誠
有祭則受福之語猶墨之明鬼韓子之所
以推墨而附於孔子者其說如此然謂墨
之尚賢明鬼有合於孔子者猶之可也謂
孔子尚同兼愛與墨子同則謬甚矣自今
觀之孔子之畏大人不非其邦之大夫乃
用下敬上之義而其所以譏專臣者則至
公之道存焉夫豈同乎流俗者哉孔子之
===

仁者則親疎之别在焉夫豈愛無差等者
哉盖聖人之道匪立異也而不主於苟同
聖人之愛無不周也而不容以混施乃槩
以尚同兼愛目之不亦謬乎程子謂退之
斯言有樂取人善之心而失之持教不嚴
誠哉是言也使韓子之說行得無立異端
之赤幟乎夫孔墨之殊固不待辨而言出
於退之則有可疑者退之嘗作原道以抑

哉蓋聖人之道匪立異也而不主於苟同
聖人之愛無不周也而不容以混施乃槩
以尚同兼愛目之不亦謬乎程子謂退之
斯言有樂取人善之心而失之持敎不嚴
誠哉是言也使韓子之說行得無立異端
之赤幟乎夫孔墨之殊固不待辯而言也
於退之則有可疑者退之嘗作原道以抑
punctuated: 為聖，猶墨之兼愛；以四科進褒弟子，疾沒世而名不稱，猶墨之尚賢；有祭如在之誠，有祭則受福之語，猶墨之明鬼。韓子之所以推墨而附於孔子者，其說如此。然謂墨之尚賢、明鬼有合於孔子者，猶之可也；謂孔子尚同、兼愛與墨子同，則謬甚矣。自今觀之，孔子之畏大人、不非其邦之大夫，乃用下敬上之義，而其所以譏專臣者，則至公之道存焉，夫豈同乎流俗者哉？孔子之汎愛博濟，乃一視同仁之心，而其所謂親仁者，則親疎之别在焉，夫豈愛無差等者哉？盖聖人之道匪立異也，而不主於苟同；聖人之愛無不周也，而不容以混施。乃槩以尚同、兼愛目之，不亦謬乎？程子謂退之斯言有樂取人善之心，而失之持教不嚴。誠哉，是言也！使韓子之說行，得無立異端之赤幟乎？夫孔墨之殊，固不待辨，而言出於退之，則有可疑者。退之嘗作《原道》，以抑

…as constituting sagehood, resembles Mozi’s “impartial care”; his advancing and commending disciples according to four categories, and his distress at reaching the end of life without his name being acknowledged, resemble Mozi’s “exalting the worthy”; his sincerity in sacrificing as though the spirits were present, and his statement that sacrifice brings blessings, resemble Mozi’s “elucidating ghosts.” Such were Master Han’s arguments for commending Mozi and aligning him with Confucius. To say that Mozi’s exalting the worthy and elucidating ghosts have points of agreement with Confucius is still permissible. But to say that Confucius exalted conformity and practiced impartial care in the same way as Mozi is profoundly mistaken.

Viewed from our present standpoint, Confucius’s standing in awe of great men and not censuring the grandees of his own state enact the principle that those below should respect those above. Yet his criticism of ministers who monopolized power embodied the Way of perfect impartiality. How could this be conformity with vulgar custom? Confucius’s universal love and extensive aid expressed a heart that regarded all with equal benevolence. Yet what he called drawing close to the benevolent preserved distinctions between the close and the distant. How could this be love without degrees? The sage’s Way does not seek to establish differences, yet neither does it make indiscriminate agreement its guiding principle. The sage’s love extends everywhere, yet cannot be bestowed without distinctions. Is it not mistaken to characterize all this indiscriminately as exalting conformity and impartial care?

The differences between Confucius and Mozi certainly require no argument; yet because these words came from Tuizhi, they give rise to perplexity. title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
邪崇正為已任又嘗推尊孟氏闢楊墨之
功以為不在禹下矣今乃儕墨於孔子何
其言之自相牴牾若是邪蓋由其因文以
見道而無身體力行之學故其論道也或
明於此而不明於彼其語聖也或知其一
而不知其二無惑乎其言之失也意者讀
墨之篇乃其少作而原道之著尊孟之言
則其晚年所自得乎不然何一人之身而
向背之頓殊也今夫學不可不慎也墨子
===
蓋學為仁者而毫釐之差其流遂至於無
父不有孟子起而攻之則世之踵其術者
將接迹於後矣若文中子則庶乎知道者
也程子固嘗稱其極有格言矣採其言之
善者而用之則亦豈不足為身心之助顧
不可安於小成而以之自處耳管見如斯
未知是否惟與其進也而教之幸甚
第四問
王遵

未知是否惟與其進也而教之幸甚

punctuated:
邪崇正為已任，又嘗推尊孟氏闢楊墨之功，以為不在禹下矣。今乃儕墨於孔子，何其言之自相牴牾若是邪？蓋由其因文以見道，而無身體力行之學，故其論道也，或明於此而不明於彼；其語聖也，或知其一而不知其二。無惑乎其言之失也。意者《讀墨》之篇乃其少作，而《原道》之著、尊孟之言，則其晚年所自得乎？不然，何一人之身而向背之頓殊也？今夫學不可不慎也。墨子蓋學為仁者，而毫釐之差，其流遂至於無父。不有孟子起而攻之，則世之踵其術者將接迹於後矣。若文中子，則庶乎知道者也。程子固嘗稱其極有格言矣。採其言之善者而用之，則亦豈不足為身心之助？顧不可安於小成而以之自處耳。管見如斯，未知是否，惟與其進也而教之，幸甚。

第四問
王遵
translation_en:
…to refute heterodoxy and uphold orthodoxy as his own responsibility. He also exalted Mengzi’s achievement in repudiating Yang Zhu and Mozi, judging it no less than Yu’s. Yet now he places Mozi on a level with Confucius. How can his statements contradict one another so markedly? This is because he sought to apprehend the Way through literary composition, without the learning that comes from personal embodiment and earnest practice. Thus, when discussing the Way, he sometimes understood one aspect but not another; when speaking of the sages, he sometimes knew one thing but not a second. It is no wonder that his words went astray. Perhaps his essay Reading Mozi (Du Mo) was a youthful work, whereas his Inquiry into the Way (Yuan Dao) and his statements honoring Mengzi expressed insights he attained in his later years? Otherwise, how could the positions embraced and rejected by a single person differ so sharply?

Now, one must exercise care in learning. Mozi presumably sought to learn benevolence, yet a hair’s-breadth deviation ultimately led his teaching to the denial of fathers. Had Mengzi not arisen to attack it, those in the world who followed Mozi’s methods would have continued one after another. As for Wenzhongzi, he came close to understanding the Way. Master Cheng indeed once praised him for having some excellent maxims. If one selects what is good in his words and puts it into practice, how could this fail to aid the cultivation of body and mind? One must simply avoid resting content with a small achievement and settling at that level. Such is my limited view; I do not know whether it is correct. I would be most grateful if you would encourage my progress and instruct me.

Fourth Question
Wang Zun

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導陸批治道一策能本東萊之
說以評隲漢宋諸君反覆辨論意尤懇至其識蓋加於
人一等矣
同考試官教諭耿批此策於民財民力民情
盡不盡處敷演詳悉斷制明白蓋士之積學而有識者
考試官侍讀朱批策有考述有斟酌有議論非識
學兼備者不能及此
考試官侍讀學士蔣批東萊所以論漢事者具有成說
此策能悉之且又能推論宋事尤得東萊不盡之意其
殆善於讀書而能推類者乎
===
有天下者欲建萬世不拔之業必為萬世
可繼之政使行之於我而不可以繼之於
人行之於今而不可以繼之於後則雖足
以取快於目前而終不免貽患於身後治
天下者能不去彼取此而顧以一時之快
貽無窮之患哉是故不能不用民之財也
使經費不虧足矣不敢盡其財也不能不
役民之力也使工役不乏足矣不敢盡其

One who possesses all under Heaven, wishing to establish a foundation that cannot be uprooted for ten thousand generations, must institute government that can be continued for ten thousand generations. title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
力也不能不求民之情也使奸慝不滋足
矣不敢盡其情也是三者非不可盡也可
盡也而不可繼故不忍於盡也使可盡也
而又可繼焉則盡之可也然既盡矣必不
可以繼可一而不可再也是狥目前者之
計也非長顧却慮以為其子孫之計也彼
治天下者豈苟為目前之計而已哉固將
為子孫千萬世之計也欲為子孫千萬世
之計而於財於力於情皆使之不可繼焉
曷若以其所餘者留之於民俾其源源相
繼以供吾子孫無窮之用乎此東萊呂氏
所以有慨於宋之神宗而因追慕乎仁宗
故因論漢之文帝而深致憾於武帝豈不
以文帝仁宗之所為為有合於此乎觀夫
露臺惜百金之費後宮無曳地之衣固可
謂不敢輕用天下之財矣若夫帷幙衾裯
多用繒施不索燒羊慮戕物命未嘗不愓
然恐民財之或匱也匈奴三入而三拒之

translation_en:
…their strength. Nor can one avoid investigating the people’s circumstances; it is enough to prevent wickedness from proliferating, without daring to probe their circumstances to the utmost. These three things cannot be exhausted—not because it is impossible to exhaust them, but because, once exhausted, they cannot be sustained. Thus one cannot bear to exhaust them. If they could be exhausted and yet sustained, then exhausting them would be permissible. Yet once exhausted, they assuredly cannot be sustained: it can be done once, but never again. This is the calculation of someone who caters to the immediate moment, not someone who looks far ahead and deliberates deeply to plan for his descendants. Can those who govern the realm merely plan for the present? Surely they intend to plan for their descendants through countless generations. If, while wishing to plan for their descendants through countless generations, they render the people’s wealth, strength, and circumstances alike impossible to sustain, how could this compare with leaving the surplus among the people, allowing it to flow continuously and supply their descendants’ needs without end?
This is why Master Lü of Donglai lamented the conduct of Emperor Shenzong of the Song and looked back with admiration upon Emperor Renzong; likewise, in discussing Emperor Wendi of the Han, he expressed profound regret over Emperor Wudi. Was this not because he considered the actions of Wendi and Renzong to accord with this principle? Consider Wendi’s reluctance to spend a hundred units of gold on the Dew Terrace, and the absence in his rear palace of robes that trailed upon the ground: he may indeed be said not to have dared spend the realm’s wealth lightly. As for curtains, coverlets, and bedclothes, these were mostly made of silk [?]; he did not demand roast lamb, being concerned about taking living creatures’ lives. He was always anxiously fearful that the people’s wealth might run short. The Xiongnu invaded three times, and three times he repelled them.…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
財於力於情皆無不盡焉者矣以武帝之
雄才使不雜於多慾則亦何至是哉仁宗
再傳而為神宗散青苗錢立手實法而利
路開以王韶經略熈河以章惇經略荆湖
而邊釁啓置大理獄置京城邏卒而法網
密則於財於力於情亦無不盡焉者矣以
神宗之勵精使不誤於安石則亦何至此
哉此文帝仁宗所以為漢宋守成之賢君
而非武帝神宗之所能及也然則後之有
===
天下者可不以文帝仁宗為法而以武帝
神宗為戒乎方今
聖明在上節用愛人省刑薄斂方將法堯舜三
王以為治彼漢宋二君固不足為
今日道然
聖不自聖則在二君者寧能無一二足以上契
聖心者乎有以契之則必思有以行之草茅微
賤之臣又何足以知之哉執事幸恕其狂
瞽而進之

punctuated:
財、於力、於情，皆無不盡焉者矣。以武帝之雄才，使不雜於多慾，則亦何至是哉？仁宗再傳而為神宗，散青苗錢，立手實法，而利路開；以王韶經略熈河，以章惇經略荆湖，而邊釁啓；置大理獄，置京城邏卒，而法網密，則於財、於力、於情，亦無不盡焉者矣。以神宗之勵精，使不誤於安石，則亦何至此哉？此文帝、仁宗所以為漢、宋守成之賢君，而非武帝、神宗之所能及也。然則後之有天下者，可不以文帝、仁宗為法，而以武帝、神宗為戒乎？
方今聖明在上，節用愛人，省刑薄斂，方將法堯、舜、三王以為治。彼漢、宋二君，固不足為今日道。然聖不自聖，則在二君者，寧能無一二足以上契聖心者乎？有以契之，則必思有以行之。草茅微賤之臣，又何足以知之哉？執事幸恕其狂瞽而進之。
translation_en:
…in wealth, in strength, and in feeling, nothing remained unexhausted. With Emperor Wu’s outstanding abilities, had these not been compromised by his many desires, how could matters have come to this? Two successions after Emperor Renzong came Emperor Shenzong. He distributed Green Sprouts loan funds and instituted the system of personal declarations of household assets, opening avenues for profit-seeking. He employed Wang Shao to conduct frontier operations in Xihe and Zhang Dun to conduct them in Jinghu, provoking border conflicts. He established a prison under the Court of Judicial Review and patrol forces in the capital, tightening the net of the law. Thus, in wealth, in strength, and in feeling, nothing remained unexhausted either. Given Emperor Shenzong’s strenuous dedication, had he not been misled by Wang Anshi, how could matters have come to this? This is why Emperor Wen and Emperor Renzong were worthy rulers who preserved the inherited achievements of the Han and Song dynasties, beyond what Emperor Wu and Emperor Shenzong could match. Should not later possessors of All-under-Heaven therefore take Emperor Wen and Emperor Renzong as models, and Emperor Wu and Emperor Shenzong as warnings?
Now our sagacious sovereign reigns above, exercising economy and caring for the people, reducing punishments and lightening taxation. He is about to model his government on Yao, Shun, and the Three Kings. Those two rulers of Han and Song scarcely merit discussion today. Yet the sage does not regard himself as already sage: could there not be one or two things about those two rulers that accord with his sagely mind? If something accords with it, he will surely consider how to put it into practice. How could your lowly servant, a humble man from the countryside, be competent to know such matters? I beg you, honored examiners, to pardon my rashness and blindness and advance this submission.

第五問
孫繼先
同考試官教諭姚批此策正欲觀士子格物
窮理之學是卷條荅不遺而評品是非確有定見且篇
末數語特為三君子詳辨尤見待人之恕與善之公其
亦知言之士乎
考試官侍讀朱批論古昔人物賢否事理得失瞭
然如指諸掌可以見窮理之學矣

===
觀人者不可以一事而盖其平生論事者
不可以平生而略其一事盖君子雖有一
眚不能揜其德然論事者亦不以其人之
賢而文之也小人雖有片善不能救其惡
然論事者亦不以其人之惡而泯之也執
此以論則人之賢否事之是非皆可得而
識矣請因明問所及而條陳之三代而下
所謂忠賢者若張子房之為人程子嘗稱

translation_en:
Fifth Question
Sun Jixian

Comment by Associate Examiner Yao, Education Instructor: This policy question was intended precisely to examine the candidates’ learning in investigating things and fathoming principles. This script answers point by point without omission, and its assessments of right and wrong reveal firm and definite judgments. Moreover, the few remarks at the end offer a detailed defense of the three gentlemen, especially revealing the writer’s forbearance toward others and impartiality in acknowledging goodness. Is he not also a scholar who understands words and their implications?

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Reader-in-Waiting: His discussion of the worthiness or unworthiness of figures of antiquity, and of what was sound or mistaken in their actions and reasoning, is as clear as pointing to something in his palm. Here one can see his learning in fathoming principles.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: His assessments of historical figures are apt in every instance. He is an accomplished writer of policy essays.

Those who assess a person must not let a single deed sum up his entire life; those who discuss deeds must not let a person’s entire life cause them to overlook a single deed. For although a gentleman may have one fault, it cannot obscure his virtue; nevertheless, those who discuss deeds must not gloss over that fault because of his worthiness. Although a petty man may possess some small goodness, it cannot redeem his wickedness; nevertheless, those who discuss deeds must not efface that goodness because of his wickedness. By adhering to this approach in discussion, one can discern both people’s worthiness or unworthiness and the rightness or wrongness of their deeds. Allow me to set out my observations point by point on the matters raised in your illuminating question. Among those called loyal and worthy since the Three Dynasties, consider Zhang Zifang: Master Cheng once praised him for possessing the bearing of a Confucian scholar. Why, then, in his plan to destroy Xiang, did he violate the agreement at Honggou…

title: 正德五年應天府鄉試錄
正德五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
其可觀而克已之功或有未盡故一念之
差或不協於公道一事之誤或不愜乎輿
情固不能以是而累其人也然即其一事
而論之亦安得不謂之過哉所謂小人者
若裴矩以諛佞誤隋煬罪莫大焉及其事
唐也乃能諫贓吏之誅而直以陷人於法
為不可孰謂諛佞如矩而能持此論哉盧
杞以奸邪誤德宗惡莫甚焉然其守虢也
乃能論官豕之害而又以移患同州為不
===
可孰謂奸邪如杞而能建此議哉李義甫
之事太子獻承華之箴而以絕邪佞為言
知養正之義矣然義甫之諂得非所謂邪
佞者與王叔文之事太子因官市之論而
以預外事為戒知為子之道矣然叔文之
譎夫豈真能輔導者與王欽若何如人也
而有蠲負釋囚之請異乎剥民奉上者矣
使其每事皆然亦何訾焉豈謂政府一入
而遂縱其惡哉丁謂何如人也而建罷兵

translation_en:
…their admirable qualities, yet their efforts at self-mastery may not have been complete. Thus a single errant thought may fail to accord with public justice, and a mistake in one undertaking may fail to satisfy public sentiment. Certainly, one cannot let this discredit the person as a whole; nevertheless, judging that particular undertaking, how could one avoid calling it a fault?
As for those called petty men, consider Pei Ju, who misled Emperor Yang of the Sui through flattery: no crime could have been greater. Yet when he served the Tang, he could remonstrate against the execution of a corrupt official, bluntly declaring it unacceptable to entrap someone into breaking the law. Who would have thought that someone as sycophantic as Pei Ju could advance such an argument? Lu Qi misled Emperor Dezong through treachery: no wickedness could have been worse. Yet when he governed Guo, he could speak out about the harm caused by government-owned pigs, and further held that it was unacceptable to shift the trouble to Tongzhou. Who would have thought that someone as treacherous as Lu Qi could make such a proposal?
While serving the heir apparent, Li Yifu presented the Admonition for the Crown Prince (Chenghua), urging the rejection of the wicked and sycophantic: he understood the principle of nurturing rectitude. Yet was Li Yifu’s own flattery not precisely what is meant by wickedness and sycophancy? While serving the heir apparent, Wang Shuwen took a discussion of government purchases as an occasion to warn against involvement in affairs outside the palace: he understood the proper way to act as a son. Yet, deceitful as Wang Shuwen was, could he truly have been capable of providing guidance?
What sort of man was Wang Qinruo? Yet he requested the remission of debts and the release of prisoners, thus distinguishing himself from those who stripped the people of their wealth to supply their superiors. Had he acted this way in every matter, what grounds would there have been for criticism? Who would have thought that, once he entered the chief council, he would give free rein to his wickedness? What sort of man was Ding Wei? Yet he proposed ending military operations…

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Our Emperor Taizu Gao established his capital at Jinling and made the lands north and south of the Yangzi the metropolitan domain. In receiving the influence of his moral teaching, this region preceded all others under Heaven. The work of gradually educating and nurturing scholars born here thus has a long history.

Successive sage emperors continued this legacy down to our present Emperor, whose civilizing influence is shared by all regions. Within the Southern Metropolitan Region, however, where this gradual education and nurturing have continued longest, that influence has penetrated all the more deeply. Hence nowhere is talent more abundant. Now, in the gengwu year of the Zhengde reign [1510], when the time duly came for the Provincial Examination, your servants Mian and Xizhou reverently received…

text:
上命職應天試事竊念臣昔嘗就
試于兹目覩人才之盛若駑
駘之處于冀北之羣未嘗不
自歎也乃今謬膺校選之任
視今之人才則又盛於昔所
見者顧臣之愚何足以甄别
之哉則惟夙夜戰兢竭力從

然後列中式者氏名及其文

translation_en: …the imperial command to take charge of the examination at Yingtian. Your servant humbly reflects that, when I formerly sat the examination here and witnessed the abundance of talented men, I was like an inferior horse among the herds of northern Ji; I could never help lamenting my own inadequacy. Now, undeservedly entrusted with examining and selecting candidates, I find that the talent of today surpasses even what I saw then. Yet how could someone of my limited understanding be equal to distinguishing among them? I could only remain fearful and vigilant day and night and exert myself to the utmost, finding satisfaction only in striving to leave no worthy talent overlooked. Yet there was no end to the talent deserving selection, while we dared not exceed the prescribed quota. Thus the difficulty lay in rejecting candidates rather than accepting them. Whenever there was someone whom we wished to accept but could not, and wished to reject but could not bear to, we would review his work three or four times before setting it aside only because we had no alternative. Once the examination work was complete, we then listed the names of the successful candidates and their compositions…

translation_en: …those of expansive breadth need not fear that their language will lack polish. Those who are shallow, crude, and unable to express themselves must have gained no understanding of principle.
